Nay, answer me. Stand and unfold yourself.
No, you answer me. Stop and show who you are.
You come most carefully upon your hour.
'Tis now struck twelve. Get thee to bed, Francisco.
It has just struck twelve. Go to bed, Francisco.
For this relief much thanks. 'Tis bitter cold, / And I am sick at heart.
Thanks for taking over. It's bitterly cold, and I feel low and uneasy.
Well, good night. / If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus, / The rivals of my watch, bid them make haste.
Well, good night. If you meet Horatio and Marcellus, who are on watch with me, tell them to hurry.
I think I hear them. Stand, ho! Who is there?
I think I can hear them. Stop! Who's there?
And loyal subjects of the Danish king.
O, farewell, honest soldier, who hath reliev'd you?
Oh, goodbye, honest soldier. Who has taken over from you?
Barnardo has my place. Give you good-night.
Barnardo has my place. Good night.
What, has this thing appear'd again tonight?
So, has this thing appeared again tonight?

Horatio says 'tis but our fantasy, / And will not let belief take hold of him / Touching this dreaded sight, twice seen of us. / Therefore I have entreated him along / With us to watch the minutes of this night, / That if again this apparition come / He may approve our eyes and speak to it.

Horatio says it's only our imagination, and he won't let himself believe in this terrible thing we've seen twice. So I've begged him to come and keep watch with us tonight, so that if the ghost comes again he can confirm what we saw and speak to it.
Sit down awhile, / And let us once again assail your ears, / That are so fortified against our story, / What we two nights have seen.
Sit down for a while, and let us attack your ears once more, since they are so well defended against our story, with what we have seen these two nights.
Well, sit we down, / And let us hear Barnardo speak of this.
Well, let's sit down and hear Barnardo tell it.
Last night of all, / When yond same star that's westward from the pole, / Had made his course t'illume that part of heaven / Where now it burns, Marcellus and myself, / The bell then beating one—
Last night, when that star west of the North Star had moved across to light the part of the sky where it is shining now, Marcellus and I, just as the bell was striking one—
Peace, break thee off. Look where it comes again.
Quiet, stop! Look, here it comes again.
In the same figure, like the King that's dead.
In the same shape as the dead King.
Thou art a scholar; speak to it, Horatio.
You're an educated man; speak to it, Horatio.
Looks it not like the King? Mark it, Horatio.
Doesn't it look like the King? Look closely, Horatio.
Most like. It harrows me with fear and wonder.
Very like him. It tears through me with fear and amazement.
It wants someone to speak to it.
What art thou that usurp'st this time of night, / Together with that fair and warlike form / In which the majesty of buried Denmark / Did sometimes march? By heaven I charge thee speak.
What are you, that take over this time of night, and the fine, warlike shape in which the buried King of Denmark used to march? In heaven's name, I order you to speak!
Stay! speak, speak! I charge thee speak!
Stop! Speak, speak! I order you to speak!
It's gone, and it won't answer.
How now, Horatio! You tremble and look pale. / Is not this something more than fantasy? / What think you on't?
What's this, Horatio? You're trembling and pale. Isn't this something more than imagination? What do you think of it?
Before my God, I might not this believe / Without the sensible and true avouch / Of mine own eyes.
I swear to God, I could never have believed this without the clear, true evidence of my own eyes.
Is it not like the King?

As thou art to thyself: / Such was the very armour he had on / When he th'ambitious Norway combated; / So frown'd he once, when in an angry parle / He smote the sledded Polacks on the ice. / 'Tis strange.

As much as you are like yourself. That was the very armour he wore when he fought the ambitious King of Norway. He frowned like that once when, in an angry meeting, he struck the Poles on their sledges on the ice. It's strange.
Thus twice before, and jump at this dead hour, / With martial stalk hath he gone by our watch.
Twice before, at exactly this dead hour, it has marched past our guard post like a soldier.
In what particular thought to work I know not; / But in the gross and scope of my opinion, / This bodes some strange eruption to our state.
I don't know exactly what to think, but my general opinion is that this is a sign of some strange upheaval coming to our country.

Good now, sit down, and tell me, he that knows, / Why this same strict and most observant watch / So nightly toils the subject of the land, / And why such daily cast of brazen cannon / And foreign mart for implements of war; / Why such impress of shipwrights, whose sore task / Does not divide the Sunday from the week. / What might be toward, that this sweaty haste / Doth make the night joint-labourer with the day: / Who is't that can inform me?

Please, sit down, and whoever knows, tell me why this strict, watchful guard is kept every night, wearing out the people of the country, and why bronze cannons are cast every day and weapons bought abroad; why shipbuilders are forced to work so hard that they don't get Sundays off. What is about to happen, that this sweating haste makes night work as hard as day? Who can tell me?

That can I; / At least, the whisper goes so. Our last King, / Whose image even but now appear'd to us, / Was, as you know, by Fortinbras of Norway, / Thereto prick'd on by a most emulate pride, / Dar'd to the combat; in which our valiant Hamlet, / For so this side of our known world esteem'd him, / Did slay this Fortinbras; who by a seal'd compact, / Well ratified by law and heraldry, / Did forfeit, with his life, all those his lands / Which he stood seiz'd of, to the conqueror; / Against the which, a moiety competent / Was gaged by our King; which had return'd / To the inheritance of Fortinbras, / Had he been vanquisher; as by the same cov'nant / And carriage of the article design'd, / His fell to Hamlet. Now, sir, young Fortinbras, / Of unimproved mettle, hot and full, / Hath in the skirts of Norway, here and there, / Shark'd up a list of lawless resolutes, / For food and diet, to some enterprise / That hath a stomach in't; which is no other, / As it doth well appear unto our state, / But to recover of us by strong hand / And terms compulsatory, those foresaid lands / So by his father lost. And this, I take it, / Is the main motive of our preparations, / The source of this our watch, and the chief head / Of this post-haste and rummage in the land.

I can; at least, this is the rumour. Our last King, whose image appeared to us just now, was, as you know, challenged to single combat by Fortinbras of Norway, who was spurred on by jealous pride. In that fight our brave Hamlet, for that's how this half of the known world thought of him, killed this Fortinbras. By a sealed agreement, properly made by law and the rules of chivalry, Fortinbras lost all the lands he owned, along with his life, to the winner. Our King had staked an equal share of land, which would have gone to Fortinbras if he had won; by the same agreement and its terms, Fortinbras's lands went to Hamlet. Now, sir, young Fortinbras, untested, hot-headed and full of spirit, has rounded up a band of lawless desperadoes from the edges of Norway, men who'll fight for their food, for some bold enterprise. As our government sees it, this is nothing other than to take back from us by force the lands his father lost. And this, I think, is the main reason for our preparations, the cause of our guard duty and the chief source of all this rush and bustle in the country.
I think it be no other but e'en so: / Well may it sort that this portentous figure / Comes armed through our watch so like the King / That was and is the question of these wars.
I think that's exactly it. It would fit that this ominous figure comes armed past our guard looking so like the King who was, and still is, the cause of these wars.

A mote it is to trouble the mind's eye. / In the most high and palmy state of Rome, / A little ere the mightiest Julius fell, / The graves stood tenantless and the sheeted dead / Did squeak and gibber in the Roman streets; / As stars with trains of fire and dews of blood, / Disasters in the sun; and the moist star, / Upon whose influence Neptune's empire stands, / Was sick almost to doomsday with eclipse. / And even the like precurse of fierce events, / As harbingers preceding still the fates / And prologue to the omen coming on, / Have heaven and earth together demonstrated / Unto our climatures and countrymen.

It's a speck of dust to trouble the mind's eye. In Rome, at the height of its glory, just before the mighty Julius Caesar fell, the graves were emptied and the dead in their shrouds squeaked and gibbered in the Roman streets. There were comets with tails of fire, dews of blood, bad signs in the sun, and the moon, which controls the tides, was so darkened by eclipse it was almost like the end of the world. And the same kind of warnings of terrible events, like messengers always running ahead of fate and like a prologue to the disaster that is coming, have been shown by heaven and earth together to our country and our people.

But, soft, behold! Lo, where it comes again! / I'll cross it, though it blast me. Stay, illusion! / If thou hast any sound, or use of voice, / Speak to me. / If there be any good thing to be done, / That may to thee do ease, and grace to me, / Speak to me. / If thou art privy to thy country's fate, / Which, happily, foreknowing may avoid, / O speak! / Or if thou hast uphoarded in thy life / Extorted treasure in the womb of earth, / For which, they say, you spirits oft walk in death, / Speak of it. Stay, and speak!

But wait, look! Here it comes again! I'll stand in its way, even if it destroys me. Stop, illusion! If you can make any sound or use a voice, speak to me. If there is any good deed that could be done to give you peace and win me grace, speak to me. If you know some secret about your country's fate, which knowing in advance might help us avoid, oh, speak! Or if in your life you buried stolen treasure in the earth, which they say is why spirits often walk after death, speak of it. Stop, and speak!
Shall I strike at it with my partisan?
Shall I strike at it with my spear?
Do, if it will not stand.
Do it, if it won't stand still.
'Tis gone! / We do it wrong, being so majestical, / To offer it the show of violence, / For it is as the air, invulnerable, / And our vain blows malicious mockery.
It's gone! We do wrong to threaten it with violence when it looks so majestic. It is like the air, it can't be wounded, and our useless blows are just spiteful mockery.
It was about to speak, when the cock crew.
It was about to speak when the cock crowed.

And then it started, like a guilty thing / Upon a fearful summons. I have heard / The cock, that is the trumpet to the morn, / Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding throat / Awake the god of day; and at his warning, / Whether in sea or fire, in earth or air, / Th'extravagant and erring spirit hies / To his confine. And of the truth herein / This present object made probation.

And then it jumped, like a guilty person called to answer for something. I've heard that the cock, the trumpeter of the morning, wakes the god of day with his high, shrill throat, and when he gives his warning, any wandering spirit, whether in sea or fire, earth or air, hurries back to where it is confined. And what we've just seen proves that this is true.

It faded on the crowing of the cock. / Some say that ever 'gainst that season comes / Wherein our Saviour's birth is celebrated, / The bird of dawning singeth all night long; / And then, they say, no spirit dare stir abroad, / The nights are wholesome, then no planets strike, / No fairy takes, nor witch hath power to charm; / So hallow'd and so gracious is the time.

It faded when the cock crowed. Some say that whenever the season comes when we celebrate our Saviour's birth, the bird of dawn sings all night long. And then, they say, no spirit dares to walk abroad. The nights are healthy, no planets bring harm, no fairy casts a spell and no witch has power to charm, the time is so holy and so full of grace.

So have I heard, and do in part believe it. / But look, the morn in russet mantle clad, / Walks o'er the dew of yon high eastward hill. / Break we our watch up, and by my advice, / Let us impart what we have seen tonight / Unto young Hamlet; for upon my life, / This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him. / Do you consent we shall acquaint him with it, / As needful in our loves, fitting our duty?

So I've heard, and I partly believe it. But look, the morning, dressed in a reddish-brown cloak, is walking over the dew on that high hill in the east. Let's end our watch, and I advise that we tell young Hamlet what we've seen tonight. I'd bet my life this spirit, silent to us, will speak to him. Do you agree that we should tell him, as our love for him demands and as our duty requires?
Let's do't, I pray, and I this morning know / Where we shall find him most conveniently.
Let's do it, please. I know where we can find him most easily this morning.

Though yet of Hamlet our dear brother's death / The memory be green, and that it us befitted / To bear our hearts in grief, and our whole kingdom / To be contracted in one brow of woe; / Yet so far hath discretion fought with nature / That we with wisest sorrow think on him, / Together with remembrance of ourselves. / Therefore our sometime sister, now our queen, / Th'imperial jointress to this warlike state, / Have we, as 'twere with a defeated joy, / With one auspicious and one dropping eye, / With mirth in funeral, and with dirge in marriage, / In equal scale weighing delight and dole, / Taken to wife; nor have we herein barr'd / Your better wisdoms, which have freely gone / With this affair along. For all, our thanks. / Now follows, that you know young Fortinbras, / Holding a weak supposal of our worth, / Or thinking by our late dear brother's death / Our state to be disjoint and out of frame, / Colleagued with this dream of his advantage, / He hath not fail'd to pester us with message, / Importing the surrender of those lands / Lost by his father, with all bonds of law, / To our most valiant brother. So much for him. / Now for ourself and for this time of meeting: / Thus much the business is: we have here writ / To Norway, uncle of young Fortinbras, / Who, impotent and bed-rid, scarcely hears / Of this his nephew's purpose, to suppress / His further gait herein; in that the levies, / The lists, and full proportions are all made / Out of his subject: and we here dispatch / You, good Cornelius, and you, Voltemand, / For bearers of this greeting to old Norway, / Giving to you no further personal power / To business with the King, more than the scope / Of these dilated articles allow. / Farewell; and let your haste commend your duty.

Although the death of our dear brother Hamlet is still fresh in our memory, and it was right for us to keep our hearts in mourning and for the whole kingdom to wear one frowning face of grief, good sense has so far fought against natural feeling that we think of him with wise sorrow while also remembering ourselves. So we have married our former sister-in-law, now our queen, who shares the rule of this warlike country. We have done it with a kind of spoiled joy, with one eye hopeful and one eye weeping, with laughter at the funeral and lament at the wedding, weighing happiness and grief equally. And we did not ignore your wise advice, which freely supported this whole matter. Thank you all. Next, as you know, young Fortinbras, who either thinks little of our strength or believes that our dear brother's recent death has thrown our country into disorder, has joined that fantasy of his advantage to constant messages pestering us to hand back the lands his father lost, legally, to our brave brother. So much for him. Now for us and the reason for this meeting. This is the business: we have written to the King of Norway, young Fortinbras's uncle, who is weak and bedridden and has hardly heard of his nephew's plans, asking him to stop him going any further, since the troops, the lists of recruits and all the supplies are drawn from his own subjects. And we are sending you, good Cornelius, and you, Voltemand, to carry this greeting to old Norway. You have no personal power to deal with the King beyond what these detailed terms allow. Goodbye, and show your loyalty by your speed.
In that, and all things, will we show our duty.
In that, and in everything, we will show our loyalty.
We doubt it nothing: heartily farewell.
We don't doubt it at all. A warm farewell.

And now, Laertes, what's the news with you? / You told us of some suit. What is't, Laertes? / You cannot speak of reason to the Dane, / And lose your voice. What wouldst thou beg, Laertes, / That shall not be my offer, not thy asking? / The head is not more native to the heart, / The hand more instrumental to the mouth, / Than is the throne of Denmark to thy father. / What wouldst thou have, Laertes?

And now, Laertes, what's your news? You mentioned a request. What is it, Laertes? You can't make a reasonable request to the King of Denmark and waste your breath. What could you ask for, Laertes, that I wouldn't offer before you asked? The head is not more closely linked to the heart, nor the hand more ready to serve the mouth, than the throne of Denmark is to your father. What do you want, Laertes?

Dread my lord, / Your leave and favour to return to France, / From whence though willingly I came to Denmark / To show my duty in your coronation; / Yet now I must confess, that duty done, / My thoughts and wishes bend again toward France, / And bow them to your gracious leave and pardon.

My respected lord, your permission to go back to France. I came to Denmark willingly to show my loyalty at your coronation, but now I must admit that, with that duty done, my thoughts and wishes are turning back to France, and they bow to ask your gracious permission.
Have you your father's leave? What says Polonius?
Do you have your father's permission? What does Polonius say?
He hath, my lord, wrung from me my slow leave / By laboursome petition; and at last / Upon his will I seal'd my hard consent. / I do beseech you give him leave to go.
He has, my lord, squeezed my reluctant permission out of me by begging hard, and in the end I gave my unwilling consent to what he wanted. I beg you, let him go.
Take thy fair hour, Laertes; time be thine, / And thy best graces spend it at thy will! / But now, my cousin Hamlet, and my son—
Make the most of your youth, Laertes. Your time is your own; spend it as you like, with your best qualities! But now, Hamlet, my nephew and my son—
[Aside] A little more than kin, and less than kind.
[Aside] A bit too closely related now, and not the loving kind.
How is it that the clouds still hang on you?
Why are the clouds still hanging over you?
Not so, my lord, I am too much i' the sun.
Not at all, my lord. I'm getting too much sun, and too much of being called your 'son'.

Good Hamlet, cast thy nighted colour off, / And let thine eye look like a friend on Denmark. / Do not for ever with thy vailed lids / Seek for thy noble father in the dust. / Thou know'st 'tis common, all that lives must die, / Passing through nature to eternity.

Good Hamlet, throw off your dark mood and your black clothes, and look at the King of Denmark like a friend. Don't keep searching for your noble father in the dust with your eyes cast down. You know it's common: everything that lives must die, passing through nature to eternity.
If it be, / Why seems it so particular with thee?
If it is, why does it seem so special in your case?

Seems, madam! Nay, it is; I know not seems. / 'Tis not alone my inky cloak, good mother, / Nor customary suits of solemn black, / Nor windy suspiration of forc'd breath, / No, nor the fruitful river in the eye, / Nor the dejected haviour of the visage, / Together with all forms, moods, shows of grief, / That can denote me truly. These indeed seem, / For they are actions that a man might play; / But I have that within which passeth show; / These but the trappings and the suits of woe.

Seems, madam? No, it is. I don't know about 'seems'. It isn't just my inky black cloak, good mother, or my usual formal black clothes, or heavy sighing, or the flood of tears from my eyes, or the downcast look on my face, together with all the outward forms, moods and signs of grief, that can show what I truly feel. Those things really do seem, because they are actions a man could put on like an actor. But I have something inside me that goes beyond any show; those are just the decorations and costumes of grief.

'Tis sweet and commendable in your nature, Hamlet, / To give these mourning duties to your father; / But you must know, your father lost a father, / That father lost, lost his, and the survivor bound / In filial obligation, for some term / To do obsequious sorrow. But to persevere / In obstinate condolement is a course / Of impious stubbornness. 'Tis unmanly grief, / It shows a will most incorrect to heaven, / A heart unfortified, a mind impatient, / An understanding simple and unschool'd; / For what we know must be, and is as common / As any the most vulgar thing to sense, / Why should we in our peevish opposition / Take it to heart? Fie, 'tis a fault to heaven, / A fault against the dead, a fault to nature, / To reason most absurd, whose common theme / Is death of fathers, and who still hath cried, / From the first corse till he that died today, / 'This must be so.' We pray you throw to earth / This unprevailing woe, and think of us / As of a father; for let the world take note / You are the most immediate to our throne, / And with no less nobility of love / Than that which dearest father bears his son / Do I impart toward you. For your intent / In going back to school in Wittenberg, / It is most retrograde to our desire: / And we beseech you bend you to remain / Here in the cheer and comfort of our eye, / Our chiefest courtier, cousin, and our son.

It is sweet and admirable in your nature, Hamlet, to give your father these duties of mourning. But you must know that your father lost a father; that father lost his; and the son left behind was bound by duty to mourn for a while. But to carry on stubbornly grieving is a course of ungodly obstinacy. It is unmanly grief. It shows a will that rebels against heaven, a weak heart, an undisciplined mind, a simple, untrained understanding. Why should we, in childish resistance, take to heart something we know must happen, something as ordinary as the most common thing we see? Shame! It is an offence against heaven, an offence against the dead, an offence against nature and completely unreasonable, since reason's constant theme is the death of fathers, and it has always cried, from the first corpse to the man who died today, 'This is how it must be.' We beg you, throw away this useless grief, and think of us as a father. For let the world note that you are next in line to our throne, and that I offer you love no less noble than the dearest father feels for his son. As for your plan to go back to university in Wittenberg, it is completely against our wishes. We beg you to agree to stay here, where we can cheer and comfort you, as our leading courtier, our nephew and our son.
Let not thy mother lose her prayers, Hamlet. / I pray thee stay with us; go not to Wittenberg.
Don't let your mother's prayers go unanswered, Hamlet. Please, stay with us. Don't go to Wittenberg.
I shall in all my best obey you, madam.
I'll do my best to obey you, madam.

Why, 'tis a loving and a fair reply. / Be as ourself in Denmark. Madam, come; / This gentle and unforc'd accord of Hamlet / Sits smiling to my heart; in grace whereof, / No jocund health that Denmark drinks today / But the great cannon to the clouds shall tell, / And the King's rouse the heaven shall bruit again, / Re-speaking earthly thunder. Come away.

Why, that's a loving and a proper answer. Be as free as I am in Denmark. Madam, come. Hamlet's gentle, willing agreement makes my heart smile. To celebrate it, every merry toast the King drinks today will be announced to the clouds by the great cannon, and the heavens will echo the King's drinking, repeating the earthly thunder. Come away.

O that this too too solid flesh would melt, / Thaw, and resolve itself into a dew! / Or that the Everlasting had not fix'd / His canon 'gainst self-slaughter. O God! O God! / How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable / Seem to me all the uses of this world! / Fie on't! Oh fie! 'tis an unweeded garden / That grows to seed; things rank and gross in nature / Possess it merely. That it should come to this! / But two months dead—nay, not so much, not two: / So excellent a king; that was to this / Hyperion to a satyr; so loving to my mother, / That he might not beteem the winds of heaven / Visit her face too roughly. Heaven and earth! / Must I remember? Why, she would hang on him / As if increase of appetite had grown / By what it fed on; and yet, within a month— / Let me not think on't—Frailty, thy name is woman! / A little month, or ere those shoes were old / With which she followed my poor father's body / Like Niobe, all tears.—Why she, even she— / O God! A beast that wants discourse of reason / Would have mourn'd longer,—married with mine uncle, / My father's brother; but no more like my father / Than I to Hercules. Within a month, / Ere yet the salt of most unrighteous tears / Had left the flushing in her galled eyes, / She married. O most wicked speed, to post / With such dexterity to incestuous sheets! / It is not, nor it cannot come to good. / But break, my heart, for I must hold my tongue.

Oh, I wish this too, too solid flesh would melt, thaw and dissolve into dew! Or that God had not made his law against suicide! Oh God! God! How weary, stale, flat and pointless all the ways of this world seem to me! Damn it, damn it! It's an unweeded garden that is going to seed; rank and coarse things completely fill it. That it should come to this! Only two months dead, no, not even that, not two. Such an excellent king, compared to this one like the sun god to a goat-man. So loving to my mother that he wouldn't let the winds of heaven blow too roughly on her face. Heaven and earth! Must I remember? Why, she would cling to him as if her hunger grew by feeding on him. And yet, within a month, I won't think about it! Weakness, your name is woman! One little month, before the shoes she wore to follow my poor father's coffin were even old, weeping like Niobe, why she, even she, oh God, an animal with no power to reason would have mourned longer, married my uncle, my father's brother, but no more like my father than I am like Hercules. Within a month, before the salt of her false tears had stopped reddening her sore eyes, she married. Oh, wicked speed, to rush so nimbly into an incestuous bed! It is not good, and it can't come to any good. But break, my heart, because I must keep quiet.
I am glad to see you well: / Horatio, or I do forget myself.
I'm glad to see you well. Horatio, or I've forgotten who I am!
The same, my lord, / And your poor servant ever.
The same, my lord, and always your humble servant.
Sir, my good friend; / I'll change that name with you: / And what make you from Wittenberg, Horatio?— / Marcellus?
Sir, my good friend. I'll swap that name with you; we are friends, not master and servant. And what are you doing away from Wittenberg, Horatio? Marcellus?
I am very glad to see you.—Good even, sir.— / But what, in faith, make you from Wittenberg?
I'm very glad to see you. Good evening, sir. But really, why have you left Wittenberg?
A truant disposition, good my lord.
Because I like skipping school, my good lord.

I would not hear your enemy say so; / Nor shall you do my ear that violence, / To make it truster of your own report / Against yourself. I know you are no truant. / But what is your affair in Elsinore? / We'll teach you to drink deep ere you depart.

I wouldn't let your enemy say that, and you won't hurt my ears by making them believe you when you speak against yourself. I know you're no truant. But what are you doing in Elsinore? We'll teach you to drink heavily before you leave.
My lord, I came to see your father's funeral.
My lord, I came to see your father's funeral.
I prithee do not mock me, fellow-student. / I think it was to see my mother's wedding.
Please don't mock me, fellow student. I think it was to see my mother's wedding.
Indeed, my lord, it follow'd hard upon.
It's true, my lord, it came soon after.

Thrift, thrift, Horatio! The funeral bak'd meats / Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables. / Would I had met my dearest foe in heaven / Or ever I had seen that day, Horatio. / My father,—methinks I see my father.

It saved money, Horatio! The meat pies baked for the funeral were served cold at the wedding feast. I'd rather have met my worst enemy in heaven than have lived to see that day, Horatio. My father, I think I can see my father.
I saw him once; he was a goodly king.
I saw him once. He was a fine king.
He was a man, take him for all in all, / I shall not look upon his like again.
He was a man, take him for all he was. I'll never see anyone like him again.
My lord, I think I saw him yesternight.
My lord, I think I saw him last night.
My lord, the King your father.
My lord, the King your father.
Season your admiration for a while / With an attent ear, till I may deliver / Upon the witness of these gentlemen / This marvel to you.
Control your amazement for a moment and listen carefully, while I tell you this marvel, with these gentlemen as witnesses.
For God's love let me hear.
For God's sake, let me hear it.

Two nights together had these gentlemen, / Marcellus and Barnardo, on their watch / In the dead waste and middle of the night, / Been thus encounter'd. A figure like your father, / Armed at point exactly, cap-à-pie, / Appears before them, and with solemn march / Goes slow and stately by them: thrice he walk'd / By their oppress'd and fear-surprised eyes, / Within his truncheon's length; whilst they, distill'd / Almost to jelly with the act of fear, / Stand dumb, and speak not to him. This to me / In dreadful secrecy impart they did, / And I with them the third night kept the watch, / Where, as they had deliver'd, both in time, / Form of the thing, each word made true and good, / The apparition comes. I knew your father; / These hands are not more like.

For two nights in a row these gentlemen, Marcellus and Barnardo, on guard duty in the dead, empty middle of the night, met this. A figure like your father, armed exactly from head to foot, appears in front of them, and with a solemn march walks slowly and grandly past. Three times he walked past their frightened, astonished eyes, as close as the length of his staff, while they, almost melted to jelly with fear, stand silent and do not speak to him. They told me this in fearful secrecy, and on the third night I kept watch with them. And there, just as they had described it, at the same time and in the same shape, every word proved true, the ghost comes. I knew your father. These two hands are not more alike.
My lord, upon the platform where we watch.
My lord, on the battlements where we keep watch.
Did you not speak to it?

My lord, I did; / But answer made it none: yet once methought / It lifted up it head, and did address / Itself to motion, like as it would speak. / But even then the morning cock crew loud, / And at the sound it shrunk in haste away, / And vanish'd from our sight.

My lord, I did, but it gave no answer. Yet once I thought it lifted its head and began to move as if it wanted to speak. But just then the morning cock crowed loudly, and at the sound it shrank hurriedly away and vanished from our sight.
As I do live, my honour'd lord, 'tis true; / And we did think it writ down in our duty / To let you know of it.
As sure as I'm alive, my honoured lord, it's true, and we thought it was our duty to let you know.
Indeed, indeed, sirs, but this troubles me. / Hold you the watch tonight?
Yes, yes, sirs, but this troubles me. Are you on guard tonight?
My lord, from head to foot.
My lord, from head to foot.
Then saw you not his face?
Then you didn't see his face?
O yes, my lord, he wore his beaver up.
Oh yes, my lord, he had the visor of his helmet raised.
A countenance more in sorrow than in anger.
His face showed more sorrow than anger.
And fix'd his eyes upon you?
I would I had been there.
It would have much amaz'd you.
Very like, very like. Stay'd it long?
Very likely, very likely. Did it stay long?
While one with moderate haste might tell a hundred.
As long as it takes to count to a hundred at a steady pace.
His beard was grey, wasn't it?
It was, as I have seen it in his life, / A sable silver'd.
It was as I saw it when he was alive, black flecked with silver.
I will watch tonight; / Perchance 'twill walk again.
I'll keep watch tonight. Perhaps it will walk again.

If it assume my noble father's person, / I'll speak to it, though hell itself should gape / And bid me hold my peace. I pray you all, / If you have hitherto conceal'd this sight, / Let it be tenable in your silence still; / And whatsoever else shall hap tonight, / Give it an understanding, but no tongue. / I will requite your loves. So, fare ye well. / Upon the platform 'twixt eleven and twelve, / I'll visit you.

If it takes my noble father's shape, I'll speak to it, even if hell itself opens its mouth and tells me to be quiet. I beg you all, if you've kept this sight secret until now, keep holding it in silence. And whatever else happens tonight, understand it but don't talk about it. I will repay your love. So, goodbye. I'll come to you on the battlements between eleven and twelve.
Your loves, as mine to you: farewell.
Your love, as I give mine to you. Goodbye.

My father's spirit in arms! All is not well; / I doubt some foul play: would the night were come! / Till then sit still, my soul: foul deeds will rise, / Though all the earth o'erwhelm them, to men's eyes.

My father's ghost in armour! All is not well. I suspect some foul play. I wish night had come! Until then, be calm, my soul. Foul deeds will come to light, even if the whole earth covers them, for men to see.
My necessaries are embark'd. Farewell. / And, sister, as the winds give benefit / And convoy is assistant, do not sleep, / But let me hear from you.
My luggage is on board. Goodbye. And, sister, whenever the winds are good and a ship is going, don't be lazy; write to me.
Do you doubt that I will?

For Hamlet, and the trifling of his favour, / Hold it a fashion and a toy in blood; / A violet in the youth of primy nature, / Forward, not permanent, sweet, not lasting; / The perfume and suppliance of a minute; / No more.

As for Hamlet and his flirting attentions, think of them as a passing fashion, a whim of hot young blood, a violet in the spring of life: early, not permanent, sweet, not lasting, the scent and pastime of a minute. Nothing more.

Think it no more. / For nature crescent does not grow alone / In thews and bulk; but as this temple waxes, / The inward service of the mind and soul / Grows wide withal. Perhaps he loves you now, / And now no soil nor cautel doth besmirch / The virtue of his will; but you must fear, / His greatness weigh'd, his will is not his own; / For he himself is subject to his birth: / He may not, as unvalu'd persons do, / Carve for himself; for on his choice depends / The sanctity and health of this whole state; / And therefore must his choice be circumscrib'd / Unto the voice and yielding of that body / Whereof he is the head. Then if he says he loves you, / It fits your wisdom so far to believe it / As he in his particular act and place / May give his saying deed; which is no further / Than the main voice of Denmark goes withal. / Then weigh what loss your honour may sustain / If with too credent ear you list his songs, / Or lose your heart, or your chaste treasure open / To his unmaster'd importunity. / Fear it, Ophelia, fear it, my dear sister; / And keep you in the rear of your affection, / Out of the shot and danger of desire. / The chariest maid is prodigal enough / If she unmask her beauty to the moon. / Virtue itself 'scapes not calumnious strokes: / The canker galls the infants of the spring / Too oft before their buttons be disclos'd, / And in the morn and liquid dew of youth / Contagious blastments are most imminent. / Be wary then, best safety lies in fear. / Youth to itself rebels, though none else near.

Think of it as nothing more. When a person grows up, it isn't only muscles and size that grow; as the body, this temple, gets bigger, the mind and soul inside it grow too. Perhaps he loves you now, and no stain or deceit spoils his honest intentions. But you must be careful: considering his rank, his will is not his own, because he is bound by his birth. He can't choose for himself, as unimportant people do, because the safety and health of the whole country depend on his choice. So his choice must be limited by the agreement and approval of the nation he will lead. So if he says he loves you, you would be wise to believe it only as far as a man in his particular position can act on what he says, which is no further than the main body of Denmark agrees. Then think what damage your honour may suffer if you listen too trustingly to his love songs, or lose your heart, or open your chaste treasure to his uncontrolled pleading. Be afraid of it, Ophelia, be afraid of it, my dear sister. Keep back behind your feelings, out of range of the shots and dangers of desire. The most careful girl is reckless enough if she shows her beauty even to the moon. Virtue itself can't escape the blows of slander. The canker worm eats the young flowers of spring too often before their buds have opened, and in the dewy morning of youth, infection is most likely to strike. So be careful. The safest thing is fear. Youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near.

I shall th'effect of this good lesson keep / As watchman to my heart. But good my brother, / Do not as some ungracious pastors do, / Show me the steep and thorny way to heaven; / Whilst like a puff'd and reckless libertine / Himself the primrose path of dalliance treads, / And recks not his own rede.

I'll keep the message of this good lesson as a guard over my heart. But, my good brother, don't be like some bad priests who show me the steep and thorny path to heaven, while they, like proud and reckless pleasure-seekers, walk the easy primrose path of pleasure and ignore their own advice.
O, fear me not. / I stay too long. But here my father comes.
Oh, don't worry about me. I've stayed too long. But here comes my father.
A double blessing is a double grace; / Occasion smiles upon a second leave.
Two blessings mean double grace. Luck has given me a chance to say goodbye twice.
Yet here, Laertes? Aboard, aboard, for shame. / The wind sits in the shoulder of your sail, / And you are stay'd for. There, my blessing with you.
Still here, Laertes? On board, on board, for shame! The wind is filling your sails and they are waiting for you. There, take my blessing with you.

And these few precepts in thy memory / Look thou character. Give thy thoughts no tongue, / Nor any unproportion'd thought his act. / Be thou familiar, but by no means vulgar. / Those friends thou hast, and their adoption tried, / Grapple them unto thy soul with hoops of steel; / But do not dull thy palm with entertainment / Of each new-hatch'd, unfledg'd comrade. Beware / Of entrance to a quarrel; but being in, / Bear't that th'opposed may beware of thee. / Give every man thine ear, but few thy voice: / Take each man's censure, but reserve thy judgement. / Costly thy habit as thy purse can buy, / But not express'd in fancy; rich, not gaudy: / For the apparel oft proclaims the man; / And they in France of the best rank and station / Are of a most select and generous chief in that. / Neither a borrower nor a lender be: / For loan oft loses both itself and friend; / And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry. / This above all: to thine own self be true; / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man. / Farewell: my blessing season this in thee.

And make sure you write these few rules in your memory. Don't say what you are thinking, and don't act on any unwise thought. Be friendly, but not overfamiliar with everyone. Once you have friends and have tested them, hold them to your soul with hoops of steel, but don't wear out your hand shaking hands with every new, untried companion. Be careful not to get into a quarrel, but once you are in one, act so that your opponent learns to beware of you. Listen to everyone, but speak to few. Hear everyone's opinion, but keep your own judgement to yourself. Buy clothes as expensive as you can afford, but not showy; rich, not flashy, because clothes often show what a man is, and the French of the highest rank are especially choosy and refined in this. Don't be a borrower or a lender, because a loan often loses both the money and the friend, and borrowing blunts the habit of thrift. Above all: be true to yourself, and it must follow, as night follows day, that you can't then be false to anyone. Goodbye. May my blessing make this advice grow in you.
Most humbly do I take my leave, my lord.
Most humbly I say goodbye, my lord.
The time invites you; go, your servants tend.
It's time to go. Your servants are waiting.
Farewell, Ophelia, and remember well / What I have said to you.
Goodbye, Ophelia, and remember what I've said to you.
'Tis in my memory lock'd, / And you yourself shall keep the key of it.
It's locked in my memory, and you will keep the key yourself.
What is't, Ophelia, he hath said to you?
What has he been saying to you, Ophelia?
So please you, something touching the Lord Hamlet.
If you must know, something about Lord Hamlet.

Marry, well bethought: / 'Tis told me he hath very oft of late / Given private time to you; and you yourself / Have of your audience been most free and bounteous. / If it be so,—as so 'tis put on me, / And that in way of caution,—I must tell you / You do not understand yourself so clearly / As it behoves my daughter and your honour. / What is between you? Give me up the truth.

Indeed, that's a good thought. I've been told he has very often spent time alone with you lately, and that you have been very free and generous in letting him see you. If that is true, as I've been told by people warning me, I must tell you that you don't understand your position as clearly as my daughter should, for the sake of your honour. What is going on between you? Tell me the truth.
He hath, my lord, of late made many tenders / Of his affection to me.
He has, my lord, recently made many offers of his love to me.
Affection! Pooh! You speak like a green girl, / Unsifted in such perilous circumstance. / Do you believe his tenders, as you call them?
Love! Pah! You talk like an inexperienced girl who knows nothing about such dangerous situations. Do you believe his 'offers', as you call them?
I do not know, my lord, what I should think.
I don't know, my lord, what I should think.

Marry, I'll teach you; think yourself a baby; / That you have ta'en these tenders for true pay, / Which are not sterling. Tender yourself more dearly; / Or,—not to crack the wind of the poor phrase, / Running it thus,—you'll tender me a fool.

Well, I'll teach you. Think of yourself as a baby for taking these offers as real money when they are fake. Offer yourself at a higher price, or, not to run the poor word into the ground, you'll offer me a fool, and make me look like one.
My lord, he hath importun'd me with love / In honourable fashion.
My lord, he has pressed his love on me in an honourable way.
Ay, fashion you may call it; go to, go to.
Yes, 'way' is the word, a passing fashion. Come on, come on.
And hath given countenance to his speech, my lord, / With almost all the holy vows of heaven.
And he has backed up his words, my lord, with almost every holy vow there is.

Ay, springes to catch woodcocks. I do know, / When the blood burns, how prodigal the soul / Lends the tongue vows: these blazes, daughter, / Giving more light than heat, extinct in both, / Even in their promise, as it is a-making, / You must not take for fire. From this time / Be something scanter of your maiden presence; / Set your entreatments at a higher rate / Than a command to parley. For Lord Hamlet, / Believe so much in him that he is young; / And with a larger tether may he walk / Than may be given you. In few, Ophelia, / Do not believe his vows; for they are brokers, / Not of that dye which their investments show, / But mere implorators of unholy suits, / Breathing like sanctified and pious bawds, / The better to beguile. This is for all: / I would not, in plain terms, from this time forth / Have you so slander any moment leisure / As to give words or talk with the Lord Hamlet. / Look to't, I charge you; come your ways.

Yes, traps to catch stupid birds. I know how generously the soul supplies the tongue with vows when passion is burning. These flames, daughter, give more light than heat, and both die out even while the promise is being made. You must not take them for real fire. From now on, be a little more sparing with your company. Don't be so ready to talk just because he asks you to. As for Lord Hamlet, believe this much: he is young, and he can do more of what he likes than you can. In short, Ophelia, don't believe his vows. They are go-betweens, not what they appear to be, just pleaders for sinful requests, speaking like holy, religious pimps to trick you better. This is my final word: plainly, from now on, I don't want you to waste a single spare moment talking to Lord Hamlet. See to it, I order you. Come along.
The air bites shrewdly; it is very cold.
The air bites sharply. It's very cold.
It is a nipping and an eager air.
I think it lacks of twelve.
I think it's not quite twelve.
Indeed? I heard it not. It then draws near the season / Wherein the spirit held his wont to walk.
Really? I didn't hear it. Then it's nearly the time when the ghost usually walks.
What does this mean, my lord?
What does this mean, my lord?

The King doth wake tonight and takes his rouse, / Keeps wassail, and the swaggering upspring reels; / And as he drains his draughts of Rhenish down, / The kettle-drum and trumpet thus bray out / The triumph of his pledge.

The King is staying up late tonight, drinking and partying, dancing wild, staggering dances. And as he drains his cups of German wine, the drums and trumpets blare out like this to celebrate each toast he downs.

Ay marry is't; / And to my mind, though I am native here, / And to the manner born, it is a custom / More honour'd in the breach than the observance. / This heavy-headed revel east and west / Makes us traduc'd and tax'd of other nations: / They clepe us drunkards, and with swinish phrase / Soil our addition; and indeed it takes / From our achievements, though perform'd at height, / The pith and marrow of our attribute. / So oft it chances in particular men / That for some vicious mole of nature in them, / As in their birth, wherein they are not guilty, / Since nature cannot choose his origin, / By their o'ergrowth of some complexion, / Oft breaking down the pales and forts of reason; / Or by some habit, that too much o'erleavens / The form of plausive manners;—that these men, / Carrying, I say, the stamp of one defect, / Being Nature's livery or Fortune's star,— / His virtues else,—be they as pure as grace, / As infinite as man may undergo, / Shall in the general censure take corruption / From that particular fault. The dram of evil / Doth all the noble substance of a doubt / To his own scandal.

Yes, it is. And to my mind, though I was born here and brought up in these ways, it's a custom it would be more honourable to break than to keep. This drunken partying makes us mocked and criticised by other nations, east and west. They call us drunkards and dirty our name by calling us pigs. And it does take away the heart and core of our reputation from our achievements, however great they are. It often happens the same way with individual men. Because of some natural flaw in them, perhaps from their birth, which isn't their fault, since nobody can choose where he comes from; or because one part of their temperament grows too strong and breaks down the fences and forts of reason; or because of some habit that spoils their good manners; these men, I say, who carry the mark of one defect, whether it came from nature or from bad luck, even if their other virtues are as pure as grace and as great as any man can have, will be thought corrupt by everyone because of that one fault. A tiny drop of evil can spoil all the noble substance and bring it into disgrace.

Angels and ministers of grace defend us! / Be thou a spirit of health or goblin damn'd, / Bring with thee airs from heaven or blasts from hell, / Be thy intents wicked or charitable, / Thou com'st in such a questionable shape / That I will speak to thee. I'll call thee Hamlet, / King, father, royal Dane. O, answer me! / Let me not burst in ignorance; but tell / Why thy canoniz'd bones, hearsed in death, / Have burst their cerements; why the sepulchre, / Wherein we saw thee quietly inurn'd, / Hath op'd his ponderous and marble jaws / To cast thee up again! What may this mean, / That thou, dead corse, again in complete steel, / Revisit'st thus the glimpses of the moon, / Making night hideous, and we fools of nature / So horridly to shake our disposition / With thoughts beyond the reaches of our souls? / Say, why is this? Wherefore? What should we do?

Angels and messengers of God, protect us! Whether you are a good spirit or a damned demon, whether you bring heavenly air or blasts from hell, whether your purpose is evil or kind, you come in such a shape that invites questions, so I will speak to you. I'll call you Hamlet, King, father, royal Dane. Oh, answer me! Don't let me burst with not knowing, but tell me why your holy bones, buried with full rites, have broken out of their burial clothes; why the tomb where we saw you quietly laid has opened its heavy marble jaws to throw you up again. What can it mean, that you, a dead body, in full armour again, come back to the moonlit world, making the night hideous, and making us, mere fools of nature, shake so horribly with thoughts beyond what our souls can reach? Say, why is this? Why? What should we do?
It beckons you to go away with it, / As if it some impartment did desire / To you alone.
It's beckoning you to go away with it, as if it wanted to tell something to you alone.
Look with what courteous action / It waves you to a more removed ground. / But do not go with it.
Look how politely it waves you to a more private place. But don't go with it.
It will not speak; then will I follow it.
It won't speak here, so I'll follow it.
Why, what should be the fear? / I do not set my life at a pin's fee; / And for my soul, what can it do to that, / Being a thing immortal as itself? / It waves me forth again. I'll follow it.

Why, what is there to fear? I don't value my life at the price of a pin. And as for my soul, what can it do to that, since it is immortal like the ghost itself? It's waving me on again. I'll follow it.

What if it tempt you toward the flood, my lord, / Or to the dreadful summit of the cliff / That beetles o'er his base into the sea, / And there assume some other horrible form / Which might deprive your sovereignty of reason, / And draw you into madness? Think of it. / The very place puts toys of desperation, / Without more motive, into every brain / That looks so many fathoms to the sea / And hears it roar beneath.

What if it tempts you toward the sea, my lord, or to the terrifying top of the cliff that hangs over its base into the sea, and there takes on some other horrible shape that might rob you of your reason and drive you mad? Think about it. The place itself, without any other reason, puts desperate thoughts into the head of anyone who looks down so far to the sea and hears it roaring below.
It waves me still. / Go on, I'll follow thee.
It's still waving to me. Go on, I'll follow you.
You shall not go, my lord.
Be rul'd; you shall not go.
My fate cries out, / And makes each petty artery in this body / As hardy as the Nemean lion's nerve.
My fate is calling, and it makes every tiny vein in my body as strong as the sinews of the Nemean lion that Hercules fought.
Still am I call'd. Unhand me, gentlemen.
It's still calling me. Let go of me, gentlemen.
By heaven, I'll make a ghost of him that lets me. / I say, away!—Go on, I'll follow thee.
By heaven, I'll make a ghost of anyone who stops me! I said get away! Go on, I'll follow you.
His imagination is making him desperate.
Let's follow; 'tis not fit thus to obey him.
Let's follow. It's not right to obey him in this.
Have after. To what issue will this come?
Let's go after him. How will this end?
Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
Heaven will take care of it.
Whither wilt thou lead me? Speak, I'll go no further.
Where are you taking me? Speak. I won't go any further.
My hour is almost come, / When I to sulph'rous and tormenting flames / Must render up myself.
It is almost time for me to give myself up again to the burning, tormenting flames.
Pity me not, but lend thy serious hearing / To what I shall unfold.
Don't pity me, but listen seriously to what I am going to tell you.
Speak, I am bound to hear.
Speak. I am bound to listen.
So art thou to revenge, when thou shalt hear.
And you will be bound to take revenge when you have heard.

I am thy father's spirit, / Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night, / And for the day confin'd to fast in fires, / Till the foul crimes done in my days of nature / Are burnt and purg'd away. But that I am forbid / To tell the secrets of my prison-house, / I could a tale unfold whose lightest word / Would harrow up thy soul; freeze thy young blood, / Make thy two eyes like stars start from their spheres, / Thy knotted and combined locks to part, / And each particular hair to stand on end / Like quills upon the fretful porpentine. / But this eternal blazon must not be / To ears of flesh and blood. List, list, O, list! / If thou didst ever thy dear father love—

I am your father's spirit, condemned for a fixed time to walk at night, and in the day shut away to starve in fire until the foul sins I committed while I was alive are burnt and cleansed away. If I were not forbidden to tell the secrets of my prison, I could tell a story whose lightest word would tear up your soul, freeze your young blood, make your eyes jump out of their sockets like shooting stars, part your neatly combed hair and make each separate hair stand on end like the quills of an angry porcupine. But this description of eternity must not be told to ears of flesh and blood. Listen, listen, oh, listen! If you ever loved your dear father—
Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.
Avenge his foul and most unnatural murder.
Murder most foul, as in the best it is; / But this most foul, strange, and unnatural.
Murder is always foul, even at best, but this was the foulest, strangest and most unnatural.
Haste me to know't, that I, with wings as swift / As meditation or the thoughts of love / May sweep to my revenge.
Hurry and tell me, so that with wings as quick as thought or the thoughts of love I can sweep to my revenge.

I find thee apt; / And duller shouldst thou be than the fat weed / That rots itself in ease on Lethe wharf, / Wouldst thou not stir in this. Now, Hamlet, hear. / 'Tis given out that, sleeping in my orchard, / A serpent stung me; so the whole ear of Denmark / Is by a forged process of my death / Rankly abus'd; but know, thou noble youth, / The serpent that did sting thy father's life / Now wears his crown.

I see you are ready. You'd be duller than the fat weed that lazily rots on the banks of Lethe, the river of forgetting, if this didn't stir you. Now, Hamlet, listen. It has been announced that a snake stung me while I was sleeping in my orchard, so all of Denmark has been grossly deceived by a false story of my death. But know this, noble young man: the snake that took your father's life now wears his crown.
O my prophetic soul! / Mine uncle!
Oh, my soul guessed it! My uncle!

Ay, that incestuous, that adulterate beast, / With witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts,— / O wicked wit, and gifts, that have the power / So to seduce!—won to his shameful lust / The will of my most seeming-virtuous queen. / O Hamlet, what a falling off was there, / From me, whose love was of that dignity / That it went hand in hand even with the vow / I made to her in marriage; and to decline / Upon a wretch whose natural gifts were poor / To those of mine. But virtue, as it never will be mov'd, / Though lewdness court it in a shape of heaven; / So lust, though to a radiant angel link'd, / Will sate itself in a celestial bed / And prey on garbage. / But soft! methinks I scent the morning air; / Brief let me be. Sleeping within my orchard, / My custom always of the afternoon, / Upon my secure hour thy uncle stole / With juice of cursed hebenon in a vial, / And in the porches of my ears did pour / The leperous distilment, whose effect / Holds such an enmity with blood of man / That swift as quicksilver it courses through / The natural gates and alleys of the body; / And with a sudden vigour it doth posset / And curd, like eager droppings into milk, / The thin and wholesome blood. So did it mine; / And a most instant tetter bark'd about, / Most lazar-like, with vile and loathsome crust / All my smooth body. / Thus was I, sleeping, by a brother's hand, / Of life, of crown, of queen at once dispatch'd: / Cut off even in the blossoms of my sin, / Unhous'led, disappointed, unanel'd; / No reckoning made, but sent to my account / With all my imperfections on my head. / O horrible! O horrible! most horrible! / If thou hast nature in thee, bear it not; / Let not the royal bed of Denmark be / A couch for luxury and damned incest. / But howsoever thou pursu'st this act, / Taint not thy mind, nor let thy soul contrive / Against thy mother aught; leave her to heaven, / And to those thorns that in her bosom lodge, / To prick and sting her. Fare thee well at once! / The glow-worm shows the matin to be near, / And 'gins to pale his uneffectual fire. / Adieu, adieu, adieu. Remember me.

Yes, that incestuous, adulterous beast. With his clever witchcraft and treacherous gifts, oh, wicked cleverness and gifts that have the power to seduce like that, he won over my queen, who seemed so virtuous, to his shameful lust. Oh, Hamlet, what a fall that was! From me, whose love was so honourable that it kept faithfully to the vow I made her at our wedding, down to a wretch whose natural gifts were poor compared to mine. But just as virtue will never be tempted, even if lust courts it disguised as an angel, so lust, even if it is joined to a shining angel, will get tired of a heavenly bed and feed on garbage. But wait! I think I can smell the morning air. Let me be quick. While I was sleeping in my orchard, as I always did in the afternoon, your uncle crept up on me in that unguarded hour with a bottle of the juice of cursed hebenon, and poured the poisonous liquid into the entrances of my ears. Its effect is so hostile to human blood that it runs as fast as mercury through the natural gates and passages of the body, and with sudden force it thickens and curdles the thin, healthy blood, like acid dropped into milk. That is what it did to mine. And at once a scaly rash covered my smooth body with a vile, disgusting crust like a leper's. So, while I slept, by my brother's hand I lost my life, my crown and my queen all at once. I was cut off with my sins in full bloom, without the last sacrament, unprepared, without the last rites, with no chance to settle my account, but sent to judgement with all my faults on my head. Oh, horrible! Horrible! Most horrible! If you have natural feeling in you, don't put up with it. Don't let the royal bed of Denmark be a bed for lust and damned incest. But however you carry out this act, don't corrupt your mind, and don't let your soul plot anything against your mother. Leave her to heaven, and to the thorns of conscience inside her to prick and sting her. Goodbye now! The glow-worm shows that morning is near, and its light is fading. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye. Remember me.

O all you host of heaven! O earth! What else? / And shall I couple hell? O, fie! Hold, my heart; / And you, my sinews, grow not instant old, / But bear me stiffly up. Remember thee? / Ay, thou poor ghost, while memory holds a seat / In this distracted globe. Remember thee? / Yea, from the table of my memory / I'll wipe away all trivial fond records, / All saws of books, all forms, all pressures past, / That youth and observation copied there; / And thy commandment all alone shall live / Within the book and volume of my brain, / Unmix'd with baser matter. Yes, by heaven! / O most pernicious woman! / O villain, villain, smiling damned villain! / My tables. Meet it is I set it down, / That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain! / At least I am sure it may be so in Denmark.

Oh, all you angels in heaven! Oh, earth! What else? Shall I call on hell too? Oh, no! Hold on, my heart, and you, my muscles, don't grow suddenly old, but hold me firmly up. Remember you? Yes, you poor ghost, as long as memory has a place in this confused head. Remember you? Yes, from the notebook of my memory I'll wipe out all trivial, foolish notes, all sayings from books, all images and impressions from the past that youth and observation copied there, and your command alone shall live in the book of my brain, not mixed with less important things. Yes, by heaven! Oh, most wicked woman! Oh, villain, villain, smiling, damned villain! My notebook. It's right that I write it down, that one may smile, and smile, and be a villain. At least I'm sure it can be so in Denmark.
So, uncle, there you are. Now to my word; / It is 'Adieu, adieu, remember me.' / I have sworn't.
So, uncle, there you are. Now for my motto. It is 'Goodbye, goodbye, remember me.' I have sworn it.
Hillo, ho, ho, boy! Come, bird, come.
Hello, ho, ho, boy! Come, bird, come.
How are you, my noble lord?
Not I, my lord, by heaven.
Not me, my lord, I swear by heaven.
How say you then, would heart of man once think it?— / But you'll be secret?
What do you say, then? Would anyone ever have imagined it? But you'll keep it secret?
There's ne'er a villain dwelling in all Denmark / But he's an arrant knave.
There's not a villain living in all Denmark who isn't a complete scoundrel.
There needs no ghost, my lord, come from the grave / To tell us this.
We don't need a ghost to come from the grave to tell us that, my lord.

Why, right; you are i' the right; / And so, without more circumstance at all, / I hold it fit that we shake hands and part: / You, as your business and desire shall point you,— / For every man hath business and desire, / Such as it is;—and for my own poor part, / Look you, I'll go pray.

Why, right, you're right. And so, without any more fuss, I think it's best that we shake hands and part. You go wherever your business and wishes take you, since every man has business and wishes, whatever they are. And as for my own poor self, look, I'll go and pray.
These are but wild and whirling words, my lord.
These are wild, whirling words, my lord.
I'm sorry they offend you, heartily; / Yes faith, heartily.
I'm sorry they offend you, truly, yes, in faith, truly.

Yes, by Saint Patrick, but there is, Horatio, / And much offence too. Touching this vision here, / It is an honest ghost, that let me tell you. / For your desire to know what is between us, / O'ermaster't as you may. And now, good friends, / As you are friends, scholars, and soldiers, / Give me one poor request.

Yes, by Saint Patrick, there is, Horatio, and a great offence too. About this vision: it's an honest ghost, I can tell you that. As for your wish to know what passed between us, control it as best you can. And now, good friends, since you are friends, scholars and soldiers, grant me one small request.
What is't, my lord? We will.
What is it, my lord? We will.
Never make known what you have seen tonight.
Never tell anyone what you've seen tonight.
In faith, my lord, not I.
On my word, my lord, I won't.
Nor I, my lord, in faith.
Nor I, my lord, on my word.
We have sworn, my lord, already.
Ha, ha boy, sayst thou so? Art thou there, truepenny? / Come on, you hear this fellow in the cellarage. / Consent to swear.
Ha, ha, boy, is that what you say? Are you there, old fellow? Come on, you hear this fellow down in the cellar. Agree to swear.
Tell us the oath, my lord.
Never to speak of this that you have seen. / Swear by my sword.
Never to speak of what you've seen. Swear by my sword.
Hic et ubique? Then we'll shift our ground. / Come hither, gentlemen, / And lay your hands again upon my sword. / Never to speak of this that you have heard. / Swear by my sword.
Here and everywhere? Then we'll move. Come over here, gentlemen, and put your hands on my sword again. Never to speak of what you've heard. Swear by my sword.
Well said, old mole! Canst work i' th'earth so fast? / A worthy pioner! Once more remove, good friends.
Well said, old mole! Can you dig through the earth so fast? A fine soldier-miner! Move once more, good friends.
O day and night, but this is wondrous strange.
By day and night, this is incredibly strange!

And therefore as a stranger give it welcome. / There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, / Than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But come, / Here, as before, never, so help you mercy, / How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself,— / As I perchance hereafter shall think meet / To put an antic disposition on— / That you, at such times seeing me, never shall, / With arms encumber'd thus, or this head-shake, / Or by pronouncing of some doubtful phrase, / As 'Well, we know', or 'We could and if we would', / Or 'If we list to speak'; or 'There be and if they might', / Or such ambiguous giving out, to note / That you know aught of me:—this not to do. / So grace and mercy at your most need help you, / Swear.

Then welcome it as you would a stranger. There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than your philosophy dreams of. But come. Swear, as before, as you hope for God's mercy, that however strange or odd I behave, since I may later think it right to act crazy, when you see me at those times you will never fold your arms like this, or shake your head like this, or say something mysterious like 'Well, we know', or 'We could if we wanted', or 'If we chose to speak', or 'There are some who could if they were allowed', or any such hint, to show that you know anything about me. Swear you won't do this, so may grace and mercy help you when you need it most.

Rest, rest, perturbed spirit. So, gentlemen, / With all my love I do commend me to you; / And what so poor a man as Hamlet is / May do t'express his love and friending to you, / God willing, shall not lack. Let us go in together, / And still your fingers on your lips, I pray. / The time is out of joint. O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right. / Nay, come, let's go together.

Rest, rest, troubled spirit! So, gentlemen, I give you all my love, and whatever a poor man like Hamlet can do to show his love and friendship, God willing, he will do. Let's go in together, and keep your fingers on your lips, I beg you. The times are out of joint. Oh, cursed bad luck that I was ever born to set them right! No, come on, let's go together.
Give him this money and these notes, Reynaldo.
Give him this money and these letters, Reynaldo.
You shall do marvellous wisely, good Reynaldo, / Before you visit him, to make inquiry / Of his behaviour.
It would be very wise of you, good Reynaldo, to find out how he is behaving before you visit him.
My lord, I did intend it.

Marry, well said; very well said. Look you, sir, / Enquire me first what Danskers are in Paris; / And how, and who, what means, and where they keep, / What company, at what expense; and finding / By this encompassment and drift of question, / That they do know my son, come you more nearer / Than your particular demands will touch it. / Take you as 'twere some distant knowledge of him, / As thus, 'I know his father and his friends, / And in part him'—do you mark this, Reynaldo?

Indeed, well said, very well said. Look, sir, first find out for me which Danes are in Paris, and how and who they are, what money they have, where they live, who they mix with and what they spend. And when you discover, by this roundabout way of asking, that they know my son, then get closer to the point than direct questions would. Pretend to know him a little, from a distance, like this: 'I know his father and his friends, and a bit of him.' Are you following this, Reynaldo?

'And in part him, but,' you may say, 'not well; / But if't be he I mean, he's very wild; / Addicted so and so;' and there put on him / What forgeries you please; marry, none so rank / As may dishonour him; take heed of that; / But, sir, such wanton, wild, and usual slips / As are companions noted and most known / To youth and liberty.

'And a bit of him, but,' you might say, 'not well. But if it's the man I mean, he's very wild, given to this and that.' And then accuse him of whatever invented faults you like; but none so bad as to dishonour him, be careful of that. Just, sir, the sort of reckless, wild and usual slips that are well known to go with youth and freedom.
Ay, or drinking, fencing, swearing, / Quarrelling, drabbing. You may go so far.
Yes, or drinking, fencing, swearing, quarrelling, whoring. You can go that far.
My lord, that would dishonour him.
My lord, that would dishonour him.

Faith no, as you may season it in the charge. / You must not put another scandal on him, / That he is open to incontinency; / That's not my meaning: but breathe his faults so quaintly / That they may seem the taints of liberty; / The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind, / A savageness in unreclaimed blood, / Of general assault.

No, really, not if you soften it as you make the charge. You mustn't add a different scandal, that he is given to unbridled lust; that's not what I mean. But hint at his faults so skilfully that they seem the flaws of freedom, the flash and outburst of a fiery mind, the wildness of untamed blood, the kind that happens to everyone.
Ay, my lord, I would know that.
Yes, my lord, I'd like to know that.

Marry, sir, here's my drift, / And I believe it is a fetch of warrant. / You laying these slight sullies on my son, / As 'twere a thing a little soil'd i' th' working, / Mark you, / Your party in converse, him you would sound, / Having ever seen in the prenominate crimes / The youth you breathe of guilty, be assur'd / He closes with you in this consequence; / 'Good sir,' or so; or 'friend,' or 'gentleman'— / According to the phrase or the addition / Of man and country.

Well, sir, here is my plan, and I believe it's a trick that works. When you put these slight stains on my son, as if he were something a little soiled in the making, listen to me: the man you are talking to, the one you want to sound out, if he has ever seen the young man you mention committing those faults, you can be sure he will agree with you like this: 'Good sir', or something like it, or 'friend', or 'gentleman', depending on how people speak and address each other in that country.
And then, sir, does he this,— / He does—What was I about to say? / By the mass, I was about to say something. Where did I leave?
And then, sir, he does this, he does... what was I going to say? By the Mass, I was about to say something. Where did I stop?
At 'closes in the consequence.' / At 'friend or so,' and 'gentleman.'
At 'will agree with you like this'. At 'friend, or something like it', and 'gentleman'.

At 'closes in the consequence' ay, marry! / He closes with you thus: 'I know the gentleman, / I saw him yesterday, or t'other day, / Or then, or then, with such and such; and, as you say, / There was he gaming, there o'ertook in's rouse, / There falling out at tennis': or perchance, / 'I saw him enter such a house of sale'— / Videlicet, a brothel, or so forth. See you now; / Your bait of falsehood takes this carp of truth; / And thus do we of wisdom and of reach, / With windlasses, and with assays of bias, / By indirections find directions out. / So by my former lecture and advice / Shall you my son. You have me, have you not?

At 'will agree with you', yes, indeed! He'll agree with you like this: 'I know the gentleman. I saw him yesterday, or the other day, or then, or then, with so-and-so, and, as you say, he was gambling there, there he was drunk, there quarrelling over tennis.' Or perhaps, 'I saw him go into a house of business', that is, a brothel, and so on. You see now: your bait of lies catches this fish of truth. And that's how we wise and far-sighted men, by roundabout ways and indirect approaches, find out the direct truth. So, by my lecture and advice, you'll find out about my son. You understand me, don't you?
God b' wi' you, fare you well.
And let him ply his music.
And let him get on with his music.
How now, Ophelia, what's the matter?
What's this, Ophelia? What's the matter?
Alas, my lord, I have been so affrighted.
Oh, my lord, I've been so frightened!
With what, in the name of God?

My lord, as I was sewing in my chamber, / Lord Hamlet, with his doublet all unbrac'd, / No hat upon his head, his stockings foul'd, / Ungart'red, and down-gyved to his ankle, / Pale as his shirt, his knees knocking each other, / And with a look so piteous in purport / As if he had been loosed out of hell / To speak of horrors, he comes before me.

My lord, as I was sewing in my room, Lord Hamlet came in front of me with his jacket all unfastened, no hat on his head, his stockings dirty, with no garters, and fallen down round his ankles like chains, as pale as his shirt, his knees knocking together, and with a look as pitiful as if he had been let out of hell to tell of horrors.
My lord, I do not know, but truly I do fear it.
My lord, I don't know, but I'm truly afraid so.

He took me by the wrist and held me hard; / Then goes he to the length of all his arm; / And with his other hand thus o'er his brow, / He falls to such perusal of my face / As he would draw it. Long stay'd he so, / At last,—a little shaking of mine arm, / And thrice his head thus waving up and down, / He rais'd a sigh so piteous and profound / As it did seem to shatter all his bulk / And end his being. That done, he lets me go, / And with his head over his shoulder turn'd / He seem'd to find his way without his eyes, / For out o' doors he went without their help, / And to the last bended their light on me.

He took me by the wrist and held me tight. Then he moved back the whole length of his arm, and with his other hand over his forehead like this, he started studying my face as if he were going to draw it. He stayed like that a long time. At last, shaking my arm a little and nodding his head up and down three times like this, he gave a sigh so pitiful and deep that it seemed to shatter his whole body and end his life. After that, he let me go, and with his head turned over his shoulder, he seemed to find his way without his eyes, because he went out of the door without their help, and kept them fixed on me to the end.

Come, go with me. I will go seek the King. / This is the very ecstasy of love, / Whose violent property fordoes itself, / And leads the will to desperate undertakings, / As oft as any passion under heaven / That does afflict our natures. I am sorry,— / What, have you given him any hard words of late?

Come, come with me. I'll go and find the King. This is the very madness of love, which by its violent nature destroys itself and drives people to desperate actions as often as any passion under heaven that afflicts us. I'm sorry. What, have you said anything harsh to him recently?
No, my good lord; but as you did command, / I did repel his letters and denied / His access to me.
No, my good lord, but as you ordered, I sent back his letters and refused to see him.

That hath made him mad. / I am sorry that with better heed and judgement / I had not quoted him. I fear'd he did but trifle, / And meant to wreck thee. But beshrew my jealousy! / It seems it is as proper to our age / To cast beyond ourselves in our opinions / As it is common for the younger sort / To lack discretion. Come, go we to the King. / This must be known, which, being kept close, might move / More grief to hide than hate to utter love.

That has made him mad. I'm sorry I didn't watch him with more care and judgement. I was afraid he was only playing with you and meant to ruin you. Curse my suspicion! It seems old men are as likely to go too far in our opinions as young people are to lack good sense. Come, let's go to the King. He must know about this. Keeping it secret might cause more grief than the anger we'll cause by revealing this love.

Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. / Moreover that we much did long to see you, / The need we have to use you did provoke / Our hasty sending. Something have you heard / Of Hamlet's transformation; so I call it, / Since nor th'exterior nor the inward man / Resembles that it was. What it should be, / More than his father's death, that thus hath put him / So much from th'understanding of himself, / I cannot dream of. I entreat you both / That, being of so young days brought up with him, / And since so neighbour'd to his youth and humour, / That you vouchsafe your rest here in our court / Some little time, so by your companies / To draw him on to pleasures and to gather, / So much as from occasion you may glean, / Whether aught to us unknown afflicts him thus / That, open'd, lies within our remedy.

Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Besides wanting very much to see you, we sent for you in a hurry because we need your help. You have heard something about Hamlet's transformation; I call it that because neither his outward appearance nor his inner self is like it was. What it can be, other than his father's death, that has put him so far out of his right mind, I can't imagine. I beg you both, since you were brought up with him from childhood and know his youth and temperament so well, to agree to stay here at our court for a little while, so that your company may draw him into some pleasures, and to find out, from whatever chances you get, whether something we don't know about is troubling him, which, once revealed, we could cure.

Good gentlemen, he hath much talk'd of you, / And sure I am, two men there are not living / To whom he more adheres. If it will please you / To show us so much gentry and good will / As to expend your time with us awhile, / For the supply and profit of our hope, / Your visitation shall receive such thanks / As fits a king's remembrance.
