Good gentlemen, he has talked about you a lot, and I'm sure there are no two men alive he is more attached to. If you will be kind and generous enough to spend some time with us, to help and further our hopes, your visit will be rewarded with the thanks a king remembers.
Both your majesties / Might, by the sovereign power you have of us, / Put your dread pleasures more into command / Than to entreaty.
Your majesties both have royal power over us, and could give your wishes to us as orders rather than requests.
We both obey, / And here give up ourselves, in the full bent, / To lay our service freely at your feet / To be commanded.
We both obey, and offer ourselves completely, to lay our service freely at your feet, ready for your commands.
Thank you, Rosencrantz and gentle Guildenstern.
Thanks, Guildenstern and gentle Rosencrantz. / And I beseech you instantly to visit / My too much changed son. Go, some of you, / And bring these gentlemen where Hamlet is.
Thank you, Guildenstern and gentle Rosencrantz. And I beg you to visit my son, who has changed so much, at once. Some of you, go and take these gentlemen to Hamlet.
Heavens make our presence and our practices / Pleasant and helpful to him.
May heaven make our presence and our actions pleasant and helpful to him!
Th'ambassadors from Norway, my good lord, / Are joyfully return'd.
The ambassadors from Norway, my good lord, have returned with good news.
Thou still hast been the father of good news.
You have always been the father of good news.

Have I, my lord? Assure you, my good liege, / I hold my duty, as I hold my soul, / Both to my God and to my gracious King: / And I do think,—or else this brain of mine / Hunts not the trail of policy so sure / As it hath us'd to do—that I have found / The very cause of Hamlet's lunacy.

Have I, my lord? I assure you, my good King, I keep my duty, as I keep my soul, both to my God and to my gracious King. And I think, unless this brain of mine doesn't follow the trail of political cunning as surely as it used to, that I have found the real cause of Hamlet's madness.
O speak of that, that do I long to hear.
Oh, speak about that! That's what I long to hear.
Give first admittance to th'ambassadors; / My news shall be the fruit to that great feast.
Receive the ambassadors first. My news will be the dessert after that great feast.
Thyself do grace to them, and bring them in.
You do them the honour yourself, and bring them in.
He tells me, my sweet queen, that he hath found / The head and source of all your son's distemper.
He tells me, my sweet queen, that he has found the root and cause of all your son's illness.
I doubt it is no other but the main, / His father's death and our o'erhasty marriage.
I suspect it is nothing other than the main thing, his father's death and our too hasty marriage.
Welcome, my good friends! / Say, Voltemand, what from our brother Norway?
Welcome, my good friends! Tell me, Voltemand, what news from our brother the King of Norway?

Most fair return of greetings and desires. / Upon our first, he sent out to suppress / His nephew's levies, which to him appear'd / To be a preparation 'gainst the Polack; / But better look'd into, he truly found / It was against your Highness; whereat griev'd, / That so his sickness, age, and impotence / Was falsely borne in hand, sends out arrests / On Fortinbras; which he, in brief, obeys, / Receives rebuke from Norway; and in fine, / Makes vow before his uncle never more / To give th'assay of arms against your Majesty. / Whereon old Norway, overcome with joy, / Gives him three thousand crowns in annual fee, / And his commission to employ those soldiers / So levied as before, against the Polack: / With an entreaty, herein further shown, / [Gives a paper] / That it might please you to give quiet pass / Through your dominions for this enterprise, / On such regards of safety and allowance / As therein are set down.

He returns your greetings and good wishes most kindly. As soon as we raised the matter, he sent orders to stop his nephew's recruiting, which he had thought was preparation for a war against the Poles. But when he looked into it, he found it was really against your Highness. He was upset that his sickness, age and weakness had been taken advantage of, so he sent orders to arrest Fortinbras. In short, Fortinbras obeys, is told off by the King of Norway, and finally swears before his uncle never again to take up arms against your Majesty. At this, old Norway, overjoyed, gives him an income of three thousand crowns a year and permission to use the soldiers he raised against the Poles, with a request, set out here [Gives a paper], that you would allow them to pass peacefully through your lands for this expedition, on the terms of safety and permission written down in it.

It likes us well; / And at our more consider'd time we'll read, / Answer, and think upon this business. / Meantime we thank you for your well-took labour. / Go to your rest, at night we'll feast together:. / Most welcome home.

We are pleased with this. When we have more time to think, we'll read it, reply and consider this business. Meanwhile, we thank you for your successful work. Go and rest. Tonight we'll feast together. Welcome home!

This business is well ended. / My liege and madam, to expostulate / What majesty should be, what duty is, / Why day is day, night night, and time is time / Were nothing but to waste night, day and time. / Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit, / And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes, / I will be brief. Your noble son is mad. / Mad call I it; for to define true madness, / What is't but to be nothing else but mad? / But let that go.

This business has ended well. My King and madam, to discuss what majesty should be, what duty is, why day is day, night is night, and time is time, would only waste night, day and time. So, since keeping it short is the heart of wisdom, and long-windedness is just its limbs and outward decoration, I will be brief. Your noble son is mad. I call it mad, because what is true madness except being nothing else but mad? But let that go.
More substance, with less fancy talk.

Madam, I swear I use no art at all. / That he is mad, 'tis true: 'tis true 'tis pity; / And pity 'tis 'tis true. A foolish figure, / But farewell it, for I will use no art. / Mad let us grant him then. And now remains / That we find out the cause of this effect, / Or rather say, the cause of this defect, / For this effect defective comes by cause. / Thus it remains, and the remainder thus. Perpend, / I have a daughter—have whilst she is mine— / Who in her duty and obedience, mark, / Hath given me this. Now gather, and surmise. / [Reads] / To the celestial, and my soul's idol, the most beautified Ophelia— / That's an ill phrase, a vile phrase; 'beautified' is a vile / phrase: but you shall hear. / [Reads] / these; in her excellent white bosom, these, &c.

Madam, I swear I'm not using any fancy talk at all. That he is mad is true; it's true it's a pity; and it's a pity it's true. A foolish figure of speech, but goodbye to it, because I won't use any art. Let's agree he is mad, then. Now what remains is to find the cause of this effect, or rather the cause of this defect, because this defective effect has a cause. That's what remains, and here's the rest. Consider this. I have a daughter, have her while she's still mine, who, out of duty and obedience, mark you, has given me this. Now listen and draw your conclusions. [Reads] 'To the heavenly one, my soul's idol, the most beautified Ophelia.' That's a bad phrase, a vile phrase; 'beautified' is a vile phrase. But you'll hear. [Reads] 'These, to her excellent white breast, these...' and so on.
Came this from Hamlet to her?
Did this come from Hamlet to her?

Good madam, stay awhile; I will be faithful. / [Reads] / Doubt thou the stars are fire, / Doubt that the sun doth move, / Doubt truth to be a liar, / But never doubt I love. / O dear Ophelia, I am ill at these numbers. I have not art to reckon my / groans. But that I love thee best, O most best, believe it. Adieu. / Thine evermore, most dear lady, whilst this machine is to him, / HAMLET. / This in obedience hath my daughter show'd me; / And more above, hath his solicitings, / As they fell out by time, by means, and place, / All given to mine ear.

Good madam, wait a moment. I'll read it all faithfully. [Reads] 'Doubt that the stars are fire, doubt that the sun moves, doubt that truth is truth, but never doubt that I love. Oh, dear Ophelia, I'm bad at writing verse. I don't have the skill to count out my groans in rhyme. But that I love you best, oh, very best, believe it. Goodbye. Yours forever, dearest lady, while this body belongs to him, Hamlet.' My daughter, out of obedience, has shown me this, and besides that she has told me about all his advances, when, how and where they happened.
But how hath she receiv'd his love?
But how has she received his love?
What do you think of me?
What do you think of me?
As of a man faithful and honourable.
That you are a faithful and honourable man.

I would fain prove so. But what might you think, / When I had seen this hot love on the wing, / As I perceiv'd it, I must tell you that, / Before my daughter told me, what might you, / Or my dear Majesty your queen here, think, / If I had play'd the desk or table-book, / Or given my heart a winking, mute and dumb, / Or look'd upon this love with idle sight, / What might you think? No, I went round to work, / And my young mistress thus I did bespeak: / 'Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of thy star. / This must not be.' And then I precepts gave her, / That she should lock herself from his resort, / Admit no messengers, receive no tokens. / Which done, she took the fruits of my advice, / And he, repulsed,—a short tale to make— / Fell into a sadness, then into a fast, / Thence to a watch, thence into a weakness, / Thence to a lightness, and, by this declension, / Into the madness wherein now he raves, / And all we wail for.

I'd like to prove that I am. But what would you have thought, when I saw this passionate love taking flight, and I noticed it, I must tell you, before my daughter told me, what would you, or my dear Majesty your queen here, have thought, if I had kept it to myself like a desk or notebook, or made my heart shut its eyes and stay silent, or looked on this love without seeing it? What would you have thought? No, I got straight to work, and spoke to my young lady like this: 'Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of your sphere. This must not happen.' And then I gave her orders to lock herself away from his visits, to see no messengers and accept no gifts. I heard thee speak me a speech once, but it was never acted, or if it / was, not above once, for the play, I remember, pleased not the million, / 'twas caviare to the general. I remember one said there were no sallets in the lines to make / the matter savoury, nor no matter in the phrase that might indite the / author of affectation, but called it an honest method, as wholesome as / sweet, and by very much more handsome than fine. If it live in your / memory, begin at this line, let me see, let me see: / The rugged Pyrrhus, like th' Hyrcanian beast,— / It is not so: it begins with Pyrrhus— / The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms, / Black as his purpose, did the night resemble / When he lay couched in the ominous horse, / Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd / With heraldry more dismal. I heard you recite a speech to me once, but it was never acted, or if it was, not more than once, because the play, I remember, didn't please the masses; it was caviar to the common people. I remember someone said there were no spicy bits in the lines to make the story tasty, and nothing in the language that could charge the author with showing off, but called it an honest style, as healthy as it was sweet, and much more truly beautiful than showy. Anon he finds him, / Striking too short at Greeks. His antique sword, / Rebellious to his arm, lies where it falls, / Repugnant to command. Unequal match'd, / Pyrrhus at Priam drives, in rage strikes wide; / But with the whiff and wind of his fell sword / Th'unnerved father falls. Then senseless Ilium, / Seeming to feel this blow, with flaming top / Stoops to his base, and with a hideous crash / Takes prisoner Pyrrhus' ear. For lo, his sword, / Which was declining on the milky head / Of reverend Priam, seem'd i' th'air to stick. / So, as a painted tyrant, Pyrrhus stood, / And like a neutral to his will and matter, / Did nothing. / But as we often see against some storm, / A silence in the heavens, the rack stand still, / The bold winds speechless, and the orb below / As hush as death, anon the dreadful thunder / Doth rend the region; so after Pyrrhus' pause, / Aroused vengeance sets him new a-work, / And never did the Cyclops' hammers fall / On Mars's armour, forg'd for proof eterne, / With less remorse than Pyrrhus' bleeding sword / Now falls on Priam. / Out, out, thou strumpet Fortune! All you gods, / In general synod, take away her power; / Break all the spokes and fellies from her wheel, / And bowl the round nave down the hill of heaven, / As low as to the fiends.

'Soon he finds him, striking at the Greeks and falling short. His old sword, refusing to obey his arm, stays where it falls, disobeying orders. Unevenly matched, Pyrrhus rushes at Priam; in his rage he misses, but the rush of air from his deadly sword is enough to knock the weakened father down. Then the senseless city of Troy, seeming to feel this blow, collapses with its burning towers, and with a hideous crash catches Pyrrhus's ear. For look, his sword, which was coming down on the white head of the respected Priam, seemed to stick in the air. So Pyrrhus stood like a tyrant in a painting, and, as if halfway between his intention and the deed, did nothing. But as we often see, before a storm, a silence in the heavens, the clouds standing still, the bold winds silent and the earth below as quiet as death, then suddenly dreadful thunder rips the sky; so, after Pyrrhus's pause, reawakened vengeance sets him to work again. And the Cyclops' hammers never fell on the armour of Mars, made to last forever, with less pity than Pyrrhus's bleeding sword now falls on Priam. Out, out, you whore, Fortune! All you gods, in a general council, take away her power. Break all the spokes and rims of her wheel, and roll the round hub down the hill of heaven as low as hell!'

'Tis well. I'll have thee speak out the rest of this soon.—Good my / lord, will you see the players well bestowed? Do you hear, let them be / well used; for they are the abstracts and brief chronicles of the time. / After your death you were better have a bad epitaph than their ill / report while you live.

That's good. I'll have you recite the rest of this soon. My good lord, will you see that the actors are well looked after? Do you hear? Let them be treated well, because they sum up and record our times. After you're dead you'd be better off with a bad epitaph than a bad report from them while you live.
My lord, I will use them according to their desert.
My lord, I'll treat them as they deserve.

God's bodikin, man, much better. Use every man after his desert, and who / should 'scape whipping? Use them after your own honour and dignity. The / less they deserve, the more merit is in your bounty. Take them in.

By God's little body, man, much better! Treat every man as he deserves, and who would escape a whipping? Treat them according to your own honour and dignity. The less they deserve, the more credit your generosity earns. Take them in.
Follow him, friends. We'll hear a play tomorrow.
Follow him, friends. We'll see a play tomorrow.
Dost thou hear me, old friend? Can you play The Murder of Gonzago?
Do you hear me, old friend? Can you perform The Murder of Gonzago?
We'll ha't tomorrow night. You could for a need study a speech of some / dozen or sixteen lines, which I would set down and insert in't, could / you not?
We'll have it tomorrow night. If necessary, you could learn a speech of twelve or sixteen lines which I'll write and put into it, couldn't you?
Very well. Follow that lord, and look you mock him not.
Very good. Follow that lord, and be careful not to make fun of him.
[To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern] My good friends, I'll leave you / till night. You are welcome to Elsinore.
[To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern] My good friends, I'll leave you until tonight. You're welcome to Elsinore.

Ay, so, God b' wi' ye. Now I am alone. / O what a rogue and peasant slave am I! / Is it not monstrous that this player here, / But in a fiction, in a dream of passion, / Could force his soul so to his own conceit / That from her working all his visage wan'd; / Tears in his eyes, distraction in's aspect, / A broken voice, and his whole function suiting / With forms to his conceit? And all for nothing! / For Hecuba? / What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, / That he should weep for her? What would he do, / Had he the motive and the cue for passion / That I have? He would drown the stage with tears / And cleave the general ear with horrid speech; / Make mad the guilty, and appal the free, / Confound the ignorant, and amaze indeed, / The very faculties of eyes and ears. Yet I, / A dull and muddy-mettled rascal, peak / Like John-a-dreams, unpregnant of my cause, / And can say nothing. No, not for a king / Upon whose property and most dear life / A damn'd defeat was made. Am I a coward? / Who calls me villain, breaks my pate across? / Plucks off my beard and blows it in my face? / Tweaks me by the nose, gives me the lie i' th' throat / As deep as to the lungs? Who does me this? / Ha! 'Swounds, I should take it: for it cannot be / But I am pigeon-liver'd, and lack gall / To make oppression bitter, or ere this / I should have fatted all the region kites / With this slave's offal. Bloody, bawdy villain! / Remorseless, treacherous, lecherous, kindless villain! / Oh vengeance! / Why, what an ass am I! This is most brave, / That I, the son of a dear father murder'd, / Prompted to my revenge by heaven and hell, / Must, like a whore, unpack my heart with words / And fall a-cursing like a very drab, / A scullion! Fie upon't! Foh! / About, my brain! I have heard / That guilty creatures sitting at a play, / Have by the very cunning of the scene, / Been struck so to the soul that presently / They have proclaim'd their malefactions. / For murder, though it have no tongue, will speak / With most miraculous organ. I'll have these players / Play something like the murder of my father / Before mine uncle. I'll observe his looks; / I'll tent him to the quick. If he but blench, / I know my course. The spirit that I have seen / May be the devil, and the devil hath power / T'assume a pleasing shape, yea, and perhaps / Out of my weakness and my melancholy, / As he is very potent with such spirits, / Abuses me to damn me. I'll have grounds / More relative than this. The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King.

Yes, goodbye to you. Now I'm alone. Oh, what a rogue and low slave I am! Isn't it monstrous that this actor here, just in a story, in a dream of passion, could force his soul to feel what he imagined, so that it made his face go pale, tears in his eyes, wildness in his look, a broken voice, and his whole body acting out what he imagined? And all for nothing! For Hecuba! What is Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, that he should weep for her? What would he do if he had the reason and the cue for passion that I have? He would drown the stage with tears, split everyone's ears with terrible words, drive the guilty mad, terrify the innocent, confuse the ignorant and stun the very senses of sight and hearing. And yet I, a dull, spiritless rascal, mope around like a dreamer, not stirred by my cause, and can say nothing. No, not even for a king whose kingdom and precious life were destroyed by a damned crime. Am I a coward? Who calls me villain? Hits me across the head? Pulls off my beard and blows it in my face? Tweaks my nose? Calls me a liar to my face, as deep as my lungs? Who does this to me? Ha! By God's wounds, I would take it, because I must be as meek as a pigeon and have no bitterness to make wrongs feel bitter, or I would have fattened all the hawks in the sky with this slave's guts by now. Bloody, filthy villain! Pitiless, treacherous, lustful, unnatural villain! Oh, vengeance! Why, what an ass I am! This is really fine, that I, the son of a dear father who was murdered, urged on to my revenge by heaven and hell, must unload my heart with words like a whore, and start cursing like a common slut, a kitchen servant! Shame on it! Ugh! Get to work, my brain! I have heard that guilty people watching a play have been so struck to the soul by the skill of the scene that they have confessed their crimes on the spot. For murder, though it has no tongue, will speak by some miraculous means. I'll have these actors perform something like my father's murder in front of my uncle. I'll watch his face. I'll probe him to the quick. If he so much as flinches, I'll know what to do. The spirit I have seen may be the devil, and the devil has the power to take on a pleasing shape. Yes, and perhaps, because of my weakness and my depression, since he has great power over people in that state, he is deceiving me to damn me. I'll get evidence more solid than this. The play's the thing in which I'll catch the conscience of the King.
And can you by no drift of circumstance / Get from him why he puts on this confusion, / Grating so harshly all his days of quiet / With turbulent and dangerous lunacy?
And can't you, by steering the conversation, get out of him why he is acting so confused, spoiling his peaceful days so harshly with wild and dangerous madness?
He does confess he feels himself distracted, / But from what cause he will by no means speak.
He admits that he feels disturbed, but he won't say at all what the cause is.
Nor do we find him forward to be sounded, / But with a crafty madness keeps aloof / When we would bring him on to some confession / Of his true state.
And we don't find him willing to be questioned. With a cunning kind of madness he keeps his distance whenever we try to lead him into admitting how he really is.
But with much forcing of his disposition.
But it was clearly an effort for him.
Niggard of question, but of our demands, / Most free in his reply.
He asked few questions, but answered ours very freely.
Did you assay him to any pastime?
Did you try to interest him in any entertainment?

Madam, it so fell out that certain players / We o'er-raught on the way. Of these we told him, / And there did seem in him a kind of joy / To hear of it. They are about the court, / And, as I think, they have already order / This night to play before him.

Madam, it happened that we overtook some actors on the way. We told him about them, and he seemed to show a kind of joy at hearing it. They are here at court, and I believe they've already been told to perform for him tonight.
'Tis most true; / And he beseech'd me to entreat your Majesties / To hear and see the matter.
That's very true, and he begged me to ask your Majesties to come and watch the play.
With all my heart; and it doth much content me / To hear him so inclin'd. / Good gentlemen, give him a further edge, / And drive his purpose on to these delights.
With all my heart. It pleases me very much to hear he is in that mood. Good gentlemen, sharpen his interest further, and encourage him towards these pleasures.

Sweet Gertrude, leave us too, / For we have closely sent for Hamlet hither, / That he, as 'twere by accident, may here / Affront Ophelia. / Her father and myself, lawful espials, / Will so bestow ourselves that, seeing unseen, / We may of their encounter frankly judge, / And gather by him, as he is behav'd, / If't be th'affliction of his love or no / That thus he suffers for.

Sweet Gertrude, leave us too, because we have secretly sent for Hamlet to come here, so that, as if by accident, he may meet Ophelia face to face. Her father and I, spying for good reasons, will hide ourselves so that, seeing without being seen, we can judge their meeting clearly and work out from the way he behaves whether it is lovesickness or not that makes him suffer like this.

I shall obey you. / And for your part, Ophelia, I do wish / That your good beauties be the happy cause / Of Hamlet's wildness: so shall I hope your virtues / Will bring him to his wonted way again, / To both your honours.
I'll obey you. And as for you, Ophelia, I hope that your beauty is the happy cause of Hamlet's madness. Then I can hope your virtues will bring him back to his usual self, to the honour of you both.

Ophelia, walk you here.—Gracious, so please you, / We will bestow ourselves.—[To Ophelia] Read on this book, / That show of such an exercise may colour / Your loneliness.—We are oft to blame in this, / 'Tis too much prov'd, that with devotion's visage / And pious action we do sugar o'er / The devil himself.

Ophelia, walk here. Your Majesty, if you please, we'll hide ourselves. [To Ophelia] Read this prayer book, so that looking busy with devotion will explain why you're alone. We are often to blame in this, it's been proved too often: with a holy face and pious actions we sugar-coat the devil himself.

[Aside] O 'tis too true! / How smart a lash that speech doth give my conscience! / The harlot's cheek, beautied with plastering art, / Is not more ugly to the thing that helps it / Than is my deed to my most painted word. / O heavy burden!

[Aside] Oh, it's too true! What a sharp whip that speech lays on my conscience! The whore's cheek, made pretty with plastered make-up, is not uglier underneath than my crime is underneath my most painted words. Oh, heavy burden!
I hear him coming. Let's withdraw, my lord.
I can hear him coming. Let's hide, my lord.

To be, or not to be, that is the question: / Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer / The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, / And by opposing end them? To die—to sleep, / No more; and by a sleep to say we end / The heart-ache, and the thousand natural shocks / That flesh is heir to: 'tis a consummation / Devoutly to be wish'd. To die, to sleep. / To sleep, perchance to dream—ay, there's the rub, / For in that sleep of death what dreams may come, / When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, / Must give us pause. There's the respect / That makes calamity of so long life. / For who would bear the whips and scorns of time, / The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely, / The pangs of dispriz'd love, the law's delay, / The insolence of office, and the spurns / That patient merit of the unworthy takes, / When he himself might his quietus make / With a bare bodkin? Who would these fardels bear, / To grunt and sweat under a weary life, / But that the dread of something after death, / The undiscover'd country, from whose bourn / No traveller returns, puzzles the will, / And makes us rather bear those ills we have / Than fly to others that we know not of? / Thus conscience does make cowards of us all, / And thus the native hue of resolution / Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought, / And enterprises of great pith and moment, / With this regard their currents turn awry / And lose the name of action. Soft you now, / The fair Ophelia! Nymph, in thy orisons / Be all my sins remember'd.

To be, or not to be, that is the question: whether it is nobler to put up with all the blows and arrows that cruel fortune throws at us, or to fight against a whole sea of troubles and end them by fighting? To die, to sleep, nothing more; and if by a sleep we could end the heartache and the thousand natural shocks that the body inherits, that would be an ending we should pray for. To die, to sleep. To sleep, perhaps to dream. Yes, that's the problem, because the thought of what dreams may come in that sleep of death, once we have thrown off the tangle of this life, must make us stop and think. That's the consideration that makes us put up with misery for so long. For who would bear the whips and scorn of the world, the wrongs of the oppressor, the insults of the proud, the pain of rejected love, the slowness of the law, the rudeness of officials and the kicks that patient, deserving people get from the unworthy, when he could settle his own account with a simple dagger? Who would carry these burdens, grunting and sweating under a weary life, if it weren't that the dread of something after death, that undiscovered country from which no traveller ever comes back, confuses the will, and makes us prefer to bear the troubles we have rather than rush to others we know nothing about? So thinking makes cowards of us all, and so the natural colour of determination is covered with the pale, sickly look of thought, and great, important plans turn aside because of this and lose the name of action. But quiet now: the lovely Ophelia! Beautiful girl, remember all my sins in your prayers.
Good my lord, / How does your honour for this many a day?
My good lord, how has your lordship been all these days?
I humbly thank you; well, well, well.
I humbly thank you. Well, well, well.
My lord, I have remembrances of yours / That I have longed long to re-deliver. / I pray you, now receive them.
My lord, I have some gifts of yours that I have long wanted to give back. Please, take them now.
No, not I. / I never gave you aught.
No, not me. I never gave you anything.

My honour'd lord, you know right well you did, / And with them words of so sweet breath compos'd / As made the things more rich; their perfume lost, / Take these again; for to the noble mind / Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove unkind. / There, my lord.

My honoured lord, you know very well you did, and with them you gave words so sweetly spoken that they made the gifts richer. Now their perfume is gone, take them back, because to a noble mind rich gifts become poor when the givers turn unkind. There, my lord.
That if you be honest and fair, your honesty should admit no discourse / to your beauty.
That if you are honest and beautiful, your honesty should not allow anyone to talk to your beauty.
Could beauty, my lord, have better commerce than with honesty?
Could beauty, my lord, have a better companion than honesty?

Ay, truly; for the power of beauty will sooner transform honesty from / what it is to a bawd than the force of honesty can translate beauty / into his likeness. This was sometime a paradox, but now the time gives / it proof. I did love you once.

Yes, truly, because the power of beauty will turn honesty into a pimp sooner than the strength of honesty can make beauty like itself. This used to be a paradox, but now the times prove it. I did love you once.
Indeed, my lord, you made me believe so.
Indeed, my lord, you made me believe so.
You should not have believed me; for virtue cannot so inoculate our old / stock but we shall relish of it. I loved you not.
You shouldn't have believed me, because virtue can't be grafted onto our old sinful stock without some taste of the old stock remaining. I didn't love you.
Then I was all the more deceived.

Get thee to a nunnery. Why wouldst thou be a breeder of sinners? I am / myself indifferent honest; but yet I could accuse me of such things / that it were better my mother had not borne me. I am very proud, / revengeful, ambitious, with more offences at my beck than I have / thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape, or time to act / them in. What should such fellows as I do crawling between earth and / heaven? We are arrant knaves all, believe none of us. Go thy ways to a / nunnery. Where's your father?

Get yourself to a nunnery. Why would you want to give birth to sinners? I'm fairly honest myself, but I could still accuse myself of such things that it would be better if my mother had never given birth to me. I'm very proud, vengeful, ambitious, with more sins ready to commit than I have thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape or time to carry them out. What should fellows like me be doing, crawling between earth and heaven? We are all complete villains. Don't believe any of us. Go on, off to a nunnery. Where's your father?
Let the doors be shut upon him, that he may play the fool nowhere but / in's own house. Farewell.
Then shut the doors on him, so he can play the fool only in his own house. Goodbye.
O help him, you sweet heavens!

If thou dost marry, I'll give thee this plague for thy dowry. Be thou / as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, thou shalt not escape calumny. Get / thee to a nunnery, go: farewell. Or if thou wilt needs marry, marry a / fool; for wise men know well enough what monsters you make of them. To / a nunnery, go; and quickly too. Farewell.

If you marry, I'll give you this curse as your dowry: be as chaste as ice and as pure as snow, you still won't escape slander. Get yourself to a nunnery. Go. Goodbye. Or if you must marry, marry a fool, because wise men know well enough what monsters you turn them into. To a nunnery, go, and quickly too. Goodbye.
Oh, heavenly powers, make him well again!

I have heard of your paintings too, well enough. God hath given you one / face, and you make yourselves another. You jig, you amble, and you / lisp, and nickname God's creatures, and make your wantonness your / ignorance. Go to, I'll no more on't, it hath made me mad. I say, we / will have no more marriages. Those that are married already, all but / one, shall live; the rest shall keep as they are. To a nunnery, go.

I've heard about your make-up too, plenty. God has given you one face and you paint yourselves another. You dance and sway and lisp, you give silly nicknames to God's creatures, and you pretend your flirting is innocence. Go on, I'll have no more of it. It's made me mad. I say we'll have no more marriages. Those who are married already, all except one, will live; the rest will stay as they are. To a nunnery, go.

O, what a noble mind is here o'erthrown! / The courtier's, soldier's, scholar's, eye, tongue, sword, / Th'expectancy and rose of the fair state, / The glass of fashion and the mould of form, / Th'observ'd of all observers, quite, quite down! / And I, of ladies most deject and wretched, / That suck'd the honey of his music vows, / Now see that noble and most sovereign reason, / Like sweet bells jangled out of tune and harsh, / That unmatch'd form and feature of blown youth / Blasted with ecstasy. O woe is me, / T'have seen what I have seen, see what I see.

Oh, what a noble mind is ruined here! The eye of a courtier, the tongue of a scholar, the sword of a soldier, the hope and flower of this fair kingdom, the mirror of fashion and the model of good behaviour, the one everyone watched, completely, completely fallen! And I, the most miserable and wretched of women, who sucked the honey of his musical promises, now see that noble, commanding reason jangling out of tune and harsh like sweet bells, that unequalled shape and face of young manhood in full bloom destroyed by madness. Oh, how wretched I am, to have seen what I saw, and to see what I see!

Love? His affections do not that way tend, / Nor what he spake, though it lack'd form a little, / Was not like madness. There's something in his soul / O'er which his melancholy sits on brood, / And I do doubt the hatch and the disclose / Will be some danger, which for to prevent, / I have in quick determination / Thus set it down: he shall with speed to England / For the demand of our neglected tribute: / Haply the seas and countries different, / With variable objects, shall expel / This something settled matter in his heart, / Whereon his brains still beating puts him thus / From fashion of himself. What think you on't?

Love? His feelings don't go that way. And what he said, though it was a little disordered, wasn't like madness. There's something in his soul that his depression is sitting on like a bird on eggs, and I fear that when it hatches and comes out it will be dangerous. To prevent that, I have quickly made up my mind: he will go to England at once, to demand the payment they owe us and haven't paid. Perhaps the sea and different countries, with new things to see, will drive out this thing that has settled in his heart, which his brain keeps beating on, making him so unlike himself. What do you think?

It shall do well. But yet do I believe / The origin and commencement of his grief / Sprung from neglected love. How now, Ophelia? / You need not tell us what Lord Hamlet said, / We heard it all. My lord, do as you please, / But if you hold it fit, after the play, / Let his queen mother all alone entreat him / To show his grief, let her be round with him, / And I'll be plac'd, so please you, in the ear / Of all their conference. If she find him not, / To England send him; or confine him where / Your wisdom best shall think.

It will work well. But I still believe the origin and beginning of his grief came from rejected love. Well, Ophelia? You needn't tell us what Lord Hamlet said; we heard it all. My lord, do as you like, but if you think it right, after the play let his mother the Queen beg him alone to reveal his grief. Let her be blunt with him, and, if you agree, I'll hide where I can hear their whole conversation. If she can't find out what's wrong, send him to England, or shut him away wherever your wisdom thinks best.
It shall be so. / Madness in great ones must not unwatch'd go.
So it shall be. Madness in important people must not go unwatched.

Speak the speech, I pray you, as I pronounced it to you, trippingly on / the tongue. But if you mouth it, as many of your players do, I had as / lief the town-crier spoke my lines. Nor do not saw the air too much / with your hand, thus, but use all gently; for in the very torrent, / tempest, and, as I may say, whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and / beget a temperance that may give it smoothness. O, it offends me to the / soul to hear a robustious periwig-pated fellow tear a passion to / tatters, to very rags, to split the ears of the groundlings, who, for / the most part, are capable of nothing but inexplicable dumb shows and / noise. I would have such a fellow whipped for o'erdoing Termagant. It / out-Herods Herod. Pray you avoid it.

Say the speech, please, the way I said it to you, lightly and naturally. But if you overact it the way many of you actors do, I'd rather have the town crier speak my lines. And don't saw the air with your hand like this, but do everything gently, because even in the flood, the storm, and I might say the whirlwind of passion, you must find and create a self-control that gives it smoothness. Oh, it hurts me to the soul to hear a loud, bewigged actor tear a passion to shreds, to rags, to split the ears of the people standing in the pit, who mostly can't appreciate anything except meaningless mime and noise. I'd have that sort of actor whipped for overplaying the ranting villain. It out-Herods Herod. Please avoid it.

Be not too tame neither; but let your own discretion be your tutor. / Suit the action to the word, the word to the action, with this special / observance, that you o'erstep not the modesty of nature; for anything / so overdone is from the purpose of playing, whose end, both at the / first and now, was and is, to hold as 'twere the mirror up to nature; / to show virtue her own feature, scorn her own image, and the very age / and body of the time his form and pressure. Now, this overdone, or come / tardy off, though it make the unskilful laugh, cannot but make the / judicious grieve; the censure of the which one must in your allowance / o'erweigh a whole theatre of others. O, there be players that I have / seen play—and heard others praise, and that highly—not to speak it / profanely, that, neither having the accent of Christians, nor the gait / of Christian, pagan, nor man, have so strutted and bellowed that I have / thought some of Nature's journeymen had made men, and not made them / well, they imitated humanity so abominably.

Don't be too tame either, but let your own judgement teach you. Fit the action to the word and the word to the action, taking special care not to go beyond what is natural. Anything overdone like that goes against the purpose of acting, whose aim, from the beginning until now, was and is to hold a mirror up to nature: to show virtue its own face, scorn its own image, and the age and body of the times its shape and imprint. Now, if this is overdone or underdone, though it makes the ignorant laugh, it can only upset the judicious, and you must value the opinion of one of them more than a whole theatre full of the others. Oh, there are actors I have seen, and heard others praise highly, who, not to put it too irreverently, didn't speak or walk like Christians, pagans or even men, and strutted and bellowed so much that I thought some of Nature's apprentice workmen had made them, and made them badly, they imitated humanity so horribly.
I hope we have reform'd that indifferently with us, sir.
I hope we have more or less corrected that in our company, sir.

O reform it altogether. And let those that play your clowns speak no / more than is set down for them. For there be of them that will / themselves laugh, to set on some quantity of barren spectators to laugh / too, though in the meantime some necessary question of the play be then / to be considered. That's villainous, and shows a most pitiful ambition / in the fool that uses it. Go make you ready.

Oh, correct it completely. And don't let the actors who play your clowns say any more than is written for them. Some of them will laugh themselves to set off some stupid spectators laughing too, even though some important point in the play needs attention at that moment. That's wicked, and shows a pathetic ambition in the fool who does it. Go and get ready.
How now, my lord? / Will the King hear this piece of work?
Well, my lord? Will the King come to see this play?
And the Queen too, and that presently.
And the Queen too, very soon.
Will you two help to hasten them?
Will you two help to hurry them?
Here, sweet lord, at your service.
Here, sweet lord, at your service.
Horatio, thou art e'en as just a man / As e'er my conversation cop'd withal.
Horatio, you are as honest and balanced a man as I have ever met.

Nay, do not think I flatter; / For what advancement may I hope from thee, / That no revenue hast, but thy good spirits / To feed and clothe thee? Why should the poor be flatter'd? / No, let the candied tongue lick absurd pomp, / And crook the pregnant hinges of the knee / Where thrift may follow fawning. Dost thou hear? / Since my dear soul was mistress of her choice, / And could of men distinguish, her election / Hath seal'd thee for herself. For thou hast been / As one, in suffering all, that suffers nothing, / A man that Fortune's buffets and rewards / Hast ta'en with equal thanks. And blessed are those / Whose blood and judgement are so well co-mingled / That they are not a pipe for Fortune's finger / To sound what stop she please. Give me that man / That is not passion's slave, and I will wear him / In my heart's core, ay, in my heart of heart, / As I do thee. Something too much of this. / There is a play tonight before the King. / One scene of it comes near the circumstance / Which I have told thee, of my father's death. / I prithee, when thou see'st that act a-foot, / Even with the very comment of thy soul / Observe mine uncle. If his occulted guilt / Do not itself unkennel in one speech, / It is a damned ghost that we have seen; / And my imaginations are as foul / As Vulcan's stithy. Give him heedful note; / For I mine eyes will rivet to his face; / And after we will both our judgements join / In censure of his seeming.

No, don't think I'm flattering you. What reward could I hope for from you, when you have no income except your good spirits to feed and clothe you? Why should anyone flatter the poor? No, let the sugary tongue lick foolish grandeur, and let the ready knee bend where profit may follow from fawning. Do you hear? Ever since my soul could make its own choices and tell one man from another, it has chosen you for itself. Because you have been like someone who suffers everything and yet is not hurt by it, a man who has taken Fortune's blows and rewards with equal thanks. And blessed are those whose passion and judgement are so well mixed that they are not a pipe for Fortune to play whatever note she likes. Give me the man who is not a slave to passion, and I will keep him at the centre of my heart, yes, in my heart of hearts, as I do you. That's a little too much of this. There is a play tonight in front of the King. One scene in it is close to what I told you about my father's death. Please, when you see that part start, watch my uncle with all the attention of your soul. If his hidden guilt doesn't break out of hiding at one particular speech, then it is a damned ghost we have seen, and my imaginings are as filthy as the blacksmith god Vulcan's forge. Watch him carefully, because I'll fix my eyes on his face, and afterwards we'll put our judgements together to decide what his reaction showed.
Well, my lord. / If he steal aught the whilst this play is playing, / And 'scape detecting, I will pay the theft.
Very well, my lord. If he steals anything while the play is on and escapes being caught, I'll pay for the theft.

Full thirty times hath Phoebus' cart gone round / Neptune's salt wash and Tellus' orbed ground, / And thirty dozen moons with borrow'd sheen / About the world have times twelve thirties been, / Since love our hearts, and Hymen did our hands / Unite commutual in most sacred bands.

The sun god's chariot has gone round the salty sea and the round earth a full thirty times, and thirty dozen moons with borrowed light have circled the world twelve times thirty, since love joined our hearts and the god of marriage joined our hands in the most sacred bonds.

So many journeys may the sun and moon / Make us again count o'er ere love be done. / But, woe is me, you are so sick of late, / So far from cheer and from your former state, / That I distrust you. Yet, though I distrust, / Discomfort you, my lord, it nothing must: / For women's fear and love holds quantity, / In neither aught, or in extremity. / Now what my love is, proof hath made you know, / And as my love is siz'd, my fear is so. / Where love is great, the littlest doubts are fear; / Where little fears grow great, great love grows there.

May the sun and moon make as many journeys again before our love is over! But I'm so sorry, you have been so ill lately, so far from cheerful and from your old self, that I am worried about you. But although I'm worried, it mustn't upset you at all, my lord, because women's fear and love go together in equal amounts: either none of either, or too much of both. Now, you know from experience how great my love is, and my fear is as great as my love. Where love is great, the smallest doubts become fears; where little fears grow great, great love grows there.

Faith, I must leave thee, love, and shortly too: / My operant powers their functions leave to do: / And thou shalt live in this fair world behind, / Honour'd, belov'd, and haply one as kind / For husband shalt thou—

Truly, I must leave you, love, and soon too. My bodily powers are stopping working. And you will live on in this lovely world after me, honoured and loved, and perhaps one as kind will be your husband—
O confound the rest. / Such love must needs be treason in my breast. / In second husband let me be accurst! / None wed the second but who kill'd the first.
Oh, damn the rest! Such love would have to be treason in my heart. Let me be cursed if I take a second husband! No woman marries a second unless she killed the first.
The instances that second marriage move / Are base respects of thrift, but none of love. / A second time I kill my husband dead, / When second husband kisses me in bed.
The reasons that lead to a second marriage are low concerns about money, never love. I kill my dead husband a second time when a second husband kisses me in bed.

I do believe you think what now you speak; / But what we do determine, oft we break. / Purpose is but the slave to memory, / Of violent birth, but poor validity: / Which now, like fruit unripe, sticks on the tree, / But fall unshaken when they mellow be. / Most necessary 'tis that we forget / To pay ourselves what to ourselves is debt. / What to ourselves in passion we propose, / The passion ending, doth the purpose lose. / The violence of either grief or joy / Their own enactures with themselves destroy. / Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament; / Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident. / This world is not for aye; nor 'tis not strange / That even our loves should with our fortunes change, / For 'tis a question left us yet to prove, / Whether love lead fortune, or else fortune love. / The great man down, you mark his favourite flies, / The poor advanc'd makes friends of enemies; / And hitherto doth love on fortune tend: / For who not needs shall never lack a friend, / And who in want a hollow friend doth try, / Directly seasons him his enemy. / But orderly to end where I begun, / Our wills and fates do so contrary run / That our devices still are overthrown. / Our thoughts are ours, their ends none of our own. / So think thou wilt no second husband wed, / But die thy thoughts when thy first lord is dead.

I do believe you mean what you are saying now, but we often break what we decide. Intentions are only slaves to memory, strong when they are born but with little staying power. Now, like unripe fruit, they stick to the tree, but they fall without shaking once they are ripe. It is unavoidable that we forget to pay ourselves the debts we owe ourselves. What we promise ourselves in passion, we lose the purpose of once the passion ends. Violent grief or joy destroys its own actions along with itself. Where joy celebrates most, grief mourns most; grief turns to joy and joy to grief on the slightest chance. This world doesn't last forever, and it isn't strange that even our loves should change with our fortunes, because it's still an open question whether love leads fortune, or fortune love. When a great man falls, you'll see his favourite runs away; when a poor man rises, his enemies become his friends. And so far love follows fortune, because the man who doesn't need anything will never lack a friend, and the man in need who tests a false friend immediately turns him into an enemy. But to finish properly where I began, our wishes and our fates run so contrary to each other that our plans are always overthrown. Our thoughts are our own, but their outcomes are not. So you think you will never marry a second husband, but your thoughts will die when your first lord is dead.

Nor earth to me give food, nor heaven light, / Sport and repose lock from me day and night, / To desperation turn my trust and hope, / An anchor's cheer in prison be my scope, / Each opposite that blanks the face of joy, / Meet what I would have well, and it destroy! / Both here and hence pursue me lasting strife, / If, once a widow, ever I be wife.

May the earth give me no food and heaven no light, may pleasure and rest be locked away from me day and night, may my trust and hope turn to despair, may a hermit's life in prison be all I have, may everything that drains the face of joy meet what I want to go well and destroy it! In this world and the next may endless trouble pursue me, if, once a widow, I ever become a wife!
[To Ophelia] If she should break it now.
[To Ophelia] What if she broke it now!

Make you a wholesome answer. My wit's diseased. But, sir, such answer / as I can make, you shall command; or rather, as you say, my mother. / Therefore no more, but to the matter. My mother, you say,—

Give you a sensible answer. My mind is diseased. But, sir, whatever answer I can give, you can have, or rather, as you say, my mother can. So no more of this, let's get to the point. My mother, you say—

Then this is what she says: your behaviour has astonished and amazed her.

Oh, what a wonderful son, who can so astonish a mother! But is there nothing following on the heels of this mother's amazement? Tell me.
She desires to speak with you in her closet ere you go to bed.
She wants to speak to you in her private room before you go to bed.
We shall obey, were she ten times our mother. Have you any further / trade with us?
We'll obey, even if she were our mother ten times over. Do you have any more business with us?

My lord, you once loved me.

How can that be, when you have the voice of the King himself for your / succession in Denmark?

Ay, sir, but while the grass grows—the proverb is something musty.

O, the recorders. Let me see one.—To withdraw with you, why do you go / about to recover the wind of me, as if you would drive me into a toil?

O my lord, if my duty be too bold, my love is too unmannerly.
Oh, my lord, if my duty makes me too bold, it's because my love makes me forget my manners.
I do not well understand that. Will you play upon this pipe?
I don't really understand that. Will you play this pipe?

'Tis as easy as lying: govern these ventages with your finger and / thumb, give it breath with your mouth, and it will discourse most / eloquent music. Look you, these are the stops.

But these cannot I command to any utterance of harmony. I have not the / skill.

Why, look you now, how unworthy a thing you make of me! You would play / upon me; you would seem to know my stops; you would pluck out the heart / of my mystery; you would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my / compass; and there is much music, excellent voice, in this little / organ, yet cannot you make it speak. Why, look now how worthless you think I am! You would play on me. You act as if you know my stops. You want to pluck out the heart of my secret. By God's blood, do you think I'm easier to play on than a pipe? Call me whatever instrument you like: though you can fret me, you can't play on me.
My lord, the Queen would speak with you, and presently.

Do you see yonder cloud that's almost in shape of a camel?
Do you see that cloud there that's almost in the shape of a camel?

By the Mass, it does look like a camel.

'Soon' is easily said. Leave me, friends.

'Tis now the very witching time of night, / When churchyards yawn, and hell itself breathes out / Contagion to this world. Now could I drink hot blood, / And do such bitter business as the day / Would quake to look on. Soft now, to my mother. / O heart, lose not thy nature; let not ever / The soul of Nero enter this firm bosom: / Let me be cruel, not unnatural. / I will speak daggers to her, but use none; / My tongue and soul in this be hypocrites. / How in my words somever she be shent, / To give them seals never, my soul, consent.

Now it's the very time of night when witches work, when churchyards open and hell itself breathes out disease into this world. Now I could drink hot blood, and do such cruel things that the day would tremble to see them. Quiet now, I must go to my mother. Oh, heart, don't lose your natural feeling. Never let the soul of Nero, who killed his mother, enter this firm heart. Let me be cruel, but not unnatural. I'll speak daggers to her, but use none. Let my tongue and soul be hypocrites in this: however much my words shame her, my soul, never agree to turn them into actions.

I like him not, nor stands it safe with us / To let his madness range. Therefore prepare you, / I your commission will forthwith dispatch, / And he to England shall along with you. / The terms of our estate may not endure / Hazard so near us as doth hourly grow / Out of his lunacies.

I don't like him, and it isn't safe for us to let his madness run free. So get ready. I'll have your orders drawn up at once, and he will go to England with you. My position as king can't put up with dangers so close to us, which grow every hour out of his madness.
We will ourselves provide. / Most holy and religious fear it is / To keep those many many bodies safe / That live and feed upon your Majesty.
We'll get ready. It is a holy and religious concern to keep safe the many, many people who live and depend on your Majesty.

The single and peculiar life is bound / With all the strength and armour of the mind, / To keep itself from 'noyance; but much more / That spirit upon whose weal depend and rest / The lives of many. The cease of majesty / Dies not alone; but like a gulf doth draw / What's near it with it. It is a massy wheel / Fix'd on the summit of the highest mount, / To whose huge spokes ten thousand lesser things / Are mortis'd and adjoin'd; which when it falls, / Each small annexment, petty consequence, / Attends the boist'rous ruin. Never alone / Did the King sigh, but with a general groan.

Every private individual is bound, with all the strength and armour of the mind, to protect himself from harm; but much more so the man on whose well-being the lives of many depend and rest. When a king dies, he doesn't die alone, but like a whirlpool drags what's near him down with him. He is a huge wheel fixed on the top of the highest mountain, with ten thousand smaller things fitted and joined to its great spokes; when it falls, every small attachment, every little thing connected to it, goes down with the noisy ruin. The King never sighs alone, but the whole nation groans with him.
Arm you, I pray you, to this speedy voyage; / For we will fetters put upon this fear, / Which now goes too free-footed.
Prepare yourselves, please, for this quick voyage, because we will put chains on this danger, which now walks about too freely.

My lord, he's going to his mother's closet. / Behind the arras I'll convey myself / To hear the process. I'll warrant she'll tax him home, / And as you said, and wisely was it said, / 'Tis meet that some more audience than a mother, / Since nature makes them partial, should o'erhear / The speech of vantage. Fare you well, my liege, / I'll call upon you ere you go to bed, / And tell you what I know.

My lord, he's going to his mother's room. I'll hide myself behind the curtain to hear what happens. I promise you she'll tell him off thoroughly. And as you said, and it was wisely said, it's right that someone other than his mother, since mothers are naturally biased, should overhear what he says, from a good hiding place. Goodbye, my King. I'll come to you before you go to bed and tell you what I know.

O, my offence is rank, it smells to heaven; / It hath the primal eldest curse upon't,— / A brother's murder! Pray can I not, / Though inclination be as sharp as will: / My stronger guilt defeats my strong intent, / And, like a man to double business bound, / I stand in pause where I shall first begin, / And both neglect. What if this cursed hand / Were thicker than itself with brother's blood, / Is there not rain enough in the sweet heavens / To wash it white as snow? Whereto serves mercy / But to confront the visage of offence? / And what's in prayer but this twofold force, / To be forestalled ere we come to fall, / Or pardon'd being down? Then I'll look up. / My fault is past. But O, what form of prayer / Can serve my turn? Forgive me my foul murder! / That cannot be; since I am still possess'd / Of those effects for which I did the murder,— / My crown, mine own ambition, and my queen. / May one be pardon'd and retain th'offence? / In the corrupted currents of this world / Offence's gilded hand may shove by justice, / And oft 'tis seen the wicked prize itself / Buys out the law. But 'tis not so above; / There is no shuffling, there the action lies / In his true nature, and we ourselves compell'd / Even to the teeth and forehead of our faults, / To give in evidence. What then? What rests? / Try what repentance can. What can it not? / Yet what can it, when one cannot repent? / O wretched state! O bosom black as death! / O limed soul, that struggling to be free, / Art more engag'd! Help, angels! Make assay: / Bow, stubborn knees; and heart with strings of steel, / Be soft as sinews of the new-born babe. / All may be well.

Oh, my crime is foul. It stinks all the way to heaven. It carries the first and oldest curse, Cain's curse: a brother's murder. I can't pray, though my wish to is as strong as my will. My stronger guilt defeats my strong intention, and like a man bound to do two things at once, I stand hesitating over where to begin, and do neither. What if this cursed hand were coated thicker than itself with a brother's blood? Isn't there enough rain in the sweet heavens to wash it as white as snow? What is mercy for, if not to face sin head on? And what is prayer, if not this double power: to stop us before we fall, or to pardon us once we have fallen? Then I'll look up. My crime is in the past. But oh, what kind of prayer can work for me? 'Forgive me my foul murder'? That can't be, since I still have all the things I murdered for: my crown, my own ambition and my queen. Can a man be pardoned and keep what he gained from the crime? In the corrupt ways of this world, the gold-covered hand of crime can push justice aside, and often the stolen profits themselves are used to buy off the law. But it isn't like that in heaven. There's no trickery there; there the deed is seen as it really is, and we ourselves are forced to give evidence against our own faults, face to face. What then? What's left? Try what repentance can do. What can't it do? But what can it do when someone cannot repent? Oh, wretched state! Oh, heart as black as death! Oh, trapped soul, that struggles to be free and only gets more stuck! Help, angels! Make an effort. Bend, stubborn knees, and heart, with your strings of steel, be as soft as the muscles of a newborn baby! All may be well.

Now might I do it pat, now he is praying. / And now I'll do't. And so he goes to heaven; / And so am I reveng'd. That would be scann'd: / A villain kills my father, and for that / I, his sole son, do this same villain send / To heaven. O, this is hire and salary, not revenge. / He took my father grossly, full of bread, / With all his crimes broad blown, as flush as May; / And how his audit stands, who knows save heaven? / But in our circumstance and course of thought, / 'Tis heavy with him. And am I then reveng'd, / To take him in the purging of his soul, / When he is fit and season'd for his passage? No. / Up, sword, and know thou a more horrid hent: / When he is drunk asleep; or in his rage, / Or in th'incestuous pleasure of his bed, / At gaming, swearing; or about some act / That has no relish of salvation in't, / Then trip him, that his heels may kick at heaven, / And that his soul may be as damn'd and black / As hell, whereto it goes. My mother stays. / This physic but prolongs thy sickly days.

Now I could do it easily, now he's praying. And now I'll do it. And so he goes to heaven, and so I'm revenged. That needs thinking about. A villain kills my father, and for that I, his only son, send this same villain to heaven. Oh, this is like doing him a paid favour, not revenge. He killed my father when he was full of food and unprepared, with all his sins in full bloom, as lush as May. And how his account stands, who knows except heaven? But as far as we can see and think, it goes badly for him. And am I then revenged, if I kill this man while he is cleansing his soul, when he is ready and prepared for his journey? No. Back in your sheath, sword, and wait for a more horrible occasion: when he is asleep drunk, or in a rage, or enjoying the incestuous pleasures of his bed, gambling, swearing, or doing something that has no hint of salvation in it. Then trip him up, so that his heels kick at heaven and his soul is as damned and black as hell, where it is going. My mother is waiting. This medicine of prayer only lengthens your sick life.
My words fly up, my thoughts remain below. / Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
My words fly up to heaven, but my thoughts stay down here. Words without real feeling never get to heaven.

He will come straight. Look you lay home to him, / Tell him his pranks have been too broad to bear with, / And that your Grace hath screen'd and stood between / Much heat and him. I'll silence me e'en here. / Pray you be round with him.

He'll come straight away. Make sure you tell him off thoroughly. Tell him his pranks have been too outrageous to put up with, and that your Grace has protected him and stood between him and a lot of anger. I'll hide and be quiet right here. Please, be blunt with him.
I'll warrant you, Fear me not. / Withdraw, I hear him coming.
I promise you. Don't worry about me. Hide, I can hear him coming.
Hamlet, thou hast thy father much offended.
Hamlet, you have offended your father very much.
Mother, you have my father much offended.
Mother, you have offended my father very much.
Come, come, you answer with an idle tongue.
Come, come, you answer with a foolish tongue.
Go, go, you question with a wicked tongue.
Go, go, you question with a wicked tongue.
Have you forgotten who I am?
No, by the rood, not so. / You are the Queen, your husband's brother's wife, / And, would it were not so. You are my mother.
No, by the cross, not at all. You are the Queen, your husband's brother's wife, and, I wish it weren't so, you are my mother.
Nay, then I'll set those to you that can speak.
Well, then I'll send people to you who can speak to you properly.
Come, come, and sit you down, you shall not budge. / You go not till I set you up a glass / Where you may see the inmost part of you.
Come, come, sit down. You won't move. You're not going until I've set up a mirror where you can see the innermost part of yourself.
What wilt thou do? Thou wilt not murder me? / Help, help, ho!
What are you going to do? You won't murder me? Help, help, ho!
How now? A rat? [Draws] / Dead for a ducat, dead!
What's this? A rat? [Draws] Dead, I bet a ducat, dead!
O me, what hast thou done?
Oh no, what have you done?
Nay, I know not. Is it the King?
No, I don't know. Is it the King?
O what a rash and bloody deed is this!
Oh, what a rash and bloody deed this is!
A bloody deed. Almost as bad, good mother, / As kill a king and marry with his brother.
A bloody deed. Almost as bad, good mother, as killing a king and marrying his brother.

Ay, lady, 'twas my word.— / [To Polonius] Thou wretched, rash, intruding fool, farewell! / I took thee for thy better. Take thy fortune, / Thou find'st to be too busy is some danger.— / Leave wringing of your hands. Peace, sit you down, / And let me wring your heart, for so I shall, / If it be made of penetrable stuff; / If damned custom have not braz'd it so, / That it is proof and bulwark against sense.

Yes, lady, that's what I said. [To Polonius] You wretched, rash, interfering fool, goodbye! I took you for your superior. Accept your fate. You've found out that being too busy is dangerous. Stop wringing your hands. Quiet, sit down, and let me wring your heart instead, because I will, if it's made of anything that can be pierced, if damned habit hasn't turned it to brass so that it's armoured and defended against all feeling.
What have I done, that thou dar'st wag thy tongue / In noise so rude against me?
What have I done, that you dare to wag your tongue so rudely against me?

Such an act / That blurs the grace and blush of modesty, / Calls virtue hypocrite, takes off the rose / From the fair forehead of an innocent love, / And sets a blister there. Makes marriage vows / As false as dicers' oaths. O such a deed / As from the body of contraction plucks / The very soul, and sweet religion makes / A rhapsody of words. Heaven's face doth glow, / Yea this solidity and compound mass, / With tristful visage, as against the doom, / Is thought-sick at the act.

Such a deed that it stains the grace and the blush of modesty, calls virtue a hypocrite, takes the rose from the fair forehead of innocent love and puts a brand there; makes wedding vows as false as gamblers' oaths. Oh, such a deed as plucks the very soul out of the marriage contract, and turns sweet religion into a jumble of words. Heaven's face is blushing, and yes, this solid earth, with a sad face as if Judgement Day were coming, is sick at the thought of the deed.
Ay me, what act, / That roars so loud, and thunders in the index?
Oh, what deed is this, that roars so loudly and thunders even in its introduction?

Look here upon this picture, and on this, / The counterfeit presentment of two brothers. / See what a grace was seated on this brow, / Hyperion's curls, the front of Jove himself, / An eye like Mars, to threaten and command, / A station like the herald Mercury / New lighted on a heaven-kissing hill: / A combination and a form indeed, / Where every god did seem to set his seal, / To give the world assurance of a man. / This was your husband. Look you now what follows. / Here is your husband, like a mildew'd ear / Blasting his wholesome brother. Have you eyes? / Could you on this fair mountain leave to feed, / And batten on this moor? Ha! have you eyes? / You cannot call it love; for at your age / The hey-day in the blood is tame, it's humble, / And waits upon the judgement: and what judgement / Would step from this to this? Sense sure you have, / Else could you not have motion; but sure that sense / Is apoplex'd, for madness would not err / Nor sense to ecstacy was ne'er so thrall'd / But it reserv'd some quantity of choice / To serve in such a difference. What devil was't / That thus hath cozen'd you at hoodman-blind? / Eyes without feeling, feeling without sight, / Ears without hands or eyes, smelling sans all, / Or but a sickly part of one true sense / Could not so mope. O shame! where is thy blush? / Rebellious hell, / If thou canst mutine in a matron's bones, / To flaming youth let virtue be as wax, / And melt in her own fire. Proclaim no shame / When the compulsive ardour gives the charge, / Since frost itself as actively doth burn, / And reason panders will.

Look here at this picture, and at this one, the painted likenesses of two brothers. See what grace was in this face: the curls of the sun god Hyperion, the forehead of Jove himself, an eye like Mars, the god of war, to threaten and command, a stance like the messenger god Mercury just landed on a hill that kisses the sky; a combination and a shape indeed where every god seemed to put his stamp, to show the world what a real man is. This was your husband. Look now at what comes next. Here is your husband, like a diseased ear of corn infecting his healthy brother. Do you have eyes? Could you stop feeding on this fine mountain and gorge yourself on this barren moor? Ha! Do you have eyes? You can't call it love, because at your age the excitement in the blood is tamed, it's humble, and it obeys judgement. And what judgement would step down from this to this? You must have senses, or you couldn't move. But those senses must be paralysed, because even madness wouldn't make that mistake, and the senses were never so enslaved by madness that they didn't keep some power of choice to see such a difference. What devil tricked you like this in a game of blind man's buff? Eyes without touch, touch without sight, ears without hands or eyes, smell without anything else, even one sickly part of a single true sense could not be so stupid. Oh, shame! Where is your blush? Rebellious hell, if you can stir up revolt in a middle-aged woman's bones, then let virtue be like wax for passionate youth and melt in its own fire. Don't call it shameful when hot young desire attacks, since frost itself burns just as fiercely, and reason acts as a pimp for lust.
O Hamlet, speak no more. / Thou turn'st mine eyes into my very soul, / And there I see such black and grained spots / As will not leave their tinct.
Oh, Hamlet, say no more! You turn my eyes inward to my very soul, and there I see such black, deep-dyed stains that will never lose their colour.
Nay, but to live / In the rank sweat of an enseamed bed, / Stew'd in corruption, honeying and making love / Over the nasty sty.
No, but to live in the stinking sweat of a greasy bed, stewed in corruption, sweet-talking and making love in the filthy pigsty—
O speak to me no more; / These words like daggers enter in mine ears; / No more, sweet Hamlet.
Oh, say no more to me! These words go into my ears like daggers. No more, sweet Hamlet!

A murderer and a villain; / A slave that is not twentieth part the tithe / Of your precedent lord. A vice of kings, / A cutpurse of the empire and the rule, / That from a shelf the precious diadem stole / And put it in his pocket!

A murderer and a villain, a slave who is not a twentieth of a tenth of your previous husband, a clown of a king, a pickpocket of the empire and its power, who stole the precious crown from a shelf and put it in his pocket!
A king of shreds and patches!—
A king of rags and patches!
Save me and hover o'er me with your wings, / You heavenly guards! What would your gracious figure?
Save me and spread your wings over me, you heavenly guards! What does your gracious figure want?
Do you not come your tardy son to chide, / That, laps'd in time and passion, lets go by / The important acting of your dread command? / O say!
Haven't you come to scold your slow son, who has let time and passion slip by and fails to carry out your terrible command? Oh, say!

Do not forget. This visitation / Is but to whet thy almost blunted purpose. / But look, amazement on thy mother sits. / O step between her and her fighting soul. / Conceit in weakest bodies strongest works. / Speak to her, Hamlet.

Don't forget. This visit is only to sharpen your purpose, which is almost blunted. But look, your mother is overwhelmed with amazement. Oh, step in between her and her struggling soul. Imagination works most strongly on the weakest bodies. Speak to her, Hamlet.
How is it with you, lady?

Alas, how is't with you, / That you do bend your eye on vacancy, / And with the incorporal air do hold discourse? / Forth at your eyes your spirits wildly peep, / And, as the sleeping soldiers in the alarm, / Your bedded hairs, like life in excrements, / Start up and stand an end. O gentle son, / Upon the heat and flame of thy distemper / Sprinkle cool patience. Whereon do you look?

Oh, how are you, that you stare at empty space and hold a conversation with the bodiless air? Your spirits peep wildly out of your eyes, and your hair, which was lying flat, jumps up and stands on end as if it were alive, like sleeping soldiers when the alarm sounds. Oh, gentle son, sprinkle cool patience on the heat and flame of your illness. What are you looking at?

On him, on him! Look you how pale he glares, / His form and cause conjoin'd, preaching to stones, / Would make them capable.—Do not look upon me, / Lest with this piteous action you convert / My stern effects. Then what I have to do / Will want true colour; tears perchance for blood.

At him, at him! Look how pale he is, staring! His appearance and his cause together could make stones listen if he preached to them. Don't look at me, in case this pitiful look of yours turns my stern purpose aside. Then what I have to do won't be done in its true colour: tears, perhaps, instead of blood.
To whom do you speak this?
Who are you saying this to?
Nothing at all; yet all that is I see.
Nothing at all, and yet I see everything that's there.
Why, look you there! look how it steals away! / My father, in his habit as he liv'd! / Look where he goes even now out at the portal.
Why, look there! Look how it creeps away! My father, in the clothes he wore when he was alive! Look, he's going out through the door right now!
This is the very coinage of your brain. / This bodiless creation ecstasy / Is very cunning in.
This is just something your brain has made up. Madness is very skilful at inventing ghosts like this.

Ecstasy! / My pulse as yours doth temperately keep time, / And makes as healthful music. It is not madness / That I have utter'd. Bring me to the test, / And I the matter will re-word; which madness / Would gambol from. Mother, for love of grace, / Lay not that flattering unction to your soul / That not your trespass, but my madness speaks. / It will but skin and film the ulcerous place, / Whilst rank corruption, mining all within, / Infects unseen. Confess yourself to heaven, / Repent what's past, avoid what is to come; / And do not spread the compost on the weeds, / To make them ranker. Forgive me this my virtue; / For in the fatness of these pursy times / Virtue itself of vice must pardon beg, / Yea, curb and woo for leave to do him good.

Madness! My pulse beats as steadily as yours and makes just as healthy a music. It isn't madness that I have spoken. Test me, and I'll repeat everything I said word for word, which madness would leap away from. Mother, for the love of God, don't put that comforting ointment on your soul, telling yourself it is my madness speaking and not your sin. It will only put a skin over the infected place while foul corruption eats away everything inside it unseen. Confess yourself to heaven. Repent what is past. Avoid what is to come, and don't spread manure on the weeds to make them grow stronger. Forgive me for my virtue, because in these fat, bloated times virtue itself has to beg vice for pardon, yes, bow and beg for permission to do it good.
O Hamlet, thou hast cleft my heart in twain.
Oh, Hamlet, you have split my heart in two.

O throw away the worser part of it, / And live the purer with the other half. / Good night. But go not to mine uncle's bed. / Assume a virtue, if you have it not. / That monster custom, who all sense doth eat, / Of habits evil, is angel yet in this, / That to the use of actions fair and good / He likewise gives a frock or livery / That aptly is put on. Refrain tonight, / And that shall lend a kind of easiness / To the next abstinence. The next more easy; / For use almost can change the stamp of nature, / And either curb the devil, or throw him out / With wondrous potency. Once more, good night, / And when you are desirous to be bles'd, / I'll blessing beg of you. For this same lord / [Pointing to Polonius] / I do repent; but heaven hath pleas'd it so, / To punish me with this, and this with me, / That I must be their scourge and minister. / I will bestow him, and will answer well / The death I gave him. So again, good night. / I must be cruel, only to be kind: / Thus bad begins, and worse remains behind. / One word more, good lady.

Oh, throw away the worse part of it, and live more purely with the other half. Good night. But don't go to my uncle's bed. Act as if you are virtuous, even if you aren't. That monster habit, which eats up all awareness of evil habits, is still an angel in this way: it also gives us a uniform for good and fair actions that fits easily. Hold back tonight, and that will make the next time you hold back a bit easier; the next time easier still, because habit can almost change our nature, and either control the devil or throw him out with wonderful power. Once more, good night, and when you want to be blessed by God, I'll ask you to bless me. [Pointing to Polonius] As for this lord, I'm sorry. But heaven has chosen to punish me with this and him with me, so that I must be heaven's whip and its agent. I'll get rid of the body and take responsibility for killing him. So again, good night. I must be cruel only to be kind. This is a bad beginning, and worse is still to come. One more word, good lady.
