Not this, by no means, that I bid you do: / Let the bloat King tempt you again to bed, / Pinch wanton on your cheek, call you his mouse, / And let him, for a pair of reechy kisses, / Or paddling in your neck with his damn'd fingers, / Make you to ravel all this matter out, / That I essentially am not in madness, / But mad in craft. 'Twere good you let him know, / For who that's but a queen, fair, sober, wise, / Would from a paddock, from a bat, a gib, / Such dear concernings hide? Who would do so? / No, in despite of sense and secrecy, / Unpeg the basket on the house's top, / Let the birds fly, and like the famous ape, / To try conclusions, in the basket creep / And break your own neck down.

Certainly not what I tell you to do: let the bloated King tempt you to bed again, pinch your cheek lustfully, call you his mouse, and for a couple of stinking kisses, or by fondling your neck with his damned fingers, get you to reveal all this, that I am not really mad, only mad on purpose. It would be good to let him know, because what queen, who is beautiful, sensible and wise, would hide such important matters from a toad, a bat, a tomcat? Who would do that? No, forget sense and secrecy: open the basket on the roof, let the birds fly out, and, like the famous ape, climb into the basket to test it and fall and break your own neck.
Be thou assur'd, if words be made of breath, / And breath of life, I have no life to breathe / What thou hast said to me.
You can be sure, if words are made of breath and breath of life, that I have no life to breathe what you have said to me.
I must to England, you know that?
I must go to England. Do you know that?
Alack, / I had forgot. 'Tis so concluded on.
Oh no, I had forgotten. It's been decided.

There's letters seal'd: and my two schoolfellows, / Whom I will trust as I will adders fang'd,— / They bear the mandate, they must sweep my way / And marshal me to knavery. Let it work; / For 'tis the sport to have the enginer / Hoist with his own petard, and 't shall go hard / But I will delve one yard below their mines / And blow them at the moon. O, 'tis most sweet, / When in one line two crafts directly meet. / This man shall set me packing. / I'll lug the guts into the neighbour room. / Mother, good night. Indeed, this counsellor / Is now most still, most secret, and most grave, / Who was in life a foolish prating knave. / Come, sir, to draw toward an end with you. / Good night, mother.

There are sealed letters, and my two schoolfellows, whom I'll trust as much as poisonous snakes, carry the orders. They are to clear the way for me and lead me into some trap. Let it happen, because it's fun to see the bomb-maker blown up with his own bomb. It will be hard luck if I don't dig a yard under their tunnels and blow them up to the moon. Oh, it's very sweet when two plots meet head on. This man will make me pack up and leave in a hurry. I'll drag the guts into the next room. Mother, good night. This adviser really is very still now, very secretive and very serious, who in life was a foolish, chattering rogue. Come, sir, let's finish with you. Good night, mother.
There's matter in these sighs. These profound heaves / You must translate; 'tis fit we understand them. / Where is your son?
There's something behind these sighs. You must explain these deep heavings; it's right that we understand them. Where is your son?
Bestow this place on us a little while.
Leave us alone here for a little while.
Ah, my good lord, what have I seen tonight!
Oh, my good lord, what I have seen tonight!

Mad as the sea and wind, when both contend / Which is the mightier. In his lawless fit / Behind the arras hearing something stir, / Whips out his rapier, cries 'A rat, a rat!' / And in this brainish apprehension kills / The unseen good old man.

As mad as the sea and the wind when they are fighting over which is stronger. In his wild fit, hearing something move behind the curtain, he whips out his sword and shouts 'A rat, a rat!', and in this crazed imagining he kills the good old man he couldn't see.

O heavy deed! / It had been so with us, had we been there. / His liberty is full of threats to all; / To you yourself, to us, to everyone. / Alas, how shall this bloody deed be answer'd? / It will be laid to us, whose providence / Should have kept short, restrain'd, and out of haunt / This mad young man. But so much was our love / We would not understand what was most fit, / But like the owner of a foul disease, / To keep it from divulging, let it feed / Even on the pith of life. Where is he gone?

Oh, terrible deed! It would have happened to us if we had been there. His freedom is a threat to everyone, to you yourself, to us, to all. Oh dear, how shall we explain this bloody deed? It will be blamed on us, who should have had the foresight to keep this mad young man on a short lead, restrained and away from people. But our love was so great that we wouldn't see what was the right thing to do, and like someone with a foul disease who keeps it hidden, we let it feed on the very core of life. Where has he gone?
To draw apart the body he hath kill'd, / O'er whom his very madness, like some ore / Among a mineral of metals base, / Shows itself pure. He weeps for what is done.
To drag away the body he has killed. Over it his madness itself, like a vein of gold in a mine of worthless metals, shows that it is pure: he is weeping for what he has done.

O Gertrude, come away! / The sun no sooner shall the mountains touch / But we will ship him hence, and this vile deed / We must with all our majesty and skill / Both countenance and excuse.—Ho, Guildenstern!

Oh, Gertrude, come away! As soon as the sun touches the mountains, we'll ship him away from here, and we must use all our royal authority and skill both to stand behind this vile deed and to excuse it. Hey, Guildenstern!

Friends both, go join you with some further aid: / Hamlet in madness hath Polonius slain, / And from his mother's closet hath he dragg'd him. / Go seek him out, speak fair, and bring the body / Into the chapel. I pray you haste in this.

Friends, both of you go and get some more help. Hamlet in his madness has killed Polonius, and he has dragged him from his mother's room. Go and find him, speak politely to him, and bring the body into the chapel. Please hurry with this.

Come, Gertrude, we'll call up our wisest friends, / And let them know both what we mean to do / And what's untimely done, so haply slander, / Whose whisper o'er the world's diameter, / As level as the cannon to his blank, / Transports his poison'd shot, may miss our name, / And hit the woundless air. O, come away! / My soul is full of discord and dismay.

Come, Gertrude, we'll call together our wisest friends and tell them both what we intend to do and what has been done so unfortunately. Then perhaps slander, whose whisper carries its poisoned shot right across the world as straight as a cannon to its target, may miss our name and hit only the air, which can't be wounded. Oh, come away! My soul is full of confusion and dread.
What noise? Who calls on Hamlet? O, here they come.
What's that noise? Who's calling Hamlet? Oh, here they come.
What have you done, my lord, with the dead body?
What have you done with the dead body, my lord?
Compounded it with dust, whereto 'tis kin.
Mixed it with the dust, which it is related to.
Tell us where 'tis, that we may take it thence, / And bear it to the chapel.
Tell us where it is, so that we can take it from there and carry it to the chapel.
That I can keep your counsel, and not mine own. Besides, to be demanded / of a sponge—what replication should be made by the son of a king?
That I can keep your secrets and not my own. Besides, to be questioned by a sponge! What answer should a king's son give to that?
Take you me for a sponge, my lord?
Do you take me for a sponge, my lord?

Ay, sir; that soaks up the King's countenance, his rewards, his / authorities. But such officers do the King best service in the end: he / keeps them, like an ape, in the corner of his jaw; first mouthed, to be / last swallowed: when he needs what you have gleaned, it is but / squeezing you, and, sponge, you shall be dry again.

Yes, sir, one that soaks up the King's favour, his rewards, his power. But officials like you do the King the best service in the end. He keeps them in the corner of his mouth like an ape keeps food, first put in, last swallowed. When he needs what you have collected, he only has to squeeze you, and, sponge, you'll be dry again.
I understand you not, my lord.
I don't understand you, my lord.
I am glad of it. A knavish speech sleeps in a foolish ear.
I'm glad of it. A clever, wicked speech is wasted on a foolish ear.
My lord, you must tell us where the body is and go with us to the King.
My lord, you must tell us where the body is and come with us to the King.
The body is with the King, but the King is not with the body. The King / is a thing—
The body is with the King, but the King isn't with the body. The King is a thing—
Of nothing. Bring me to him. Hide fox, and all after.
Of no importance. Take me to him. Hide, fox, and everyone after him!

I have sent to seek him and to find the body. / How dangerous is it that this man goes loose! / Yet must not we put the strong law on him: / He's lov'd of the distracted multitude, / Who like not in their judgement, but their eyes; / And where 'tis so, th'offender's scourge is weigh'd, / But never the offence. To bear all smooth and even, / This sudden sending him away must seem / Deliberate pause. Diseases desperate grown / By desperate appliance are reliev'd, / Or not at all.

I've sent people to look for him and find the body. How dangerous it is that this man is free! But we mustn't use the full force of the law on him. He is loved by the confused common people, who judge by what they see, not by reason, and when that's the case, they weigh up the offender's punishment, but never the offence. To keep everything smooth and calm, sending him away suddenly like this must look like a carefully considered decision. Diseases that have become desperate can only be cured by desperate remedies, or not at all.
Where the dead body is bestow'd, my lord, / We cannot get from him.
We can't get him to tell us where the dead body is hidden, my lord.
Without, my lord, guarded, to know your pleasure.
Outside, my lord, under guard, waiting to hear what you want.
Ho, Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.
Hey, Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.

Not where he eats, but where he is eaten. A certain convocation of / politic worms are e'en at him. Your worm is your only emperor for diet. / We fat all creatures else to fat us, and we fat ourselves for maggots. / Your fat king and your lean beggar is but variable service,—two dishes, / but to one table. That's the end.

Not where he is eating, but where he is being eaten. A certain assembly of political worms is busy with him right now. The worm is the true emperor when it comes to food. We fatten all other creatures to fatten ourselves, and we fatten ourselves for maggots. A fat king and a thin beggar are just different courses, two dishes on the same table. That's how it ends.
A man may fish with the worm that hath eat of a king, and eat of the / fish that hath fed of that worm.
A man may go fishing with the worm that has eaten a king, and eat the fish that has fed on that worm.
What dost thou mean by this?
What do you mean by this?
Nothing but to show you how a king may go a progress through the guts / of a beggar.
Nothing, except to show you how a king can make a royal tour through the guts of a beggar.

In heaven. Send thither to see. If your messenger find him not there, / seek him i' th'other place yourself. But indeed, if you find him not / within this month, you shall nose him as you go up the stairs into the / lobby.

In heaven. Send someone there to look. If your messenger doesn't find him there, look for him in the other place yourself. But really, if you don't find him within a month, you'll smell him as you go up the stairs into the hall.
[To some Attendants] Go seek him there.
[To some Attendants] Go and look for him there.
He will stay till you come.

Hamlet, this deed, for thine especial safety,— / Which we do tender, as we dearly grieve / For that which thou hast done,—must send thee hence / With fiery quickness. Therefore prepare thyself; / The bark is ready, and the wind at help, / Th'associates tend, and everything is bent / For England.

Hamlet, for your own special safety, which we care about as much as we deeply grieve over what you have done, this deed means you must leave here as fast as fire. So get ready. The ship is ready and the wind is helpful, your companions are waiting and everything is set for England.
So is it, if thou knew'st our purposes.
So it is, if you knew our intentions.
I see a cherub that sees them. But, come; for England! Farewell, dear / mother.
I see an angel who sees them. But come, off to England! Goodbye, dear mother.
My mother. Father and mother is man and wife; man and wife is one / flesh; and so, my mother. Come, for England.
My mother. Father and mother are man and wife, man and wife are one flesh, and so, my mother. Come, off to England!
Follow him at foot. Tempt him with speed aboard; / Delay it not; I'll have him hence tonight. / Away, for everything is seal'd and done / That else leans on th'affair. Pray you make haste.
Follow close behind him. Get him on board quickly. Don't delay it. I want him gone tonight. Go, because everything else to do with this business is sealed and done. Please hurry.

And England, if my love thou hold'st at aught,— / As my great power thereof may give thee sense, / Since yet thy cicatrice looks raw and red / After the Danish sword, and thy free awe / Pays homage to us,—thou mayst not coldly set / Our sovereign process, which imports at full, / By letters conjuring to that effect, / The present death of Hamlet. Do it, England; / For like the hectic in my blood he rages, / And thou must cure me. Till I know 'tis done, / Howe'er my haps, my joys were ne'er begun.

And King of England, if you value my love at all, as my great power should make you do, since your scar from the Danish sword still looks raw and red and you pay us respect out of your own free fear, you can't ignore our royal command, which is set out fully in letters urging this: the immediate death of Hamlet. Do it, England, because he rages in my blood like a fever, and you must cure me. Until I know it's done, whatever my luck, my happiness can never begin.

Go, Captain, from me greet the Danish king. / Tell him that by his license, Fortinbras / Craves the conveyance of a promis'd march / Over his kingdom. You know the rendezvous. / If that his Majesty would aught with us, / We shall express our duty in his eye; / And let him know so.

Go, Captain, and greet the Danish king for me. Tell him that, with his permission, Fortinbras asks for the promised safe passage of his army across his kingdom. You know where we are to meet. If his Majesty wants anything from us, we'll pay our respects to him in person; tell him that.
Good sir, whose powers are these?
Good sir, whose army is this?
How purpos'd, sir, I pray you?
Where is it going, sir, may I ask?
The nephew to old Norway, Fortinbras.
The old King of Norway's nephew, Fortinbras.
Goes it against the main of Poland, sir, / Or for some frontier?
Is it going against the heart of Poland, sir, or some border area?

Truly to speak, and with no addition, / We go to gain a little patch of ground / That hath in it no profit but the name. / To pay five ducats, five, I would not farm it; / Nor will it yield to Norway or the Pole / A ranker rate, should it be sold in fee.

To tell the truth, without exaggerating, we're going to win a little patch of ground that has nothing to be gained from it except the name. I wouldn't rent it for five ducats, five. And neither Norway nor Poland would get a higher price for it if they sold it outright.
Why, then the Polack never will defend it.
Why, then the Poles will never defend it.
Yes, they will. It's already got soldiers in it.

Two thousand souls and twenty thousand ducats / Will not debate the question of this straw! / This is th'imposthume of much wealth and peace, / That inward breaks, and shows no cause without / Why the man dies. I humbly thank you, sir.

Two thousand lives and twenty thousand ducats won't be enough to settle the argument over this bit of straw! This is the abscess that comes from too much wealth and peace, which bursts inside and shows nothing on the outside to explain why the man dies. I humbly thank you, sir.
Will't please you go, my lord?
Will you come now, my lord?
I'll be with you straight. Go a little before.
I'll be with you in a moment. Go on a little ahead.

How all occasions do inform against me, / And spur my dull revenge. What is a man / If his chief good and market of his time / Be but to sleep and feed? A beast, no more. / Sure he that made us with such large discourse, / Looking before and after, gave us not / That capability and godlike reason / To fust in us unus'd. Now whether it be / Bestial oblivion, or some craven scruple / Of thinking too precisely on th'event,— / A thought which, quarter'd, hath but one part wisdom / And ever three parts coward,—I do not know / Why yet I live to say this thing's to do, / Sith I have cause, and will, and strength, and means / To do't. Examples gross as earth exhort me, / Witness this army of such mass and charge, / Led by a delicate and tender prince, / Whose spirit, with divine ambition puff'd, / Makes mouths at the invisible event, / Exposing what is mortal and unsure / To all that fortune, death, and danger dare, / Even for an eggshell. Rightly to be great / Is not to stir without great argument, / But greatly to find quarrel in a straw / When honour's at the stake. How stand I then, / That have a father kill'd, a mother stain'd, / Excitements of my reason and my blood, / And let all sleep, while to my shame I see / The imminent death of twenty thousand men / That, for a fantasy and trick of fame, / Go to their graves like beds, fight for a plot / Whereon the numbers cannot try the cause, / Which is not tomb enough and continent / To hide the slain? O, from this time forth, / My thoughts be bloody or be nothing worth.

How everything that happens accuses me and spurs on my slow revenge! What is a man, if the main good and use of his time is only to sleep and eat? A beast, nothing more. Surely the one who made us with such a great power of reasoning, able to look forward and back, didn't give us that ability and godlike reason to go mouldy in us unused. Now, whether it is animal forgetfulness or some cowardly worry from thinking too carefully about the outcome, a thought which, cut into four, has only one part wisdom and always three parts cowardice, I don't know why I am still alive to say 'This must be done', when I have the reason, the will, the strength and the means to do it. Examples as big as the earth urge me on. Look at this army, so large and so expensive, led by a delicate, young prince whose spirit, swollen with divine ambition, pulls faces at the unknown outcome, exposing what is mortal and uncertain to everything that fortune, death and danger can do, all for an eggshell. To be truly great is not to act without a great cause, but to find a great reason to fight over a straw when honour is at stake. Where does that leave me, then, who have a murdered father and a disgraced mother, things that should rouse my reason and my passion, and yet I let it all sleep, while to my shame I see twenty thousand men about to die, who for a fantasy and a trick of fame go to their graves as if to bed, fighting for a plot of land that isn't big enough for all the armies to fight on, and isn't even a big enough tomb to hold the dead? Oh, from now on, let my thoughts be bloody, or be worth nothing!
I will not speak with her.
She is importunate, indeed distract. / Her mood will needs be pitied.
She insists, and she really is out of her mind. Her state deserves pity.

She speaks much of her father; says she hears / There's tricks i' th' world, and hems, and beats her heart, / Spurns enviously at straws, speaks things in doubt, / That carry but half sense. Her speech is nothing, / Yet the unshaped use of it doth move / The hearers to collection; they aim at it, / And botch the words up fit to their own thoughts, / Which, as her winks, and nods, and gestures yield them, / Indeed would make one think there might be thought, / Though nothing sure, yet much unhappily. / 'Twere good she were spoken with, for she may strew / Dangerous conjectures in ill-breeding minds.

She talks a lot about her father, says she hears there is trickery in the world, coughs and beats her breast, kicks angrily at straws, and says things that are unclear and only half make sense. Her words mean nothing, and yet their confused shape makes listeners try to piece them together. They guess at her meaning and patch the words up to fit their own thoughts, and her winks, nods and gestures do make you think there might be some meaning behind them, nothing certain, but something very unhappy. It would be good to speak with her, because she may spread dangerous suspicions in minds that breed trouble.
To my sick soul, as sin's true nature is, / Each toy seems prologue to some great amiss. / So full of artless jealousy is guilt, / It spills itself in fearing to be spilt.

[Aside] To my sick soul, as is the true nature of sin, every little thing seems the start of some great disaster. Guilt is so full of clumsy suspicion that it gives itself away by being afraid of giving itself away.
Where is the beauteous Majesty of Denmark?
Where is the beautiful Queen of Denmark?
[Sings] / How should I your true love know / From another one? / By his cockle hat and staff / And his sandal shoon.
[Sings] How will I know your true love from another one? By his pilgrim's hat with its shell, his staff and his sandals.
Alas, sweet lady, what imports this song?
Oh, sweet lady, what does this song mean?
Say you? Nay, pray you mark. / [Sings] / He is dead and gone, lady, / He is dead and gone, / At his head a grass green turf, / At his heels a stone.
What did you say? No, please listen. [Sings] He is dead and gone, lady, he is dead and gone. At his head is green turf, at his feet a stone.
Pray you mark. / [Sings] / White his shroud as the mountain snow.
Please listen. [Sings] His shroud was as white as the mountain snow—
Oh, look at this, my lord!
[Sings] / Larded all with sweet flowers; / Which bewept to the grave did not go / With true-love showers.
[Sings] Covered all over with sweet flowers, which went to the grave without being wept on by true love's showers of tears.
Well, God dild you! They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we / know what we are, but know not what we may be. God be at your table!
Well, God reward you! They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but not what we may become. God be at your table!
She is brooding on her father.

Pray you, let's have no words of this; but when they ask you what it / means, say you this: / [Sings] / Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's day, / All in the morning betime, / And I a maid at your window, / To be your Valentine. / Then up he rose and donn'd his clothes, / And dupp'd the chamber door, / Let in the maid, that out a maid / Never departed more.

Please, let's not talk about this, but when they ask you what it means, say this: [Sings] Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's Day, early in the morning, and I'm a girl at your window, to be your Valentine. Then up he got and put his clothes on, and opened the bedroom door, and let the girl in, who never left it a girl again.

Indeed la, without an oath, I'll make an end on't. / [Sings] / By Gis and by Saint Charity, / Alack, and fie for shame! / Young men will do't if they come to't; / By Cock, they are to blame. / Quoth she, before you tumbled me, / You promis'd me to wed. / So would I ha' done, by yonder sun, / An thou hadst not come to my bed.

Yes, really, without swearing, I'll finish it. [Sings] By Jesus and by holy charity, oh no, and shame on them! Young men will do it if they get the chance; by God, they are to blame. She said, 'Before you tumbled me, you promised to marry me.' He answers: 'I would have done it, by that sun up there, if you hadn't come to my bed.'
How long hath she been thus?
How long has she been like this?

I hope all will be well. We must be patient. But I cannot choose but / weep, to think they would lay him i' th' cold ground. My brother shall / know of it. And so I thank you for your good counsel. Come, my coach! / Good night, ladies; good night, sweet ladies; good night, good night.

I hope all will be well. We must be patient. But I can't help crying when I think that they laid him in the cold ground. My brother will hear about it. And so I thank you for your good advice. Come, my coach! Good night, ladies. Good night, sweet ladies. Good night, good night.
Follow her close; give her good watch, I pray you.
Follow her closely. Keep a good watch on her, please.

O, this is the poison of deep grief; it springs / All from her father's death. O Gertrude, Gertrude, / When sorrows come, they come not single spies, / But in battalions. First, her father slain; / Next, your son gone; and he most violent author / Of his own just remove; the people muddied, / Thick, and unwholesome in their thoughts and whispers / For good Polonius' death; and we have done but greenly / In hugger-mugger to inter him. Poor Ophelia / Divided from herself and her fair judgement, / Without the which we are pictures or mere beasts. / Last, and as much containing as all these, / Her brother is in secret come from France, / Feeds on his wonder, keeps himself in clouds, / And wants not buzzers to infect his ear / With pestilent speeches of his father's death, / Wherein necessity, of matter beggar'd, / Will nothing stick our person to arraign / In ear and ear. O my dear Gertrude, this, / Like to a murdering piece, in many places / Gives me superfluous death.

Oh, this is the poison of deep grief. It all comes from her father's death. Oh, Gertrude, Gertrude, when sorrows come, they don't come like single spies, but in whole battalions. First her father killed; next your son gone, and he himself the violent cause of his own rightful exile; the people stirred up, muddy and unhealthy in their thoughts and whispers about good Polonius's death. And we have acted foolishly in burying him in secret. Poor Ophelia, cut off from herself and her good judgement, without which we are only pictures or mere animals. Last, and as serious as all of these together, her brother has come back secretly from France. He feeds on his suspicions, keeps himself hidden in clouds, and has no shortage of gossips to infect his ear with poisonous stories about his father's death, in which, since they don't know the facts, they won't hesitate to accuse me from ear to ear. Oh, my dear Gertrude, this, like a cannon firing scattered shot, hits me in many places and kills me more times than I need.
Where are my Switzers? Let them guard the door.
Where are my Swiss guards? Let them guard the door.

Save yourself, my lord. / The ocean, overpeering of his list, / Eats not the flats with more impetuous haste / Than young Laertes, in a riotous head, / O'erbears your offices. The rabble call him lord, / And, as the world were now but to begin, / Antiquity forgot, custom not known, / The ratifiers and props of every word, / They cry 'Choose we! Laertes shall be king!' / Caps, hands, and tongues applaud it to the clouds, / 'Laertes shall be king, Laertes king.'

Save yourself, my lord. The ocean, rising over its limits, doesn't swallow up the shore with more violent speed than young Laertes, at the head of a rioting crowd, is overpowering your officers. The mob call him lord, and as if the world were only just beginning, with tradition forgotten and custom unknown, though these are what confirm and support every title, they shout 'We choose! Laertes shall be king!' Caps, hands and tongues cheer it to the clouds: 'Laertes shall be king! Laertes king!'
How cheerfully on the false trail they cry. / O, this is counter, you false Danish dogs.
How happily they bark on the wrong trail! Oh, you're running the wrong way, you false Danish dogs!
Where is this king?—Sirs, stand you all without.
Where is this king? Sirs, all of you stay outside.
I pray you, give me leave.
I thank you. Keep the door. O thou vile king, / Give me my father.
Thank you. Guard the door. Oh, you vile king, give me back my father!
That drop of blood that's calm proclaims me bastard; / Cries cuckold to my father, brands the harlot / Even here between the chaste unsmirched brow / Of my true mother.
Any drop of blood in me that's calm proclaims I'm a bastard, calls my father a cuckold, and brands my true mother a whore right here on her chaste, unstained forehead.

What is the cause, Laertes, / That thy rebellion looks so giant-like?— / Let him go, Gertrude. Do not fear our person. / There's such divinity doth hedge a king, / That treason can but peep to what it would, / Acts little of his will.—Tell me, Laertes, / Why thou art thus incens'd.—Let him go, Gertrude:— / Speak, man.

What is the reason, Laertes, that your rebellion looks so gigantic? Let him go, Gertrude. Don't worry about our safety. A king is protected by such divine power that treason can only peep at what it wants and achieves little of its aim. Tell me, Laertes, why you are so angry. Let him go, Gertrude. Speak, man.
Let him ask all he wants.

How came he dead? I'll not be juggled with. / To hell, allegiance! Vows, to the blackest devil! / Conscience and grace, to the profoundest pit! / I dare damnation. To this point I stand, / That both the worlds, I give to negligence, / Let come what comes; only I'll be reveng'd / Most throughly for my father.

How did he die? I won't be tricked. To hell with loyalty! Vows, go to the blackest devil! Conscience and grace, to the deepest pit! I dare to be damned. This is where I stand: I don't care about this world or the next. Let whatever happens happen. I'll just get revenge, completely, for my father.
My will, not all the world. / And for my means, I'll husband them so well, / They shall go far with little.
My own will, not the whole world. And as for my resources, I'll use them so carefully that they will go far with little.
Good Laertes, / If you desire to know the certainty / Of your dear father's death, is't writ in your revenge / That, sweepstake, you will draw both friend and foe, / Winner and loser?

Good Laertes, if you want to know the truth about your dear father's death, is it part of your revenge that, like a gambler sweeping up all the stakes, you will take both friend and enemy, winner and loser?
Do you want to know who they are, then?
To his good friends thus wide I'll ope my arms; / And, like the kind life-rendering pelican, / Repast them with my blood.
To his good friends I'll open my arms this wide, and like the kind pelican, which feeds its young with its own blood, I'll feed them with mine.

Why, now you speak / Like a good child and a true gentleman. / That I am guiltless of your father's death, / And am most sensibly in grief for it, / It shall as level to your judgement 'pear / As day does to your eye.
Why, now you speak like a good son and a true gentleman. That I am innocent of your father's death and grieve for it most deeply, will become as plain to your judgement as daylight is to your eyes.
How now! What noise is that?

O heat, dry up my brains. Tears seven times salt, / Burn out the sense and virtue of mine eye. / By heaven, thy madness shall be paid by weight, / Till our scale turn the beam. O rose of May! / Dear maid, kind sister, sweet Ophelia! / O heavens, is't possible a young maid's wits / Should be as mortal as an old man's life? / Nature is fine in love, and where 'tis fine, / It sends some precious instance of itself / After the thing it loves.

Oh, heat, dry up my brain! Tears seven times salty, burn out the feeling and power of my eyes! By heaven, your madness will be paid for in full, until our side of the scales outweighs the other. Oh, rose of May! Dear girl, kind sister, sweet Ophelia! Oh, heavens! Is it possible that a young girl's mind can be as easily killed as an old man's life? Human nature is refined by love, and when it is, it sends some precious part of itself after the thing it loves.
[Sings] / They bore him barefac'd on the bier, / Hey non nonny, nonny, hey nonny / And on his grave rain'd many a tear.— / Fare you well, my dove!
[Sings] They carried him on the coffin with his face uncovered, hey non nonny, nonny, hey nonny, and on his grave fell many tears. Goodbye, my dove!
Hadst thou thy wits, and didst persuade revenge, / It could not move thus.
If you were sane and urged me to take revenge, it couldn't move me as much as this.
You must sing 'Down a-down, and you call him a-down-a.' O, how the / wheel becomes it! It is the false steward that stole his master's / daughter.
You must sing 'Down a-down', and you call him 'a-down-a'. Oh, how well the refrain fits! It's about the false steward who stole his master's daughter.
This nonsense means more than sense.
There's rosemary, that's for remembrance; pray love, remember. And / there is pansies, that's for thoughts.
There's rosemary, that's for remembrance. Please, love, remember. And there are pansies; that's for thoughts.
A document in madness, thoughts and remembrance fitted.
A lesson in madness: thoughts and remembrance put together.

There's fennel for you, and columbines. There's rue for you; and here's / some for me. We may call it herb of grace o' Sundays. O you must wear / your rue with a difference. There's a daisy. I would give you some / violets, but they wither'd all when my father died. They say he made a / good end. / [Sings] / For bonny sweet Robin is all my joy.

There's fennel for you, and columbines. There's rue for you, and here's some for me. We can call it the herb of grace on Sundays. Oh, you must wear your rue for a different reason. There's a daisy. I'd give you some violets, but they all withered when my father died. They say he died well. [Sings] For bonny sweet Robin is all my joy.
Thought and affliction, passion, hell itself / She turns to favour and to prettiness.
Sorrow and suffering, passion, hell itself, she turns into charm and prettiness.

[Sings] / And will he not come again? / And will he not come again? / No, no, he is dead, / Go to thy death-bed, / He never will come again. / His beard was as white as snow, / All flaxen was his poll. / He is gone, he is gone, / And we cast away moan. / God ha' mercy on his soul. / And of all Christian souls, I pray God. God b' wi' ye.

[Sings] And won't he come back again? And won't he come back again? No, no, he is dead. Go to your deathbed. He will never come back again. His beard was as white as snow, his hair all pale like flax. He is gone, he is gone, and we throw away our grief. God have mercy on his soul! And on all Christian souls, I pray to God. God be with you.
Do you see this, O God?
Do you see this, oh God?

Laertes, I must commune with your grief, / Or you deny me right. Go but apart, / Make choice of whom your wisest friends you will, / And they shall hear and judge 'twixt you and me. / If by direct or by collateral hand / They find us touch'd, we will our kingdom give, / Our crown, our life, and all that we call ours / To you in satisfaction; but if not, / Be you content to lend your patience to us, / And we shall jointly labour with your soul / To give it due content.

Laertes, I must share in your grief, or you deny me what is right. Just go aside, choose whichever of your wisest friends you like, and let them hear us and judge between you and me. If they find that I was involved, directly or indirectly, I will give you our kingdom, our crown, our life and everything we call ours, to make up for it. But if not, be content to be patient with us, and we will work together with you to give your soul the satisfaction it deserves.

Let this be so; / His means of death, his obscure burial,— / No trophy, sword, nor hatchment o'er his bones, / No noble rite, nor formal ostentation,— / Cry to be heard, as 'twere from heaven to earth, / That I must call't in question.

Let it be so. The way he died, his secret burial, with no monument, sword or coat of arms over his bones, no noble ceremony or formal display, all cry out to be heard, as loudly as if from heaven to earth, so I must demand an explanation.
So you shall. / And where th'offence is let the great axe fall. / I pray you go with me.
And so you shall, and where the guilt lies, let the great axe fall. Please, come with me.
What are they that would speak with me?
Who are the people who want to speak to me?
Sailors, sir. They say they have letters for you.
Sailors, sir. They say they have letters for you.
I do not know from what part of the world / I should be greeted, if not from Lord Hamlet.
I don't know who in the world would be writing to me, if not Lord Hamlet.
And may he bless you too.
He shall, sir, and't please him. There's a letter for you, sir. It / comes from th'ambassador that was bound for England; if your name be / Horatio, as I am let to know it is.
He will, sir, if he wants to. There's a letter for you, sir. It comes from the ambassador who was going to England, if your name is Horatio, as I've been told it is.

[Reads] 'Horatio, when thou shalt have overlooked this, give these / fellows some means to the King. They have letters for him. Ere we were / two days old at sea, a pirate of very warlike appointment gave us / chase. Finding ourselves too slow of sail, we put on a compelled / valour, and in the grapple I boarded them. On the instant they got / clear of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner. They have dealt / with me like thieves of mercy. But they knew what they did; I am to do / a good turn for them. Let the King have the letters I have sent, and / repair thou to me with as much haste as thou wouldst fly death. I have / words to speak in thine ear will make thee dumb; yet are they much too / light for the bore of the matter. These good fellows will bring thee / where I am. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern hold their course for England: / of them I have much to tell thee. Farewell. / He that thou knowest thine, / HAMLET.' / Come, I will give you way for these your letters, / And do't the speedier, that you may direct me / To him from whom you brought them.

[Reads] 'Horatio, when you have read this, help these fellows get to the King. They have letters for him. Before we were two days out at sea, a pirate ship very well armed chased us. Finding we were too slow, we were forced to be brave, and in the fight I boarded their ship. At that moment they got clear of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner. They have treated me like merciful thieves, but they knew what they were doing: I am to do them a favour. Let the King have the letters I have sent, and come to me as fast as you would run from death. I have things to tell you that will leave you speechless, and yet my words are far too light for the weight of the matter. These good fellows will bring you to where I am. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are still on their way to England. I have a lot to tell you about them. Goodbye. The one you know is yours, Hamlet.' Come, I'll get these letters of yours delivered, and I'll do it all the faster so that you can take me to the man who gave them to you.

Now must your conscience my acquittance seal, / And you must put me in your heart for friend, / Sith you have heard, and with a knowing ear, / That he which hath your noble father slain / Pursu'd my life.

Now your conscience must confirm that I am innocent, and you must take me into your heart as a friend, since you have heard, and understood, that the man who killed your noble father was trying to kill me.
It well appears. But tell me / Why you proceeded not against these feats, / So crimeful and so capital in nature, / As by your safety, wisdom, all things else, / You mainly were stirr'd up.
That seems clear. But tell me why you didn't take action against these deeds, so criminal and deserving death, when your own safety, your wisdom and everything else must have strongly urged you to.

O, for two special reasons, / Which may to you, perhaps, seem much unsinew'd, / But yet to me they are strong. The Queen his mother / Lives almost by his looks; and for myself,— / My virtue or my plague, be it either which,— / She's so conjunctive to my life and soul, / That, as the star moves not but in his sphere, / I could not but by her. The other motive, / Why to a public count I might not go, / Is the great love the general gender bear him, / Who, dipping all his faults in their affection, / Would like the spring that turneth wood to stone, / Convert his gyves to graces; so that my arrows, / Too slightly timber'd for so loud a wind, / Would have reverted to my bow again, / And not where I had aim'd them.

Oh, for two special reasons, which may seem very weak to you, but to me they are strong. The Queen, his mother, lives almost for the sight of him, and as for me, whether it is my virtue or my curse, she is so closely joined to my life and soul that, just as a star only moves within its own sphere, I can only move with her. The other reason I couldn't bring him to public trial is the great love the common people have for him. They dip all his faults in their affection and, like the spring that turns wood into stone, would turn his chains into honours. So my arrows, too light for such a strong wind, would have blown back to my bow and not gone where I aimed them.

And so have I a noble father lost, / A sister driven into desperate terms, / Whose worth, if praises may go back again, / Stood challenger on mount of all the age / For her perfections. But my revenge will come.

And so I have lost a noble father, and my sister has been driven into desperate madness, a girl whose worth, if I may praise what she used to be, stood high above everyone of her age, challenging anyone to match her perfections. But my revenge will come.

Break not your sleeps for that. You must not think / That we are made of stuff so flat and dull / That we can let our beard be shook with danger, / And think it pastime. You shortly shall hear more. / I lov'd your father, and we love ourself, / And that, I hope, will teach you to imagine—

Don't lose any sleep over that. You mustn't think we are made of such flat and dull stuff that we can let danger pull our beard and think it's a game. You'll hear more soon. I loved your father, and we love ourselves, and that, I hope, will teach you to imagine—
Letters, my lord, from Hamlet. / This to your Majesty; this to the Queen.
Letters, my lord, from Hamlet. This one for your Majesty, this one for the Queen.
Sailors, my lord, they say; I saw them not. / They were given me by Claudio. He receiv'd them / Of him that brought them.
Sailors, my lord, they say. I didn't see them. Claudio gave them to me. He got them from the man who brought them.
Laertes, you shall hear them. / Leave us.
Laertes, you shall hear them. Leave us.

[Reads] 'High and mighty, you shall know I am set naked on your / kingdom. Tomorrow shall I beg leave to see your kingly eyes. When I / shall, first asking your pardon thereunto, recount the occasions of my / sudden and more strange return. / HAMLET.' / What should this mean? Are all the rest come back? / Or is it some abuse, and no such thing?

[Reads] 'High and mighty King, you should know that I have been put down on your kingdom with nothing. Tomorrow I will ask permission to see your royal eyes, and then, after first asking your pardon, I'll tell you the reasons for my sudden and even stranger return. Hamlet.' What can this mean? Have all the others come back? Or is it some trick, and nothing of the kind?
'Tis Hamlet's character. 'Naked!' / And in a postscript here he says 'alone.' / Can you advise me?
It's Hamlet's writing. 'With nothing'! And in a note here he adds 'alone'. Can you advise me?
I am lost in it, my lord. But let him come, / It warms the very sickness in my heart / That I shall live and tell him to his teeth, / 'Thus diest thou.'
I'm completely confused by it, my lord. But let him come. It warms the very sickness in my heart that I'll live to tell him to his face, 'This is how you die.'
If it be so, Laertes,— / As how should it be so? How otherwise?— / Will you be rul'd by me?
If that is so, Laertes, and how can it be so? Yet how can it be otherwise? Will you let me guide you?
Ay, my lord; / So you will not o'errule me to a peace.
Yes, my lord, as long as you don't order me to make peace.

To thine own peace. If he be now return'd, / As checking at his voyage, and that he means / No more to undertake it, I will work him / To an exploit, now ripe in my device, / Under the which he shall not choose but fall; / And for his death no wind shall breathe, / But even his mother shall uncharge the practice / And call it accident.

Only to your own peace of mind. If he has come back now, turning away from his voyage, and means not to go on it any more, I'll lead him into a plan, now fully worked out in my mind, which will certainly kill him. And there won't be a breath of blame for his death; even his mother won't accuse anyone of the plot, and will call it an accident.
My lord, I will be rul'd; / The rather if you could devise it so / That I might be the organ.
My lord, I'll let you guide me, and all the more if you could arrange it so that I am the instrument.

It falls right. / You have been talk'd of since your travel much, / And that in Hamlet's hearing, for a quality / Wherein they say you shine. Your sum of parts / Did not together pluck such envy from him / As did that one, and that, in my regard, / Of the unworthiest siege.

That fits well. You've been talked about a lot since you went abroad, and in Hamlet's hearing, for one skill they say you shine at. All your other qualities together didn't make him as envious as that one did, though in my opinion it is the least important.
What part is that, my lord?
What skill is that, my lord?

A very riband in the cap of youth, / Yet needful too, for youth no less becomes / The light and careless livery that it wears / Than settled age his sables and his weeds, / Importing health and graveness. Two months since / Here was a gentleman of Normandy,— / I've seen myself, and serv'd against, the French, / And they can well on horseback, but this gallant / Had witchcraft in't. He grew unto his seat, / And to such wondrous doing brought his horse, / As had he been incorps'd and demi-natur'd / With the brave beast. So far he topp'd my thought / That I in forgery of shapes and tricks, / Come short of what he did.

A mere ribbon in the cap of youth, and yet a necessary one too, because light, carefree clothes suit youth no less than sober furs and robes suit settled old age, showing well-being and seriousness. Two months ago there was a gentleman from Normandy here. I've seen the French myself and fought against them, and they ride very well, but this young man was like a magician. He seemed to grow into his saddle, and he made his horse do such amazing things, it was as if he had become one body with the fine animal, half man, half horse. He went so far beyond what I could imagine that I can't invent the moves and tricks he did.
I know him well. He is the brooch indeed / And gem of all the nation.
I know him well. He is truly the jewel and pride of the whole nation.

He made confession of you, / And gave you such a masterly report / For art and exercise in your defence, / And for your rapier most especially, / That he cried out 'twould be a sight indeed / If one could match you. The scrimers of their nation / He swore had neither motion, guard, nor eye, / If you oppos'd them. Sir, this report of his / Did Hamlet so envenom with his envy / That he could nothing do but wish and beg / Your sudden coming o'er to play with him. / Now, out of this,—

He told us about you, and gave you such a glowing report for your skill and practice in fencing, especially with the rapier, that he exclaimed it would be a real sight if anyone could match you. He swore the fencers of his country had no movement, defence or eye when they faced you. Sir, this report of his made Hamlet so poisoned with envy that he could do nothing but wish and beg for you to come back quickly and fence with him. Now, out of this—
What out of this, my lord?
What out of this, my lord?
Laertes, was your father dear to you? / Or are you like the painting of a sorrow, / A face without a heart?
Laertes, did you love your father? Or are you like the painting of a sorrow, a face without a heart?

Not that I think you did not love your father, / But that I know love is begun by time, / And that I see, in passages of proof, / Time qualifies the spark and fire of it. / There lives within the very flame of love / A kind of wick or snuff that will abate it; / And nothing is at a like goodness still, / For goodness, growing to a pleurisy, / Dies in his own too much. That we would do, / We should do when we would; for this 'would' changes, / And hath abatements and delays as many / As there are tongues, are hands, are accidents; / And then this 'should' is like a spendthrift sigh / That hurts by easing. But to the quick o' th'ulcer: / Hamlet comes back: what would you undertake / To show yourself your father's son in deed, / More than in words?

Not because I think you didn't love your father, but because I know that love is started by time, and I see, from experience, that time weakens its spark and fire. Inside the very flame of love there lives a sort of wick or burnt end that will dim it, and nothing stays at the same level of goodness forever, because goodness, growing too full, dies of its own excess. What we want to do, we should do when we want to, because this 'want' changes and has as many weakenings and delays as there are tongues, hands and accidents, and then this 'should' is like a wasteful sigh that hurts while it eases. But to the heart of the sore: Hamlet comes back. What would you do to show yourself your father's son in actions, more than in words?
To cut his throat i' th' church.

No place, indeed, should murder sanctuarize; / Revenge should have no bounds. But good Laertes, / Will you do this, keep close within your chamber. / Hamlet return'd shall know you are come home: / We'll put on those shall praise your excellence, / And set a double varnish on the fame / The Frenchman gave you, bring you in fine together / And wager on your heads. He, being remiss, / Most generous, and free from all contriving, / Will not peruse the foils; so that with ease, / Or with a little shuffling, you may choose / A sword unbated, and in a pass of practice, / Requite him for your father.

No place, it's true, should give sanctuary to a murderer. Revenge should have no limits. But, good Laertes, if you'll do this, stay shut up in your room. When Hamlet comes back, he'll learn that you are home. We'll get people to praise your skill and put a double coat of polish on the reputation the Frenchman gave you, and finally bring you together and bet on you. He, being careless, very generous and free of all scheming, won't examine the swords, so that easily, or with a little sleight of hand, you can choose a sword without a safety tip, and with a thrust in the practice match pay him back for your father.

I will do't. / And for that purpose I'll anoint my sword. / I bought an unction of a mountebank / So mortal that, but dip a knife in it, / Where it draws blood no cataplasm so rare, / Collected from all simples that have virtue / Under the moon, can save the thing from death / This is but scratch'd withal. I'll touch my point / With this contagion, that if I gall him slightly, / It may be death.

I'll do it, and for that purpose I'll smear poison on my sword. I bought an ointment from a travelling quack so deadly that if you just dip a knife in it, where it draws blood, no remedy, however rare, made from every herb with healing powers under the moon, can save anyone from death who is even scratched with it. I'll touch the tip of my sword with this poison, so that if I graze him even slightly, it will mean death.

Let's further think of this, / Weigh what convenience both of time and means / May fit us to our shape. If this should fail, / And that our drift look through our bad performance. / 'Twere better not assay'd. Therefore this project / Should have a back or second, that might hold / If this did blast in proof. Soft, let me see. / We'll make a solemn wager on your cunnings,— / I ha't! When in your motion you are hot and dry, / As make your bouts more violent to that end, / And that he calls for drink, I'll have prepar'd him / A chalice for the nonce; whereon but sipping, / If he by chance escape your venom'd stuck, / Our purpose may hold there.

Let's think further about this, and consider what timing and means will best suit our roles. If this should fail, and our plan should show through because we carry it out badly, it would be better not to try. So this plan should have a backup, a second one that would work if this one blew up when tested. Wait, let me see. We'll make a formal bet on your skills. I've got it! When you are hot and thirsty from moving, and you should make your bouts more violent for that purpose, and he asks for a drink, I'll have prepared a cup for him for the occasion. If he just sips it, even if by chance he escapes your poisoned thrust, our plan will still succeed.
One woe doth tread upon another's heel, / So fast they follow. Your sister's drown'd, Laertes.
One sorrow treads on another's heels, they follow so fast. Your sister has drowned, Laertes.

There is a willow grows aslant a brook, / That shows his hoary leaves in the glassy stream. / There with fantastic garlands did she make / Of crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples, / That liberal shepherds give a grosser name, / But our cold maids do dead men's fingers call them. / There on the pendant boughs her coronet weeds / Clamb'ring to hang, an envious sliver broke, / When down her weedy trophies and herself / Fell in the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide, / And mermaid-like, awhile they bore her up, / Which time she chaunted snatches of old tunes, / As one incapable of her own distress, / Or like a creature native and indued / Unto that element. But long it could not be / Till that her garments, heavy with their drink, / Pull'd the poor wretch from her melodious lay / To muddy death.

There is a willow growing at an angle over a stream, showing its grey-white leaves in the glassy water. There she came with fantastic garlands she had made of buttercups, nettles, daisies and long purple flowers, which the coarse shepherds give a rude name, but our chaste girls call dead men's fingers. There, as she climbed to hang her crown of flowers on the hanging branches, a spiteful branch broke, and down she fell with her flowery trophies into the weeping stream. Her clothes spread out wide and held her up like a mermaid for a while, and all that time she sang bits of old songs, as if she didn't understand the danger she was in, or like a creature born and suited to the water. But it couldn't be long before her clothes, heavy with all the water they had soaked up, pulled the poor girl from her lovely singing down to a muddy death.

Too much of water hast thou, poor Ophelia, / And therefore I forbid my tears. But yet / It is our trick; nature her custom holds, / Let shame say what it will. When these are gone, / The woman will be out. Adieu, my lord, / I have a speech of fire, that fain would blaze, / But that this folly douts it.

You've had too much water, poor Ophelia, so I won't let myself cry. But still, it's our human nature; nature keeps to her habits, whatever shame may say. When these tears are gone, the woman in me will be gone too. Goodbye, my lord. I have a fiery speech that wants to blaze out, but this foolish weeping puts it out.
Let's follow, Gertrude; / How much I had to do to calm his rage! / Now fear I this will give it start again; / Therefore let's follow.
Let's follow, Gertrude. How hard I worked to calm his rage! Now I'm afraid this will start it up again. So let's follow.
Is she to be buried in Christian burial, when she wilfully seeks her / own salvation?
Is she going to be given a Christian burial, when she deliberately went looking for her own salvation?
I tell thee she is, and therefore make her grave straight. The crowner / hath sat on her, and finds it Christian burial.
I'm telling you she is, so dig her grave straight away. The coroner has held an inquest on her and decided it's to be a Christian burial.
How can that be, unless she drowned herself in her own defence?
How can that be, unless she drowned herself in self-defence?

It must be se offendendo, it cannot be else. For here lies the point: / if I drown myself wittingly, it argues an act: and an act hath three / branches. It is to act, to do, and to perform: argal, she drowned / herself wittingly.

It must have been 'self-offence'; it can't be anything else. Because here's the point: if I drown myself on purpose, that shows an act, and an act has three branches: to act, to do and to perform. Ergo, she drowned herself on purpose.
Nay, but hear you, goodman delver,—

Give me leave. Here lies the water; good. Here stands the man; good. If / the man go to this water and drown himself, it is, will he nill he, he / goes,—mark you that. But if the water come to him and drown him, he / drowns not himself. Argal, he that is not guilty of his own death / shortens not his own life.

Let me finish. Here's the water, good. Here stands the man, good. If the man goes to this water and drowns himself, it is, whether he likes it or not, he goes, mark that. But if the water comes to him and drowns him, he doesn't drown himself. Ergo, the man who isn't guilty of his own death doesn't shorten his own life.
Ay, marry, is't, crowner's quest law.
Yes, it certainly is, coroner's inquest law.
Will you ha' the truth on't? If this had not been a gentlewoman, she / should have been buried out o' Christian burial.
Do you want the truth of it? If she hadn't been a gentlewoman, she wouldn't have been given a Christian burial.

Why, there thou say'st. And the more pity that great folk should have / countenance in this world to drown or hang themselves more than their / even Christian. Come, my spade. There is no ancient gentlemen but / gardeners, ditchers, and grave-makers: they hold up Adam's profession.

Why, you've said it. And it's a great pity that important people should have more permission in this world to drown or hang themselves than their fellow Christians. Come, my spade. There are no gentlemen of older family than gardeners, ditch-diggers and gravediggers. They carry on Adam's profession.
He was the first that ever bore arms.
He was the first man ever to bear arms.
Why, he didn't have a coat of arms.

What, art a heathen? How dost thou understand the Scripture? The / Scripture says Adam digg'd. Could he dig without arms? I'll put another / question to thee. If thou answerest me not to the purpose, confess / thyself—
What, are you a heathen? How do you understand the Bible? The Bible says Adam dug. Could he dig without arms? I'll ask you another question. If you don't answer me properly, confess yourself—
What is he that builds stronger than either the mason, the shipwright, / or the carpenter?
Who builds stronger than the stonemason, the shipbuilder or the carpenter?
The gallows-maker; for that frame outlives a thousand tenants.
The gallows-maker, because his frame outlives a thousand tenants.

I like thy wit well in good faith, the gallows does well. But how does / it well? It does well to those that do ill. Now, thou dost ill to say / the gallows is built stronger than the church; argal, the gallows may / do well to thee. To't again, come.

I like your wit, honestly. The gallows does well. But how does it do well? It does well for those who do evil. Now, you do evil to say the gallows is built stronger than the church. Ergo, the gallows may do well for you. Try again, come on.
Who builds stronger than a mason, a shipwright, or a carpenter?
Who builds stronger than a stonemason, a shipbuilder or a carpenter?
Ay, tell me that, and unyoke.
Yes, tell me that, and you can stop work.
Well, now I can tell you.
By the Mass, I can't tell you.

Cudgel thy brains no more about it, for your dull ass will not mend his / pace with beating; and when you are asked this question next, say 'a / grave-maker'. The houses he makes last till doomsday. Go, get thee to / Yaughan; fetch me a stoup of liquor.

Don't beat your brains about it any more, because your dull donkey won't go any faster for being beaten. And when you're asked this question next time, say 'a gravedigger'. The houses he makes last till the Day of Judgement. Go on, off to Yaughan's and fetch me a jug of drink.
In youth when I did love, did love, / Methought it was very sweet; / To contract, O, the time for, a, my behove, / O methought there was nothing meet.
[Sings] In my youth, when I loved, I loved, I thought it was very sweet, to pass the time for my own pleasure. Oh, I thought nothing was so fitting.
Has this fellow no feeling of his business, that he sings at / grave-making?
Doesn't this fellow have any feeling for what he's doing, that he sings while digging graves?
Custom hath made it in him a property of easiness.
Habit has made it easy for him.
'Tis e'en so; the hand of little employment hath the daintier sense.
That's true. The hand that does little work has more delicate feelings.
[Sings] / But age with his stealing steps / Hath claw'd me in his clutch, / And hath shipp'd me into the land, / As if I had never been such.
[Sings] But old age, creeping up with stealthy steps, has grabbed me in his claws and shipped me off into the earth, as if I had never been young.

That skull had a tongue in it, and could sing once. How the knave jowls / it to th' ground, as if 'twere Cain's jawbone, that did the first / murder! This might be the pate of a politician which this ass now / o'er-offices, one that would circumvent God, might it not?

That skull had a tongue in it and could sing once. How the rogue throws it to the ground, as if it were the jawbone of Cain, who did the first murder! This might be the head of a scheming politician, which this donkey now gets the better of, one who would try to get round God himself, mightn't it?

Or of a courtier, which could say 'Good morrow, sweet lord! How dost / thou, good lord?' This might be my lord such-a-one, that praised my / lord such-a-one's horse when he meant to beg it, might it not?
Or of a courtier, who could say 'Good morning, sweet lord! How are you, good lord?' This might be Lord So-and-so, who praised Lord So-and-so's horse when he meant to beg for it, mightn't it?

Why, e'en so: and now my Lady Worm's; chapless, and knocked about the / mazard with a sexton's spade. Here's fine revolution, an we had the / trick to see't. Did these bones cost no more the breeding but to play / at loggets with 'em? Mine ache to think on't.

Why, exactly, and now it belongs to my Lady Worm, with no jaw, and knocked about the head with a gravedigger's spade. Here's a fine reversal of fortune, if only we had the trick of seeing it. Did these bones cost so little to bring up that they're only fit for playing skittles with? Mine ache to think about it.
[Sings] / A pickaxe and a spade, a spade, / For and a shrouding-sheet; / O, a pit of clay for to be made / For such a guest is meet.
[Sings] A pickaxe and a spade, a spade, and a sheet to wrap the body in; oh, a pit of clay to be dug is just right for such a guest.

There's another. Why may not that be the skull of a lawyer? Where be / his quiddits now, his quillets, his cases, his tenures, and his tricks? / Why does he suffer this rude knave now to knock him about the sconce / with a dirty shovel, and will not tell him of his action of battery? / Hum. This fellow might be in's time a great buyer of land, with his / statutes, his recognizances, his fines, his double vouchers, his / recoveries. Is this the fine of his fines, and the recovery of his / recoveries, to have his fine pate full of fine dirt? Will his vouchers / vouch him no more of his purchases, and double ones too, than the / length and breadth of a pair of indentures? The very conveyances of his / lands will scarcely lie in this box; and must the inheritor himself / have no more, ha?

There's another. Why couldn't that be the skull of a lawyer? Where are his quibbles now, his fine distinctions, his cases, his property rights and his tricks? Why does he let this rough rogue knock him on the head with a dirty shovel, and not threaten to sue him for assault? Hm. This fellow might have been a great buyer of land in his time, with his contracts, his bonds, his transfers, his double guarantees, his legal recoveries. Is this the end of his transfers and the recovery of his recoveries, to have his fine head full of fine dirt? Will all his guarantees, even the double ones, guarantee him no more land than the length and width of a pair of contracts? The deeds to his lands would hardly fit in this box, and must the owner himself have no more than this, ha?
Not a jot more, my lord.
Not a bit more, my lord.
Is not parchment made of sheep-skins?
Ay, my lord, and of calf-skins too.
Yes, my lord, and of calfskin too.
They are sheep and calves which seek out assurance in that. I will / speak to this fellow.—Whose grave's this, sir?
People are sheep and calves to look for security in that. I'll speak to this fellow. Whose grave is this, sir?
Mine, sir. / [Sings] / O, a pit of clay for to be made / For such a guest is meet.
Mine, sir. [Sings] Oh, a pit of clay to be dug is just right for such a guest.
I think it be thine indeed, for thou liest in't.
I think it really is yours, because you are lying in it.
You lie out on't, sir, and therefore 'tis not yours. / For my part, I do not lie in't, yet it is mine.
You're lying outside it, sir, so it isn't yours. As for me, I'm not lying in it, and yet it's mine.
Thou dost lie in't, to be in't and say it is thine. 'Tis for the dead, / not for the quick; therefore thou liest.
You are lying in it, to be in it and say it's yours. It's for the dead, not for the living, so you are lying.
'Tis a quick lie, sir; 't will away again from me to you.
It's a living lie, sir. It will jump away from me to you again.
What man dost thou dig it for?
What man are you digging it for?
Who is to be buried in't?
Who is going to be buried in it?
One that was a woman, sir; but, rest her soul, she's dead.
One who was a woman, sir, but, God rest her soul, she's dead.

How absolute the knave is! We must speak by the card, or equivocation / will undo us. By the Lord, Horatio, these three years I have taken note / of it, the age is grown so picked that the toe of the peasant comes so / near the heel of the courtier he galls his kibe.—How long hast thou / been a grave-maker?

How precise the rogue is! We must speak exactly, or double meanings will defeat us. By God, Horatio, I've noticed it these last three years: the times have become so refined that the peasant's toe comes so close to the courtier's heel that he rubs his chilblain. How long have you been a gravedigger?
Of all the days i' th' year, I came to't that day that our last King / Hamlet o'ercame Fortinbras.
Of all the days in the year, I started on the day our last King Hamlet defeated Fortinbras.
Cannot you tell that? Every fool can tell that. It was the very day / that young Hamlet was born,—he that is mad, and sent into England.
Can't you tell that? Any fool can tell that. It was the very day young Hamlet was born, the one who is mad and has been sent to England.
Ay, marry, why was he sent into England?
Yes, indeed. Why was he sent to England?
Why, because he was mad; he shall recover his wits there; or if he do / not, it's no great matter there.
Why, because he was mad. He'll get his wits back there, or if he doesn't, it doesn't much matter there.
'Twill not be seen in him there; there the men are as mad as he.
It won't be noticed in him there. The men there are as mad as he is.
Faith, e'en with losing his wits.
Why, here in Denmark. I have been sexton here, man and boy, thirty / years.
Why, here in Denmark. I've been gravedigger here, man and boy, for thirty years.
How long will a man lie i' th'earth ere he rot?
How long will a man lie in the earth before he rots?

Faith, if he be not rotten before he die,—as we have many pocky corses / nowadays that will scarce hold the laying in,—he will last you some / eight year or nine year. A tanner will last you nine year.

Well, if he isn't rotten before he dies, since we get a lot of corpses these days so riddled with the pox that they hardly last till they're buried, he'll last you about eight or nine years. A tanner will last you nine years.
Why him more than anyone else?

Why, sir, his hide is so tann'd with his trade that he will keep out / water a great while. And your water is a sore decayer of your whoreson / dead body. Here's a skull now; this skull hath lain in the earth / three-and-twenty years.

Why, sir, his skin is so tanned by his trade that it keeps out water for a long time, and water is a terrible destroyer of your damned dead body. Here's a skull now. This skull has been lying in the earth for twenty-three years.
A whoreson, mad fellow's it was. Whose do you think it was?
A damned mad fellow's it was. Whose do you think it was?
A pestilence on him for a mad rogue! A pour'd a flagon of Rhenish on my / head once. This same skull, sir, was Yorick's skull, the King's jester.
A plague on him for a mad rogue! He poured a jug of German wine over my head once. This very skull, sir, was Yorick's skull, the King's jester.

Let me see. [Takes the skull] Alas, poor Yorick. I knew him, / Horatio, a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy. He hath / borne me on his back a thousand times; and now, how abhorred in my / imagination it is! My gorge rises at it. Here hung those lips that I / have kiss'd I know not how oft. Where be your gibes now? your gambols? / your songs? your flashes of merriment, that were wont to set the table / on a roar? Not one now, to mock your own grinning? Quite chop-fallen? / Now get you to my lady's chamber, and tell her, let her paint an inch / thick, to this favour she must come. Make her laugh at that.—Prithee, / Horatio, tell me one thing.

Let me see. [Takes the skull] Oh, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio, a fellow of endless jokes and the most brilliant imagination. He carried me on his back a thousand times, and now how disgusting it is to think of! It makes me feel sick. Here hung those lips that I kissed I don't know how often. Where are your jokes now? Your capers? Your songs? Your flashes of fun that used to set the whole table roaring? Not one left now to mock your own grin? Your jaw has quite dropped. Now go to my lady's room and tell her that even if she paints her make-up on an inch thick, she must come to this face in the end. Make her laugh at that. Please, Horatio, tell me one thing.
Dost thou think Alexander looked o' this fashion i' th'earth?
Do you think Alexander the Great looked like this in the earth?
To what base uses we may return, Horatio! Why may not imagination trace / the noble dust of Alexander till he find it stopping a bung-hole?
To what low uses we may come back, Horatio! Why couldn't the imagination follow the noble dust of Alexander until it finds it plugging a hole in a beer barrel?
'Twere to consider too curiously to consider so.
It would be thinking too elaborately to think like that.

No, faith, not a jot. But to follow him thither with modesty enough, / and likelihood to lead it; as thus. Alexander died, Alexander was / buried, Alexander returneth into dust; the dust is earth; of earth we / make loam; and why of that loam whereto he was converted might they not / stop a beer-barrel? / Imperious Caesar, dead and turn'd to clay, / Might stop a hole to keep the wind away. / O, that that earth which kept the world in awe / Should patch a wall t'expel the winter's flaw. / But soft! but soft! aside! Here comes the King.

No, honestly, not a bit. Just follow him there reasonably, with likelihood to lead the way, like this: Alexander died, Alexander was buried, Alexander turns back into dust; the dust is earth; from earth we make clay; and why couldn't they use the clay he turned into to plug a beer barrel? Mighty Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might plug a hole to keep the wind away. Oh, that the earth which kept the world in awe should patch a wall to keep out the winter's gusts! But quiet! Quiet! Step aside! Here comes the King.

The Queen, the courtiers. Who is that they follow? / And with such maimed rites? This doth betoken / The corse they follow did with desperate hand / Fordo it own life. 'Twas of some estate. / Couch we awhile and mark.

The Queen, the courtiers. Who is it they are following? And with such cut-down ceremonies? This shows that the body they follow took its own life with a desperate hand. It was someone of high rank. Let's hide for a while and watch.
That is Laertes, a very noble youth. Mark.
That's Laertes, a very noble young man. Watch.

Her obsequies have been as far enlarg'd / As we have warranties. Her death was doubtful; / And but that great command o'ersways the order, / She should in ground unsanctified have lodg'd / Till the last trumpet. For charitable prayers, / Shards, flints, and pebbles should be thrown on her. / Yet here she is allowed her virgin rites, / Her maiden strewments, and the bringing home / Of bell and burial.

Her funeral has been given as many rites as we are allowed. Her death was suspicious, and if the King's orders hadn't overruled the normal rules, she would have been buried in unholy ground until the trumpet sounds on Judgement Day. Instead of charitable prayers, broken pots, flints and pebbles would have been thrown on her. Yet here she is allowed the garlands of a virgin, flowers scattered for a maiden, and to be brought to her last home with the bell and a proper burial.
Must there no more be done?
No more be done. / We should profane the service of the dead / To sing sage requiem and such rest to her / As to peace-parted souls.
Nothing more must be done. We would be dishonouring the service for the dead to sing a solemn requiem and pray for rest for her as we do for souls who died in peace.
Lay her i' th'earth, / And from her fair and unpolluted flesh / May violets spring. I tell thee, churlish priest, / A minist'ring angel shall my sister be / When thou liest howling.
Lay her in the earth, and may violets grow from her lovely, pure body! I tell you, you mean priest, my sister will be a ministering angel in heaven while you lie howling in hell.
[Scattering flowers] Sweets to the sweet. Farewell. / I hop'd thou shouldst have been my Hamlet's wife; / I thought thy bride-bed to have deck'd, sweet maid, / And not have strew'd thy grave.
[Scattering flowers] Sweet flowers for the sweet girl. Goodbye. I hoped you would be my Hamlet's wife. I thought I'd be decorating your wedding bed, sweet girl, not scattering flowers on your grave.

O, treble woe / Fall ten times treble on that cursed head / Whose wicked deed thy most ingenious sense / Depriv'd thee of. Hold off the earth a while, / Till I have caught her once more in mine arms. / [Leaps into the grave] / Now pile your dust upon the quick and dead, / Till of this flat a mountain you have made, / To o'ertop old Pelion or the skyish head / Of blue Olympus.

Oh, may three times the sorrow fall ten times three times on that cursed head whose wicked deed robbed you of your fine mind! Hold back the earth for a while, until I've held her in my arms once more. [Leaps into the grave] Now pile your dust on the living and the dead, until you've made a mountain out of this flat ground, higher than old Mount Pelion or the sky-high top of blue Olympus.

[Advancing] / What is he whose grief / Bears such an emphasis? whose phrase of sorrow / Conjures the wand'ring stars, and makes them stand / Like wonder-wounded hearers? This is I, / Hamlet the Dane. / [Leaps into the grave]

[Advancing] Who is this whose grief is shown with such emphasis, whose words of sorrow cast a spell on the wandering planets and make them stand still like listeners struck with wonder? This is I, Hamlet the Dane! [Leaps into the grave]
[Grappling with him] The devil take thy soul!
[Grappling with him] The devil take your soul!
Thou pray'st not well. / I prithee take thy fingers from my throat; / For though I am not splenative and rash, / Yet have I in me something dangerous, / Which let thy wiseness fear. Away thy hand!

That's not a good prayer. Please take your fingers off my throat, because although I'm not hot-tempered and rash, I still have something dangerous in me, which you would be wise to fear. Take your hand away!
Why, I will fight with him upon this theme / Until my eyelids will no longer wag.
Why, I'll fight with him over this until my eyelids can no longer move.
I lov'd Ophelia; forty thousand brothers / Could not, with all their quantity of love, / Make up my sum. What wilt thou do for her?
I loved Ophelia. Forty thousand brothers, with all their love added together, couldn't make up the total of mine. What will you do for her?
For love of God forbear him!
For the love of God, leave him alone!

'Swounds, show me what thou'lt do: / Woul't weep? woul't fight? woul't fast? woul't tear thyself? / Woul't drink up eisel? eat a crocodile? / I'll do't. Dost thou come here to whine? / To outface me with leaping in her grave? / Be buried quick with her, and so will I. / And if thou prate of mountains, let them throw / Millions of acres on us, till our ground, / Singeing his pate against the burning zone, / Make Ossa like a wart. Nay, an thou'lt mouth, / I'll rant as well as thou.

By God's wounds, show me what you'll do. Will you weep? Will you fight? Will you starve yourself? Will you tear yourself to pieces? Will you drink vinegar? Eat a crocodile? I'll do it. Did you come here to whine? To outdo me by leaping into her grave? Be buried alive with her, and so will I. And if you babble about mountains, let them throw millions of acres on top of us, until the pile scorches its head against the burning sun and makes Mount Ossa look like a wart. No, if you're going to rant, I'll rant as well as you.
This is mere madness: / And thus awhile the fit will work on him; / Anon, as patient as the female dove, / When that her golden couplets are disclos'd, / His silence will sit drooping.
This is pure madness, and the fit will work on him like this for a while. Then, as patient as the female dove when her golden pair of chicks have hatched, he'll sit silent and drooping.
Hear you, sir; / What is the reason that you use me thus? / I lov'd you ever. But it is no matter. / Let Hercules himself do what he may, / The cat will mew, and dog will have his day.
Listen, sir, why do you treat me like this? I always loved you. But it doesn't matter. Let Hercules himself do what he can, the cat will mew, and the dog will have his day.
I pray thee, good Horatio, wait upon him.
Please, good Horatio, go and look after him.
