[To Laertes] Strengthen your patience in our last night's speech; / We'll put the matter to the present push.— / Good Gertrude, set some watch over your son. / This grave shall have a living monument. / An hour of quiet shortly shall we see; / Till then in patience our proceeding be.

[To Laertes] Be patient, remembering what we said last night. We'll put the plan into action at once. Good Gertrude, have your son watched. This grave will have a living monument. We'll soon have an hour of peace. Until then, let us go about things patiently.
So much for this, sir. Now let me see the other; / You do remember all the circumstance?
So much for that, sir. Now you'll hear the rest. Do you remember all the details?

Sir, in my heart there was a kind of fighting / That would not let me sleep. Methought I lay / Worse than the mutinies in the bilboes. Rashly, / And prais'd be rashness for it,—let us know, / Our indiscretion sometime serves us well, / When our deep plots do pall; and that should teach us / There's a divinity that shapes our ends, / Rough-hew them how we will.

Sir, there was a kind of fighting in my heart that wouldn't let me sleep. I felt I was lying in a worse state than mutineers in chains. On impulse, and thank God for impulse, because we should know that our rashness sometimes works well for us when our careful plans fail, and that should teach us there's a divine power that shapes how things end, however roughly we carve them ourselves—

Up from my cabin, / My sea-gown scarf'd about me, in the dark / Grop'd I to find out them; had my desire, / Finger'd their packet, and in fine, withdrew / To mine own room again, making so bold, / My fears forgetting manners, to unseal / Their grand commission; where I found, Horatio, / Oh royal knavery! an exact command, / Larded with many several sorts of reasons, / Importing Denmark's health, and England's too, / With ho! such bugs and goblins in my life, / That on the supervise, no leisure bated, / No, not to stay the grinding of the axe, / My head should be struck off.

I got up from my cabin, wrapped my sea-coat round me, and groped in the dark to find them. I got what I wanted, fingered their package of letters, and finally went back to my own room, being so bold, since my fears made me forget my manners, as to break the seal on their important orders. And there I found, Horatio, oh, royal villainy! an exact command, padded with lots of different reasons about the welfare of Denmark and of England too, with such bogeymen and goblins if I were left alive, that as soon as the letter was read, with no time wasted, not even to wait for the axe to be sharpened, my head should be cut off.
Here's the commission, read it at more leisure. / But wilt thou hear me how I did proceed?
Here are the orders. Read them when you have more time. But do you want to hear how I went on?

Being thus benetted round with villanies,— / Or I could make a prologue to my brains, / They had begun the play,—I sat me down, / Devis'd a new commission, wrote it fair: / I once did hold it, as our statists do, / A baseness to write fair, and labour'd much / How to forget that learning; but, sir, now / It did me yeoman's service. Wilt thou know / The effect of what I wrote?

Being caught like this in a net of villainy, before I could even begin to think about it, my brain had started the play. I sat down, invented a new set of orders and wrote it out neatly. I used to think, as our statesmen do, that neat handwriting was something for lowly clerks, and I worked hard to forget that skill, but, sir, now it did me loyal service. Do you want to know what I wrote?

An earnest conjuration from the King, / As England was his faithful tributary, / As love between them like the palm might flourish, / As peace should still her wheaten garland wear / And stand a comma 'tween their amities, / And many such-like 'as'es of great charge, / That on the view and know of these contents, / Without debatement further, more or less, / He should the bearers put to sudden death, / Not shriving-time allow'd.

A solemn request from the King, since England was his loyal subject state, since love between them should flourish like the palm tree, since peace should always wear her garland of wheat and stand like a link between their friendships, and many more such 'since's of great importance, that as soon as he had seen and read these contents, without any more discussion of any kind, he should put the bearers to immediate death, with no time allowed for confession.

Why, even in that was heaven ordinant. / I had my father's signet in my purse, / Which was the model of that Danish seal: / Folded the writ up in the form of the other, / Subscrib'd it: gave't th'impression; plac'd it safely, / The changeling never known. Now, the next day / Was our sea-fight, and what to this was sequent / Thou know'st already.

Why, even in that, heaven was on my side. I had my father's seal ring in my purse, which was the original of the Danish royal seal. I folded the letter in the same way as the other one, signed it, stamped it with the seal and put it back safely; the substitute was never noticed. Now, the next day was our sea fight, and what happened after that you already know.
So Guildenstern and Rosencrantz go to't.
So Guildenstern and Rosencrantz go to their deaths.

Why, man, they did make love to this employment. / They are not near my conscience; their defeat / Does by their own insinuation grow. / 'Tis dangerous when the baser nature comes / Between the pass and fell incensed points / Of mighty opposites.

Why, man, they courted this job. They don't weigh on my conscience. Their destruction comes from their own meddling. It's dangerous when lesser people come between the thrusts and fierce, angry sword points of mighty enemies.
Why, what a king is this!
Why, what a king this is!

Does it not, thinks't thee, stand me now upon,— / He that hath kill'd my king, and whor'd my mother, / Popp'd in between th'election and my hopes, / Thrown out his angle for my proper life, / And with such cozenage—is't not perfect conscience / To quit him with this arm? And is't not to be damn'd / To let this canker of our nature come / In further evil?

Don't you think it's now my duty, against the man who has killed my king and made my mother a whore, who pushed in between the election and my hopes of the throne, who cast his fishing line for my own life, and with such trickery, isn't it right in all conscience to pay him back with this arm? And wouldn't I be damned to let this cancer on humanity go on to do more evil?
It must be shortly known to him from England / What is the issue of the business there.
He'll soon hear from England how the business there has turned out.

It will be short. The interim is mine; / And a man's life's no more than to say 'One'. / But I am very sorry, good Horatio, / That to Laertes I forgot myself; / For by the image of my cause I see / The portraiture of his. I'll court his favours. / But sure the bravery of his grief did put me / Into a tow'ring passion.

It will be soon. The time in between is mine, and a man's life is no longer than it takes to say 'one'. But I'm very sorry, good Horatio, that I forgot myself with Laertes, because in the picture of my own cause I can see the likeness of his. I'll try to win his friendship. But the showiness of his grief really put me into a towering rage.
Your lordship is right welcome back to Denmark.
Your lordship is very welcome back to Denmark.
I humbly thank you, sir. Dost know this waterfly?
I humbly thank you, sir. [Aside to Horatio] Do you know this mayfly?

Thy state is the more gracious; for 'tis a vice to know him. He hath / much land, and fertile; let a beast be lord of beasts, and his crib / shall stand at the king's mess; 'tis a chough; but, as I say, spacious / in the possession of dirt.

You're all the better for it, because it's a vice to know him. He has a lot of land, and good land. Let an animal be lord of animals, and his feeding trough will stand at the King's table. He's a chattering jackdaw, but, as I say, he owns a great deal of dirt.
Sweet lord, if your lordship were at leisure, I should impart a thing / to you from his Majesty.
Sweet lord, if your lordship had time, I'd tell you something from his Majesty.
I will receive it with all diligence of spirit. Put your bonnet to his / right use; 'tis for the head.
I'll receive it with all my attention. Put your hat to its proper use. It's for the head.
I thank your lordship, 'tis very hot.
I thank your lordship, it's very hot.
No, believe me, 'tis very cold, the wind is northerly.
No, believe me, it's very cold. The wind is from the north.
It is indifferent cold, my lord, indeed.
It is fairly cold, my lord, indeed.
Methinks it is very sultry and hot for my complexion.
But I think it's very sultry and hot for someone like me.
Exceedingly, my lord; it is very sultry,—as 'twere—I cannot tell how. / But, my lord, his Majesty bade me signify to you that he has laid a / great wager on your head. Sir, this is the matter,—
Very, my lord. It's very sultry, as if, I can't say how. But, my lord, his Majesty asked me to tell you that he has made a large bet on you. Sir, this is the matter—

Nay, in good faith; for mine ease, in good faith. Sir, here is newly / come to court Laertes; believe me, an absolute gentleman, full of most / excellent differences, of very soft society and great showing. Indeed, / to speak feelingly of him, he is the card or calendar of gentry; for / you shall find in him the continent of what part a gentleman would see.

No, really, I'm comfortable, really. Sir, Laertes has just come to court. Believe me, a perfect gentleman, full of the most excellent qualities, very pleasant company and very impressive. Indeed, to speak of him fittingly, he is the map and guide of good breeding, because you will find in him every quality a gentleman would want to see.

Sir, his definement suffers no perdition in you, though I know, to / divide him inventorially would dizzy th'arithmetic of memory, and yet / but yaw neither, in respect of his quick sail. But, in the verity of / extolment, I take him to be a soul of great article and his infusion of / such dearth and rareness as, to make true diction of him, his semblable / is his mirror and who else would trace him his umbrage, nothing more.

Sir, his description loses nothing in your telling, though I know that to list his qualities one by one would make the memory dizzy with counting, and even then it would only stagger along behind his speed. But, to praise him truthfully, I take him to be a soul of great importance, and his nature so precious and rare that, to speak truly of him, the only thing like him is his own mirror, and anyone else who tried to follow him would be his shadow, nothing more.
Your lordship speaks most infallibly of him.
Your lordship speaks of him with complete accuracy.
The concernancy, sir? Why do we wrap the gentleman in our more rawer / breath?
The point, sir? Why are we wrapping the gentleman in our cruder breath?
Is't not possible to understand in another tongue? You will do't, sir, / really.
Isn't it possible to understand in a different language? You'll manage it, sir, really.
What imports the nomination of this gentleman?
Why are we mentioning this gentleman?
His purse is empty already, all's golden words are spent.
[Aside] His purse is empty already. All his golden words are spent.
I know you are not ignorant,—
I know you are not ignorant—
I would you did, sir; yet in faith if you did, it would not much / approve me. Well, sir?
I wish you did know it, sir, though honestly, if you did, it wouldn't be much of a compliment to me. Well, sir?
You are not ignorant of what excellence Laertes is,—
You are not ignorant of how excellent Laertes is—
I dare not confess that, lest I should compare with him in excellence; / but to know a man well were to know himself.
I don't dare admit that, in case I seem to compare myself with him in excellence. To know another man well, you'd have to know yourself.
I mean, sir, for his weapon; but in the imputation laid on him, by them / in his meed he's unfellowed.
I mean, sir, with his weapon. In the reputation people give him, he has no equal in his skill.
That's two of his weapons. But well.
That's two of his weapons. But go on.

The King, sir, hath wager'd with him six Barbary horses, against the / which he has imponed, as I take it, six French rapiers and poniards, / with their assigns, as girdle, hangers, and so. Three of the carriages, / in faith, are very dear to fancy, very responsive to the hilts, most / delicate carriages, and of very liberal conceit.

The King, sir, has bet him six Arab horses, and against them he has staked, as I understand it, six French rapiers and daggers, with their accessories, such as belts, hangers and so on. Three of the 'carriages', honestly, are very fine to look at, very well matched to the hilts, very delicate carriages and very elaborately designed.
What do you call the carriages?
I knew you must be edified by the margin ere you had done.
[Aside to Hamlet] I knew you'd need the footnotes before you'd finished.
The carriages, sir, are the hangers.
The carriages, sir, are the hangers.

The phrase would be more german to the matter if we could carry cannon / by our sides. I would it might be hangers till then. But on. Six / Barbary horses against six French swords, their assigns, and three / liberal conceited carriages: that's the French bet against the Danish. / Why is this all imponed, as you call it?

The word would be more fitting if we carried cannon at our sides. Until then I'd prefer 'hangers'. But go on. Six Arab horses against six French swords, their accessories and three elaborately designed carriages: that's the French bet against the Danish. Why is all this 'staked', as you call it?

The King, sir, hath laid that in a dozen passes between you and him, he / shall not exceed you three hits. He hath laid on twelve for nine. And / it would come to immediate trial if your lordship would vouchsafe the / answer.

The King, sir, has bet that in a dozen bouts between you and Laertes, he won't beat you by more than three hits. Laertes has bet he'll win twelve for nine. And it would be tried at once if your lordship would agree to answer.
I mean, my lord, the opposition of your person in trial.
I mean, my lord, the meeting of your person with him in the contest.

Sir, I will walk here in the hall. If it please his Majesty, it is the / breathing time of day with me. Let the foils be brought, the gentleman / willing, and the King hold his purpose, I will win for him if I can; if / not, I will gain nothing but my shame and the odd hits.

Sir, I'll be walking here in the hall. If it pleases his Majesty, this is my time of day for exercise. Let the swords be brought. If the gentleman is willing and the King still wants it, I'll win for him if I can. If not, I'll gain nothing but my shame and the odd hits.
Shall I re-deliver you e'en so?
Shall I take back your answer like that?
To this effect, sir; after what flourish your nature will.
Along those lines, sir, with whatever decorations you like.
I commend my duty to your lordship.
I offer my service to your lordship.
He does well to commend it himself, there are no tongues else for's / turn.
He does well to offer it himself. There's no one else's tongue that would do it for him.
This lapwing runs away with the shell on his head.
This baby bird is running off with the shell still on its head.

He did comply with his dug before he suck'd it. Thus has he,—and many / more of the same bevy that I know the drossy age dotes on,— only got / the tune of the time and outward habit of encounter; a kind of yeasty / collection, which carries them through and through the most fanned and / winnowed opinions; and do but blow them to their trial, the bubbles are / out.

He bowed and scraped to his mother's breast before he sucked it. Like him, and many more of the same flock that I know this worthless age dotes on, he has only learned the fashionable tune of the times and the outward manners of conversation, a kind of frothy collection of phrases that carries them through even the most refined and sifted opinions. But just blow on them to test them, and the bubbles burst.

My lord, his Majesty commended him to you by young Osric, who brings / back to him that you attend him in the hall. He sends to know if your / pleasure hold to play with Laertes or that you will take longer time.

My lord, his Majesty sent his greetings to you through young Osric, who has told him that you are waiting for him in the hall. He wants to know if you still want to fence with Laertes, or if you'd like more time.
I am constant to my purposes, they follow the King's pleasure. If his / fitness speaks, mine is ready. Now or whensoever, provided I be so able / as now.
I stick to my intentions; they follow the King's wishes. If he's ready, so am I, now or at any time, as long as I'm as fit as I am now.
The King and Queen and all are coming down.
The King and Queen and everyone are coming down.
The Queen desires you to use some gentle entertainment to Laertes / before you fall to play.
The Queen wants you to be friendly to Laertes before you start fencing.
You will lose this wager, my lord.
You'll lose this bet, my lord.
I do not think so. Since he went into France, I have been in continual / practice. I shall win at the odds. But thou wouldst not think how ill / all's here about my heart: but it is no matter.

I don't think so. Since he went to France, I've been practising all the time. I'll win with the odds I've been given. But you wouldn't believe how bad I feel here around my heart. But it doesn't matter.
It is but foolery; but it is such a kind of gain-giving as would / perhaps trouble a woman.
It's only foolishness, but it's the kind of uneasy feeling that might worry a woman.
If your mind dislike anything, obey it. I will forestall their repair / hither, and say you are not fit.
If your mind is uneasy about anything, obey it. I'll stop them coming here and say you're not well.

Not a whit, we defy augury. There's a special providence in the fall of / a sparrow. If it be now, 'tis not to come; if it be not to come, it / will be now; if it be not now, yet it will come. The readiness is all. / Since no man has aught of what he leaves, what is't to leave betimes?

Not at all. We defy omens. There's a special providence even in the fall of a sparrow. If it is now, it is not to come; if it is not to come, it will be now; if it is not now, still it will come. Being ready is everything. Since no one keeps any of what he leaves behind, what does it matter if he leaves early?
Come, Hamlet, come, and take this hand from me.
Come, Hamlet, come, and take this hand from me.

Give me your pardon, sir. I have done you wrong; / But pardon't as you are a gentleman. / This presence knows, and you must needs have heard, / How I am punish'd with sore distraction. / What I have done / That might your nature, honour, and exception / Roughly awake, I here proclaim was madness. / Was't Hamlet wrong'd Laertes? Never Hamlet. / If Hamlet from himself be ta'en away, / And when he's not himself does wrong Laertes, / Then Hamlet does it not, Hamlet denies it. / Who does it, then? His madness. If't be so, / Hamlet is of the faction that is wrong'd; / His madness is poor Hamlet's enemy. / Sir, in this audience, / Let my disclaiming from a purpos'd evil / Free me so far in your most generous thoughts / That I have shot my arrow o'er the house / And hurt my brother.

Forgive me, sir. I have done you wrong, but forgive it, as you are a gentleman. Everyone here knows, and you must have heard, how I have been punished with a terrible madness. Whatever I have done that might have roughly roused your feelings, your honour and your resentment, I declare here was madness. Was it Hamlet who wronged Laertes? Never Hamlet. If Hamlet is taken away from himself, and when he's not himself he wrongs Laertes, then Hamlet doesn't do it. Hamlet denies it. Who does it, then? His madness. If that's so, Hamlet is on the side of the injured. His madness is poor Hamlet's enemy. Sir, in front of these people, let my denial that I meant any harm free me so far in your generous thoughts as if I had shot an arrow over the house and accidentally hurt my brother.

I am satisfied in nature, / Whose motive in this case should stir me most / To my revenge. But in my terms of honour / I stand aloof, and will no reconcilement / Till by some elder masters of known honour / I have a voice and precedent of peace / To keep my name ungor'd. But till that time / I do receive your offer'd love like love, / And will not wrong it.

As far as my natural feelings go, which in this case should push me hardest towards revenge, I am satisfied. But as far as honour goes, I hold back, and I won't make peace until some older experts in matters of honour give me their opinion and a precedent for peace, so that my name is not stained. But until then, I accept your offered love as love, and I won't wrong it.
I embrace it freely, / And will this brother's wager frankly play.— / Give us the foils; come on.
I welcome that wholeheartedly, and I'll fence in this brotherly contest with an open heart. Give us the swords. Come on.
I'll be your foil, Laertes; in mine ignorance / Your skill shall like a star i' th' darkest night, / Stick fiery off indeed.
I'll be your foil, Laertes. Next to my lack of skill, yours will shine out like a star in the darkest night.
No, I swear by this hand.
Give them the foils, young Osric. Cousin Hamlet, / You know the wager?
Give them the swords, young Osric. Nephew Hamlet, you know the bet?
Very well, my lord. / Your Grace has laid the odds o' the weaker side.
Very well, my lord. Your Grace has bet on the weaker side.
I do not fear it. I have seen you both; / But since he is better'd, we have therefore odds.
I'm not worried. I've seen you both fence. But since he has improved, we've been given odds.
This is too heavy. Let me see another.
This one's too heavy. Let me see another.
This likes me well. These foils have all a length?
I like this one. Are these swords all the same length?

Set me the stoups of wine upon that table. / If Hamlet give the first or second hit, / Or quit in answer of the third exchange, / Let all the battlements their ordnance fire; / The King shall drink to Hamlet's better breath, / And in the cup an union shall he throw / Richer than that which four successive kings / In Denmark's crown have worn. Give me the cups; / And let the kettle to the trumpet speak, / The trumpet to the cannoneer without, / The cannons to the heavens, the heavens to earth, / 'Now the King drinks to Hamlet.' Come, begin. / And you, the judges, bear a wary eye.

Put the jugs of wine on that table for me. If Hamlet makes the first or second hit, or gets even in the third bout, let all the cannons on the battlements fire. The King will drink to Hamlet's health, and he'll throw a pearl into the cup, richer than the one four kings in a row have worn in Denmark's crown. Give me the cups, and let the kettledrum tell the trumpet, the trumpet the gunner outside, the cannons the heavens, and the heavens the earth: 'Now the King drinks to Hamlet!' Come, begin. And you judges, watch carefully.
A hit, a very palpable hit.
A hit, a very clear hit.
Stay, give me drink. Hamlet, this pearl is thine; / Here's to thy health.
Wait, give me a drink. Hamlet, this pearl is yours. Here's to your health!
I'll play this bout first; set it by awhile.
I'll fence this bout first. Put it down for a while.
Come. Another hit; what say you?
Come on. Another hit. What do you say?
A touch, a touch, I do confess.
A touch, a touch, I admit.
He's fat, and scant of breath. / Here, Hamlet, take my napkin, rub thy brows. / The Queen carouses to thy fortune, Hamlet.
He's sweaty and out of breath. Here, Hamlet, take my handkerchief and wipe your forehead. The Queen drinks to your good luck, Hamlet.
I will, my lord; I pray you pardon me.
I will, my lord. Please excuse me.
[Aside] It is the poison'd cup; it is too late.
[Aside] It's the poisoned cup. It's too late.
I dare not drink yet, madam. By and by.
I don't dare drink yet, madam. Soon.
Come, let me wipe thy face.
Come, let me wipe your face.
My lord, I'll hit him now.
My lord, I'll hit him now.
[Aside] And yet it's almost against my conscience.
Come for the third, Laertes. You do but dally. / I pray you pass with your best violence. / I am afeard you make a wanton of me.
Come on, the third bout, Laertes. You're only playing about. Please attack with all your force. I'm afraid you're treating me like a spoilt child.
Is that what you say? Come on.
Look to the Queen there, ho!
Look after the Queen there, ho!
They bleed on both sides. How is it, my lord?
They are both bleeding. How are you, my lord?
Why, as a woodcock to my own springe, Osric. / I am justly kill'd with mine own treachery.
Why, like a stupid bird caught in my own trap, Osric. I'm justly killed by my own treachery.
She swoons to see them bleed.
She's fainted at seeing them bleed.
No, no, the drink, the drink! O my dear Hamlet! / The drink, the drink! I am poison'd.
No, no, the drink, the drink! Oh, my dear Hamlet! The drink, the drink! I've been poisoned.
O villany! Ho! Let the door be lock'd: / Treachery! Seek it out.
Oh, villainy! Ho! Lock the door! Treachery! Find out who did it!

It is here, Hamlet. Hamlet, thou art slain. / No medicine in the world can do thee good. / In thee there is not half an hour of life; / The treacherous instrument is in thy hand, / Unbated and envenom'd. The foul practice / Hath turn'd itself on me. Lo, here I lie, / Never to rise again. Thy mother's poison'd. / I can no more. The King, the King's to blame.

It's here, Hamlet. Hamlet, you are killed. No medicine in the world can help you. You don't have half an hour to live. The treacherous weapon is in your hand, unblunted and poisoned. The foul trick has turned back on me. Look, here I lie, never to get up again. Your mother has been poisoned. I can't say any more. The King, the King is to blame.
The point envenom'd too! / Then, venom, to thy work.
The tip poisoned too! Then, poison, do your work!
O yet defend me, friends. I am but hurt.
Oh, defend me still, friends. I'm only wounded.
Here, thou incestuous, murderous, damned Dane, / Drink off this potion. Is thy union here? / Follow my mother.
Here, you incestuous, murdering, damned Dane, drink up this potion! Is your pearl in here? Follow my mother!
He is justly serv'd. / It is a poison temper'd by himself. / Exchange forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet. / Mine and my father's death come not upon thee, / Nor thine on me.
He has got what he deserves. It's a poison he mixed himself. Let's forgive each other, noble Hamlet. May my death and my father's not be on your head, nor yours on mine!

Heaven make thee free of it! I follow thee. / I am dead, Horatio. Wretched Queen, adieu. / You that look pale and tremble at this chance, / That are but mutes or audience to this act, / Had I but time,—as this fell sergeant, death, / Is strict in his arrest,—O, I could tell you,— / But let it be. Horatio, I am dead, / Thou liv'st; report me and my cause aright / To the unsatisfied.

May heaven free you from guilt for it! I'll follow you. I'm dead, Horatio. Wretched Queen, goodbye! You who look pale and tremble at what has happened, who are only silent extras or audience to this act, if only I had time, since this cruel officer, death, is strict in his arrest, oh, I could tell you— But let it be. Horatio, I'm dead. You are alive. Tell my story and my cause truthfully to those who don't know.
Never believe it. / I am more an antique Roman than a Dane. / Here's yet some liquor left.
Never believe it. I'm more like an ancient Roman than a Dane. There's still some poison left.

As th'art a man, / Give me the cup. Let go; by Heaven, I'll have't. / O good Horatio, what a wounded name, / Things standing thus unknown, shall live behind me. / If thou didst ever hold me in thy heart, / Absent thee from felicity awhile, / And in this harsh world draw thy breath in pain, / To tell my story.

As you are a man, give me the cup. Let go! By heaven, I'll have it. Oh, good Horatio, what a damaged name I'll leave behind me if things stay unknown like this! If you ever held me in your heart, keep away from the happiness of death for a while, and in this harsh world breathe in pain, to tell my story.
Young Fortinbras, with conquest come from Poland, / To the ambassadors of England gives / This warlike volley.
Young Fortinbras, coming back victorious from Poland, fires this military salute to the ambassadors from England.

O, I die, Horatio. / The potent poison quite o'er-crows my spirit: / I cannot live to hear the news from England, / But I do prophesy th'election lights / On Fortinbras. He has my dying voice. / So tell him, with the occurrents more and less, / Which have solicited. The rest is silence.

Oh, I'm dying, Horatio. The strong poison completely overpowers my spirit. I can't live to hear the news from England. But I predict that the election will fall on Fortinbras. He has my dying vote. So tell him, along with the events, large and small, that have led to this. The rest is silence.
Now cracks a noble heart. Good night, sweet prince, / And flights of angels sing thee to thy rest. / Why does the drum come hither?
Now a noble heart breaks. Good night, sweet prince, and may flights of angels sing you to your rest! Why is the drum coming this way?
What is it you would see? / If aught of woe or wonder, cease your search.
What is it you want to see? If it's anything of sorrow or horror, look no further.
This quarry cries on havoc. O proud death, / What feast is toward in thine eternal cell, / That thou so many princes at a shot / So bloodily hast struck?
This pile of bodies cries out of slaughter. Oh, proud Death, what feast is being prepared in your eternal cell, that you have struck down so many princes with one shot, so bloodily?

The sight is dismal; / And our affairs from England come too late. / The ears are senseless that should give us hearing, / To tell him his commandment is fulfill'd, / That Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead. / Where should we have our thanks?

The sight is terrible, and our business from England has come too late. The ears that should hear us, to be told his order has been carried out and that Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead, can no longer hear. Who will thank us now?

Not from his mouth, / Had it th'ability of life to thank you. / He never gave commandment for their death. / But since, so jump upon this bloody question, / You from the Polack wars, and you from England / Are here arriv'd, give order that these bodies / High on a stage be placed to the view, / And let me speak to th' yet unknowing world / How these things came about. So shall you hear / Of carnal, bloody and unnatural acts, / Of accidental judgements, casual slaughters, / Of deaths put on by cunning and forc'd cause, / And, in this upshot, purposes mistook / Fall'n on the inventors' heads. All this can I / Truly deliver.

Not his mouth, even if it had the life to thank you. He never ordered their deaths. But since you have arrived here so soon after this bloody business, you from the Polish wars and you from England, give orders that these bodies be put high on a platform for everyone to see, and let me tell the world, which doesn't know yet, how these things happened. Then you will hear of lustful, bloody and unnatural acts, of accidental judgements and chance killings, of deaths caused by cunning and by force, and, in this ending, of plans gone wrong that fell back on the heads of those who made them. All this I can truthfully tell you.

Let us haste to hear it, / And call the noblest to the audience. / For me, with sorrow I embrace my fortune. / I have some rights of memory in this kingdom, / Which now to claim my vantage doth invite me.

Let's hurry to hear it, and call the noblest people to listen. As for me, I accept my good fortune with sorrow. I have some long-remembered rights to this kingdom, which my position now invites me to claim.

Of that I shall have also cause to speak, / And from his mouth whose voice will draw on more. / But let this same be presently perform'd, / Even while men's minds are wild, lest more mischance / On plots and errors happen.

I'll have reason to speak of that too, on behalf of one whose vote will bring others with it. But let this be done at once, while people's minds are still wild, in case more disasters happen through plots and mistakes.

Let four captains / Bear Hamlet like a soldier to the stage, / For he was likely, had he been put on, / To have prov'd most royally; and for his passage, / The soldiers' music and the rites of war / Speak loudly for him. / Take up the bodies. Such a sight as this / Becomes the field, but here shows much amiss. / Go, bid the soldiers shoot.

Let four captains carry Hamlet like a soldier onto the platform, because he would probably have proved a great king, if he had been given the chance. And to mark his passing, let soldiers' music and the rites of war speak loudly for him. Take up the bodies. A sight like this belongs on a battlefield, but here it looks very wrong. Go, tell the soldiers to fire.
